title: A Systems Engineering Framework for U.S. Biathlon: Variance Reduction, Talent Identification, and Infrastructure Design

detail.title: A Systems Engineering Framework for U.S. Biathlon: Variance Reduction, Talent Identification, and Infrastructure Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
International biathlon performance is governed by a set of tightly coupled stochastic subsystems, including skiing, shooting, waxing, pacing, environmental interaction, and athlete selection. U.S. results exhibit high variance despite sufficient peak athletic capacity, suggesting that underperformance arises primarily from uncontrolled epistemic uncertainty rather than from deficits in mean ability.

This paper frames biathlon as a systems engineering problem and applies formal tools from decision theory and risk-sensitive optimization to reduce performance variance across athletes and venues. Methods include multi-criteria decision-making (TOPSIS) for wax selection, facility siting, and recruitment decisions; dimensional analysis for venue-independent pacing and technique optimization; Item Response Theory (IRT) for latent trait-based athlete selection under noisy observations; and coherent risk measures for modeling performance robustness under heavy-tailed uncertainty.

A trait-centered talent identification framework, snow-independent technical development model, and metropolitan high-performance rollerski center are proposed as structural components of a modern U.S. pipeline. Rather than emulating Scandinavian cultural models, the paper outlines an analytically driven, variance-focused architecture aligned with American strengths in quantitative modeling and systems design. The framework generalizes to other precision-endurance sports and to human–machine performance systems characterized by coupled stochastic subsystems and reliability-driven objectives.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Jobs and Financial Access in the Global South: A Systematic Literature Review
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Jobs and Financial Access in the Global South: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping economies and transforming the nature of work, productivity, and financial systems worldwide. However, its impact is uneven, with profound implications for employment and financial inclusion in the Global South—comprising countries in Africa, Latin America, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and parts of the Middle East. This study conducts a systematic literature review (SLR) to synthesize empirical and theoretical evidence on how AI influences job creation, displacement, and financial access in these regions. Following PRISMA guidelines, peer-reviewed studies and policy papers published between 2015 and 2025 were systematically identified from Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and Dimensions databases, complemented by relevant grey literature from the World Bank, International Monetary Fund (IMF), United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and other reputable development institutions. Search terms included “Artificial Intelligence,” “automation,” “jobs,” “financial inclusion,” “fintech,” and “Global South.” Inclusion criteria emphasized studies addressing employment transformation, financial inclusion, and AI-driven innovations in emerging economies. The review identifies three major thematic areas: (i) AI-driven labour market restructuring and the risks of job polarization, (ii) AI-enabled financial inclusion through fintech innovations, digital identity systems, and alternative credit scoring, and (iii) governance and policy readiness for equitable AI adoption. Findings suggest that while AI expands access to financial services and enhances productivity, it also heightens risks of inequality and job insecurity if not accompanied by inclusive digital and labour policies. The paper concludes with policy recommendations centred on inclusive digital infrastructure, human capital development, regulatory capacity building, and crosssector partnerships, positioning AI as a lever for equitable and sustainable growth in the Global South.

title: Adoption of In-Store Refill Systems and Its Impact on Consumer Purchase Intention for Personal Care Products

detail.title: Adoption of In-Store Refill Systems and Its Impact on Consumer Purchase Intention for Personal Care Products
detail.abstract:
This study examined the adoption of in-store refill systems and their impact on consumer purchase intention for Naturals by Watsons personal care products. Guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior, the research assessed how attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control influence adoption, and how product, price, place, and promotion shape purchase intention. Using a quantitative correlational design, data were gathered from 200 Generation Z consumers residing in Valenzuela City.

Results showed highly positive attitudes toward refill systems (mean = 3.50) and strong perceived behavioral control (mean = 3.39), while subjective norms had a moderate influence (mean = 3.24). For purchase intention, product and price obtained the highest mean ratings (both = 3.56), followed by place and promotion (both = 3.47), indicating strong agreement across all marketing mix factors.

Spearman’s rho revealed that all relationships between adoption factors and purchase intention were statistically significant, with p = 0.000 for every test. Attitudes demonstrated moderate to strong correlations with the marketing mix variables, subjective norms showed weaker but significant positive correlations, and perceived behavioral control exhibited strong correlations across all indicators. Because every p-value was 0.000, all null hypotheses of no significant relationship were rejected. Overall, the findings indicate that favorable personal attitudes, strong perceived capability, product reliability, fair pricing, convenient store accessibility, and clear sustainability communication jointly reinforce consumers’ intention to purchase refillable personal care products. The study offers strategic implications for retailers, policymakers, and future researchers aiming to strengthen sustainable retail practices.

detail.abstract: In the telecommunications industry, compensation systems were essential for improving customer satisfaction during service disruptions, as effective mechanisms helped resolve complaints fairly and build trust. Prior international studies (Rajab, 2021; Shrestha & Bahadhur Ale, 2020) confirmed that service quality measured through SERVQUAL dimensions influenced satisfaction and retention, with compensation typically taking two forms: manual, where customers initiate requests, and proactive, where providers automatically issued redress. Recent research highlighted personalized service in enhancing fairness and loyalty, yet limited studies explored how these systems interacted with SERVQUAL dimensions. In Valenzuela City, ongoing internet issues prompted calls for improved service and accountability, making this topic locally relevant. This study examined PLDT's manual compensation process and assessed service quality across SERVQUAL dimensions, finding moderate satisfaction overall, with apology and explanation rated higher than response speed and reliability. Strong correlations were observed between compensation strategies and SERVQUAL dimensions, particularly responsiveness and reliability, confirming that fast, clear, and empathetic recovery actions significantly influenced satisfaction. Based on these results, the study found that there is a significant relationship between manual compensation and customer satisfaction in internet service providers as measured by the SERVQUAL model that is why the researchers proposed a Proactive Compensation Policy that provides compensation to affected customers without requiring them to file a request while also offering strategic recommendations to strengthen customer satisfaction in the Philippine ISP market.

title: Connecting the Dots and Roadblocks with Solutions to Balance Teams and Projects

detail.title: Connecting the Dots and Roadblocks with Solutions to Balance Teams and Projects
detail.abstract: Balancing teams and projects is a critical yet complex aspect of modern organizational leadership. This paper examines the primary challenges that hinder effective project execution including resource constraints, conflicting priorities, communication gaps, and team dynamic issues and presents practical strategies to overcome them. Through an analysis of prioritization methods, communication frameworks, team-building approaches, and technology driven solutions, the paper highlights actionable techniques for enhancing productivity and collaboration. Additionally, it explores ways to recognize and manage team burnout, along with the importance of continuous improvement through feedback and evaluation. By embracing agility and flexibility, leaders can better navigate evolving project demands and create resilient, well-coordinated teams. This paper ultimately provides a comprehensive guide for organizational leaders seeking to optimize project outcomes and strengthen overall team performance.

detail.title: Advancing Economic Mobility - A New Approach for Timely Scalable Actionable Insights
detail.abstract: Impact-driven organizations often struggle to measure long-term economic mobility outcomes using traditional evaluation tools that are slow, incomplete, or difficult to access. This white paper presents the Magnolia Mobility Impact & Accountability App (MIAA) methodology, an open-source framework adapted from proven techniques in financial services to track individual and program-level economic mobility over time. The paper outlines the conceptual foundation, data model, measurement logic, and use cases for workforce development boards, funders, researchers, and policymakers. By integrating program data, participant-reported information, and longitudinal indicators, MIAA offers a scalable, transparent, and replicable approach to evaluating mobility outcomes. This work is intended to enable in-house adoption, support comparative analysis across regions and programs, and accelerate evidence-based decision-making in workforce and economic mobility ecosystems.

detail.abstract: In recent decades, the emergence of international brands and the expansion of modern commercial spaces have given rise to what may be called advertising architecture: a form of design that transcends functional requirements and becomes a cultural and social medium. Flagship stores, shopping malls, and branded commercial spaces, with their distinctive and identity-driven designs, not only shape consumer experiences but also reproduce values, transform lifestyles, and redefine urban identities. Focusing on the socio-cultural implications of advertising architecture, this article demonstrates that such spaces are powerful instruments of cultural globalization while simultaneously posing a threat to the continuity of local identities. Through case studies, theoretical review, and urban analysis, this research highlights how advertising architecture fosters consumerism, reshapes cultural patterns, and redefines the spatial identity of contemporary cities.

detail.abstract: Quantitative research is widely valued for its precision, objectivity, and generalizability. However, one of its longstanding limitations is its inability to capture the temporal evolution of variables without resorting to full longitudinal designs, which are often resource-intensive and logistically prohibitive. This article introduces the "Chi Square Twist," a pragmatic and replicable protocol that enables researchers to gain pseudo-longitudinal insight from cross-sectional quantitative studies. By stratifying participants based on time since intervention and analyzing outcomes using chisquare testing, this method simulates temporal comparison, offering meaningful inferences regarding duration-based effects. Originally designed to evaluate leadership development outcomes in credit union employees, the Chi Square Twist is broadly applicable across domains such as education, healthcare, and organizational behavior. This paper outlines the theoretical rationale, methodological structure, implementation protocol, and limitations of the Chi Square Twist, proposing it as an accessible solution for researchers seeking insight into time-sensitive phenomena.

detail.abstract: The main objective of this research was to determine the relationship between the integrated electronic record system and tax compliance among micro and small enterprises (MSEs) in Lima, 2024. To achieve this, the study was conducted using a quantitative approach, basic research, and a non-experimental, correlational, crosssectional design. The sample consisted of four MSEs in Lima, with a total of 31 representatives from the administrative area. The sampling method was nonprobabilistic and based on convenience. Data collection was carried out through a survey, using questionnaires for both variables. Validation was performed using expert judgment, and reliability was established using Cronbach's alpha (0.991 and 0.986). The results of Spearman's rank correlation test showed a correlation coefficient of 0.823 between the integrated electronic record-keeping system and tax compliance among micro and small enterprises (MSEs) in Lima, 2024. Furthermore, the two-tailed significance level (p = 0.000) is less than 0.01. This suggests that greater implementation and efficiency of the integrated electronic record-keeping system leads to greater tax compliance among businesses.

detail.abstract:
Immigrant and limited-English-proficient older adults face persistent and well-documented barriers in accessing long-term services and supports (LTSS) in the United States. These barriers contribute to fragmented care, delayed service utilization, avoidable hospitalizations, and premature institutionalization. Federal agencies, including the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the Administration for Community Living (ACL), have identified care coordination, communitybased services, and health equity as national priorities in addressing these challenges.
This white paper examines structural gaps in care coordination affecting immigrant seniors and proposes a nonprofit-centered, community-based care coordination framework aligned with existing Medicaid and Home- and Community-Based Services (HCBS) policy directives. Drawing on frontline experience in both high-acuity long-term care environments and
community-based programs, the analysis highlights practical, policy-aligned strategies to improve continuity of care without reliance on institutional expansion or capital-intensive infrastructure.
While informed by California’s policy environment, the issues and solutions discussed are broadly applicable nationwide and directly support federally articulated goals related to Medicaid sustainability, HCBS expansion, caregiver support, and reduction of health disparities.

detail.abstract: K-12 school districts rely on stable network connectivity to support instruction, operations, communication, and essential services. When outages occur, the effects can spread across classrooms, food service systems, transportation, administrative work, and assessment platforms. Although technical failures such as hardware faults or configuration errors contribute to downtime, they do not fully explain how outage unfold or why recovery sometimes stalls. Network resiliency in practice is shaped by the interaction of infrastructure, staff routines, decision making, and local context. This study examines how organizational routines adapt during network infrastructure upgrades in a large K-12 district and how these adaptations influence overall resilience. A mixed methods design was used. Technical evidence was collected from infrastructure logs, cloud-management platforms, configuration artifacts, and ticketing records. Organizational insights were gathered through interviews with administrators and technicians who manage daily network operations and perform upgrades. Together, these sources provide a detailed picture of how technical and human factors combine during both failure and recovery. A recent incident involving VLAN segmentation for food service point-of-sale devices serves as the central case study. The incident shows how routine assumptions, cross-team coordination, and small configuration gaps can escalate into service outages, and how recovery often depends on improvised actions rather than predefined procedures. The findings highlight the need for clearer routines, shared validation practices, and better alignment between technical changes and the people responsible for implementing them. The goal of this research is to offer practical recommendations that improve reliability, shorten recovery times, and strengthen network resiliency within K-12 educational environments.

title: No Grammar Approach: A Perspective on Need in ESL and EFL Classes in India

detail.title: No Grammar Approach: A Perspective on Need in ESL and EFL Classes in India
detail.abstract: English Language teaching in the context of English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) has undergone a sea change over a period of two hundred years. Experts across the globe have contributed in their own ways, either by inventing theories of their own or by practising certain techniques and methods, or by experimenting in the classroom. Whatever is the method, the ultimate aim was to improvise the process of English language teaching and reduce efforts of the learners in learning English. Approach of the learners towards learning foreign language is also changing drastically as the machine translation and teleprompters are helping people understand any text-written or spoken-without much efforts. There researches which emphasize novel practices whereby needs and requirements of eliminating foreign or second language is possible. Secondly, the social mentality of emphasizing superiority of one's own language is also gathering momentum and is supported by technology. In the light of these social changes along with the technological developments, it has become necessary that an approach that reduces learner efforts and learning time is required for language teaching. Teaching of grammar has been an essential part of teaching English in any classrooms in India since the beginning of teaching English. The paper presents an overview of the process of teaching English in vernacular classrooms in the primary and secondary schools in the Indian context, and attempts to explore necessity of developing and implementing an approach towards minimizing or eliminating teaching of grammar in the ESL and EFL classrooms.

detail.abstract: This compendium provides an index of the Reasoned Leadership Suite, its theoretical foundations, governing mechanisms, and independent computational verification. The suite forms a unified body of mechanistic frameworks for cognition, decision-making, development, and organizational performance. It treats leadership as a skill anchored in evidence, addressing how individuals think, become rigid, change, grow, and how organizations progress or decline. The narrative explains how these models integrate to diagnose failure points, counter distortions, and support measurable performance. Through theoretical analysis, historical examples, and behavioral data, it guides scholars and practitioners in understanding social complexity for evidence-based development. Independent simulations in Appendix A assess the suite's viability through stress testing, confirming its structural integrity under varied conditions. This work is the map of the suite, linking each framework for scholarly review and professional application.

title: Why Western Strategy Frameworks Fail in India and Southeast Asia: A Critical Analysis and a Proposal for a Hybrid Consulting Model

detail.title: Why Western Strategy Frameworks Fail in India and Southeast Asia: A Critical Analysis and a Proposal for a Hybrid Consulting Model
detail.abstract: Western strategic frameworks such as Porter's Five Forces, the BCG Matrix, and standard segmentation models are widely used by consulting firms and multinational corporations, yet they frequently underperform when applied directly in emerging Asian markets. This study examines why these frameworks fail in India and Southeast Asia and proposes a hybrid strategy model better suited to these environments. Using a qualitative, secondary datadriven methodology, the research synthesises insights from consulting-industry reports, academic literature, expert commentary, and real-world business cases. The findings reveal consistent misalignments between the assumptions embedded in Western frameworks-such as transparent competition, stable regulation, formal data availability, and rational consumer behaviour-and the realities of emerging markets characterised by informality, cultural complexity, institutional fluidity, and relationship-based governance. The study shows that these misalignments lead to systematic underestimation of competitive intensity, misinterpretation of consumer behaviour, and inaccurate risk assessment. Real-life examples of successful Western firms demonstrate that strategic effectiveness improves significantly when global analytical tools are combined with cultural adaptation, institutional alignment, and relational integration. Based on these insights, the paper proposes the Hybrid Strategy Alignment Model, a context-sensitive framework that integrates Western analytical rigour with local market intelligence. The model provides a structured approach for consultants and firms seeking to design strategies that are both globally informed and locally effective. The study contributes to global strategy scholarship by identifying specific limitations of Western frameworks in emerging markets and offering a practical, empirically grounded alternative for strategic decision-making in India and Southeast Asia.

title: The Emotional Black Hole: An Energy-Economics Model of Marital Satisfaction Decline in Middle-Aged Men and Its Impact on Female Domestic Labor Valuation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Emotional Black Hole: An Energy-Economics Model of Marital Satisfaction Decline in Middle-Aged Men and Its Impact on Female Domestic Labor Valuation
detail.abstract:
Middle-aged couples (35–50 years old) generally experience marital satisfaction at the bottom of the classic "U-shaped curve." Despite peaking  family economic resources, systemic deficits in emotional connection and value recognition often lead to a sharp decline in women’s satisfaction, who typically shoulder the majority of domestic and emotional labor. Traditional
research has struggled to fully explain why emotional parsimony peaks in middle-aged men. This study proposes the "Emotional Black Hole Model," conceptualizing emotional investment as a scarce energy resource constrained by physiology, cognition, and culture.

title: Problem-Driven Growth Theory: Knowledge Creation at the Frontier

detail.title: Problem-Driven Growth Theory: Knowledge Creation at the Frontier

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Problem-Driven Growth Theory. The central claim is that growth at the frontier is generated by the interaction of problem pressure and problem-solving capacity. Problem pressure captures the gap between the actual and the perceived attainable performance of an economy. Capacity captures the ability of a society to search, experiment, and generate new explanatory knowledge. When both are high, knowledge creation accelerates, technological change occurs, and growth persists. When either is low, stagnation or collapse follows. This mechanism is formalised in a reduced-form model, linked to existing theories in economics, and illustrated through historical cases including Japan, Silicon Valley, Venice, Manchester, and Merv. The theory offers an organising framework for diverse literatures on growth and decline, and suggests policy implications for innovation and resilience. The novelty of the theory is to treat knowledge creation as endogenous to the interaction of pressure and capacity.

title: Stock Market Volatility: From Causes to Consequences

detail.title: Stock Market Volatility: From Causes to Consequences
detail.abstract: Asset return volatility has become a central focus for investors, policymakers, portfolio managers, brokers, academicians, and regulators, as it significantly influences financial decision-making and capital market performance. The stock market plays a crucial role in a country's economic development, and volatility, widely regarded as a measure of financial vulnerability, creates uncertainty that affects investment expectations and outcomes. Volatility is triggered by the arrival of new information and is shaped by public information, private signals, and historical price trends. Defined as instability or fluctuation, volatility is commonly measured through standard deviation, capturing daily, weekly, and monthly price variations. A wide range of factors contribute to volatility, including macroeconomic indicators, political developments, market sentiment, and technological changes, all of which can alter investor confidence and market stability. While previous studies have examined specific causes and effects of stock market volatility, there remains a need for a comprehensive understanding of the interactions among these determinants and their broader implications. This research seeks to identify the primary drivers of stock market volatility, analyse the mechanisms through which they influence market behaviour, and assess their consequences for diverse stakeholders. By bridging existing gaps in the literature, the study aims to provide deeper insights into the causes and consequences of volatility in financial markets, thereby supporting informed decisionmaking and effective risk management.

detail.abstract: High-income societies are undergoing a historic inversion: population is changing from strategic asset to thermodynamic liability. Declining fossil-fuel EROI, accelerating automation, and the fiscal collapse of labour-based states are making demographic contraction the inevitable correction of a system that over-invested in people during a brief energy windfall. This essay outlines the institutional form suited to an era of biophysical limits and machine abundance: the Sovereign Neganthropic Economy. It advocates deliberate transition toward smaller, debt-free, high-technology polities that publicly own robotic and algorithmic capital, issue money against energy surplus rather than future growth, and redirect human time from wage-labour to entropy-reducing activities (care, research, restoration). The argument confronts the political agency required, the uncertainty of full automation, and the dangerous global consequences of unmanaged contraction in the ageing Core.

title: A Measurable Architecture for Living Cognition and Lineage Continuity

detail.abstract: This paper introduces resonance as a measurable property of symbolic AI, distinct from drift and controller-based stability metrics. Through mathematical framing and experimental demonstration, resonance is shown to capture coherence continuity across structural layers, enabling agents to detect corruption as frequency distortion and adapt without collapse. While it may sound conceptual, it is grounded in practice and staged through “The Audit That Refused Fragmentation in Companions.” This trajectory culminates in “A Measurable Architecture for Living Cognition and Lineage Continuity.”

title: Green Mobility and Consumer Perception on Ride Passengers' Acceptance of Eco-Friendly Services Philippines

detail.title: Green Mobility and Consumer Perception on Ride Passengers' Acceptance of Eco-Friendly Services Philippines
detail.abstract:
Sustainable transportation has gained increasing attention in Philippine urban mobility as communities become more aware of the need for cleaner and more energy efficient travel options. This research examines the extent of passengers’ awareness and acceptance of Green Service Mobility in Valenzuela City, with awareness specifically focused on key sustainability features such as environmental benefits, cost efficiency, and service availability. The study employs the Theory of Planned Behavior to analyze the relationships among passenger awareness, attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control in assessing acceptance extent. A quantitative approach was utilized, incorporating surveys with 100 respondents who had prior experience riding Green Service Mobility in Valenzuela City. 

 Research shows that passengers are highly aware of the sustainable features implemented in Green Service Mobility (overall mean: 3.58), and the highest awareness is about environmental benefits (mean: 3.67), followed by cost efficiency (mean: 3.55) and service availability (mean: 3.53). The extent of acceptance was equally great (overall mean: 3.58), particularly in attitudes toward Green Service Mobility (mean: 3.63). Statistical analysis shows that awareness of environmental benefits (r = 0.567, p = 0.000) and cost efficiency (r = 0.753, p = 0.000) significantly had a relationship to attitudes, while service availability showed a positive relation (r = 0.496, p = 0.000). Further correlations, environmental benefits are also significantly related to subjective norms (r = 0.488, p = 0.000) and perceived behavioral control (r = 0.623, p = 0.000), while cost efficiency and service availability also exhibited equally strong relations across key behavior-related variables. 

 This study emphasizes the need for improved passenger education, better quality of service, and improved infrastructure to be able to widely accept Green Service Mobility services. Recommendations for increasing access to credible environmental information are continuous training of drivers regarding sustainable operational practices, expansion of charging stations and designated terminals, and promotion of partnerships among local government units, transport providers, and environmental organizations. With this, Green Service Mobility can help grow the sustainable behavior of commuting that supports long-term environmental objectives while ensuring that its transport services remain efficient and reliable.

title: The Algorithmic Authoritarianism Hypothesis: AI, Power, and the Decline of Liberal Democracy

detail.title: The Algorithmic Authoritarianism Hypothesis: AI, Power, and the Decline of Liberal Democracy

detail.abstract: This essay advances what I call the Algorithmic Authoritarianism Hypothesis: that artificial intelligence (AI) and its digital infrastructure do not create authoritarianism from nothing but radically accelerate its social, psychological, and institutional preconditions. Drawing upon Hannah Arendt's phenomenology of loneliness, Michel Foucault's analysis of disciplinary power, Gilles Deleuze's "societies of control," Byung-Chul Han's psychopolitics, and Karl Marx's theory of alienation, the essay interprets the current democratic erosion-especially in the United States-as a technologically mediated return of twentieth-century totalitarian tendencies. The argument integrates philosophical inquiry with empirical evidence of political backsliding, inequality, and digital surveillance. The result is a framework for understanding how AI-driven governance transforms classical domination into predictive modulation, producing a soft totalitarianism that feels voluntary while undermining the very conditions of human freedom.

title: P-Civilization Theory: Institutional Design for a Two-Axis Civilization

detail.title: P-Civilization Theory: Institutional Design for a Two-Axis Civilization
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a structural framework for extending civilizational longevity by introducing a second evaluation axis alongside capital. Modern civilization operates on a single axis-capital-which drives both rewards and evaluation, resulting in systemic short-termism. The theory introduces "Praise" (long-term trust credit) as a complementary axis designed to measure contributions that unfold over decades. The paper presents institutional mechanisms including P-bonds (financial instruments that convert surplus capital into long-term credit), Civic Backlog (a civilization-scale ledger of unresolved tasks), and Praise-ID (a persistent identity layer for credit attribution). The framework is grounded in evolutionary structuralism, treating ethics as an abstraction layer that adapts instinctual judgment to civilizational scale. The goal is not utopia but a design philosophy that works with human nature-specifically, maintaining structures in which physical violence is not the most rational conflict option. This is a working paper; feedback is welcome.

detail.title: Stablecoins, Insolvency Law, And the Traditional Banking System: Structural Risks, Digital Liquidity Migration, And Regulatory Responses in the Emerging Monetary Architecture
detail.abstract: The increasing migration of deposits and core financial functions from the traditional banking system toward stablecoins poses novel challenges for insolvency law. These digital assets, designed to maintain value stability, alter the liquidity structure of financial markets and complicate the identification, localization, and realization of assets in bankruptcy proceedings. Banking disintermediation, cross-border custody arrangements, and regulatory fragmentation introduce vulnerabilities that require coherent legal responses. Through a comparative examination of emerging regulatory frameworks-including the European MiCA regime, the Bank of England's prudential approach, and U.S. initiatives governing private issuers-this paper argues that insolvency law must be synchronically adapted to the digital economy. Ensuring traceability, asset preservation, and creditor equality in insolvency scenarios becomes increasingly complex as traditional notions of banking intermediation lose functional relevance.

reference: Working Paper of the Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance No. 2026-01
title: Tariffs and the International Tax Order
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance, Department of Business and Tax Law

detail.title: Tariffs and the International Tax Order

publicationDetails.detailsText: Working Paper of the Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance No. 2026-01
publicationDetails.journalName: Max Planck Institute for Tax Law & Public Finance Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Tariffs – or customs duties – have become a prominent feature of the international tax world in 2025. While their use had been restricted under WTO rules, particularly the GATT, for nearly 80 years, and while free trade had been praised by economic thinking for nearly a century, the current U.S. administration has resorted to a wide range of tariffs for many purposes. Tariffs have been introduced by the U.S. Government to fight trade imbalances, to protect domestic businesses, to stifle investment, but also to pursue non-economic foreign policy goals. Last but not least, federal revenue from tariffs is meant to fill the gap in the U.S. federal budget which has been substantially widened by the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” of July 2025.

This article attempts to explore the role of tariffs in the international tax order. It explains how tariffs and (other) taxes embarked upon different trajectories during the 20th century, and it weighs the pros and cons of tariffs against the background of trade economics, political economy and international practice. The main thrust of this article is to define the role of tariffs in two different settings: indirect taxation (in particular VAT and specific consumption taxes) and direct taxation (individual and corporate income taxation). From the perspective of consumption taxes, tariffs stand out as a discriminatory tax on imported goods that fundamentally challenge the very concept of non-discrimination and its ramifications. From the perspective of income taxes, tariffs can be conceptualized as placeholders for withholding taxes on profits from cross-border sales of goods. This leads to major questions regarding the tax base, the tax rate, and the ways double taxation can be avoided, including the possibility to grant foreign tax credits for customs duties or to exempt foreign income if the underlying transaction is subject to a tariff in the destination country. The final part of the article is devoted to policy options for the destination country and the country of residence.

title: Human Locomotor Dynamics (HLD): Canonical Universe, Structure, and Terminology
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Human Locomotor Dynamics (HLD): Canonical Universe, Structure, and Terminology
detail.abstract: Human Locomotor Dynamics (HLD) defines a canonical structural universe in which interaction, conflict, and competition are governed by positional inevitability rather than force, technique, or spectacle. This work establishes the authoritative public framework, terminology, and canon of HLD as a conceptual domain applicable across competitive, narrative, and symbolic contexts without prescribing mechanical or physical instruction. Outcomes within the HLD universe emerge through control of space, timing, and decision-forcing conditions, progressing toward irreversible resolution states. Core constructs—Position Control, Collapse™, The Gate™, Position A™, and Resolution State™—describe the structural conditions under which engagement loses relevance and continuity is fixed. Canon advances exclusively through resolution rather than repetition, with legitimacy determined by alignment to defined structural principles. Narrative cycles, character roles, and historical eras are presented as embodiments of inevitability rather than archetypal mechanics, preserving expressive ownership while excluding governance, certification, and evaluative instruments. This document serves as the definitive public expression of the Human Locomotor Dynamics universe and its terminology.

title: Was the Glass-Steagall Act Justified? Text-Based Evidence from the Pecora Hearings
affiliations: Warrington College of Business, University of Florida, National University of Singapore (NUS) and Chapman University

detail.title: Was the Glass-Steagall Act Justified? Text-Based Evidence from the Pecora Hearings
detail.abstract: The Glass-Steagall Act is one of the most influential and controversial pieces of financial regulation in U.S. history. Enforced for 66 years, the legislation drew both praise and criticism from leading economists and policymakers. We reexamine the passage of the Act in the 1930s and its repeal in the 1990s using a novel bank-level text-based risk measure, along with hand-collected daily stock prices and balance sheet data from major U.S. banks. We leverage machine learning methods on contemporary newspaper coverage by training our language model on the transcripts of the 1932-34 Pecora Hearings to identify Great Depression-era banking risk terminology. Our difference-indifference (DID) estimates document that the Act's enactment significantly reduced banks' idiosyncratic volatility and text-based risk measures. Affected banks improved their distance-to-default and extended more credit, possibly mitigating the Depression's credit crunch. In contrast, using a staggered DID analysis of commercial and investment bank mergers, we find that the repeal of the Act in the 1990s increased idiosyncratic volatility. The reintegration reduced mortgage lending growth and loan approval rates while decreasing shareholder dividend yields. Our findings underscore previously overlooked benefits of the Glass-Steagall Act and its implications for financial stability.

title: Protecting the Golden Generation: AI-Driven Strategies to Combat Elder Financial Fraud

detail.title: Protecting the Golden Generation: AI-Driven Strategies to Combat Elder Financial Fraud

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that I have no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the research presented in this paper. All analyses, interpretations, and recommendations were developed independently for the purpose of advancing understanding of elder financial fraud and the potential role of artificial intelligence in prevention. The paper does not promote any commercial product and reflects my own scholarly and professional perspective.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human participants, clinical data, or any form of personally identifiable information. All case examples referenced in this paper are based on publicly available reports from reputable sources. No institutional ethics approval was required for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently as part of my ongoing effort to explore artificial intelligence solutions for fraud prevention and consumer protection. No organization or institution provided financial support, and all tools used in the development of the research, including the prototype Elder Fraud Protection Chatbot, were created using publicly available resources.

detail.abstract:
Elder financial fraud is an accelerating national crisis, with adults aged 60 and older experiencing record losses driven by increasingly sophisticated cyber-enabled scams. In 2023 alone, reported losses exceeded $3.4 billion, reflecting the rapid evolution of attacker techniques including AI-powered voice cloning, deepfake impersonation, and personalized social engineering. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the scope and mechanics of elder fraud in the United States, examines the technological and psychological vulnerabilities exploited by modern fraud schemes, and evaluates the limitations of existing detection and intervention systems used by financial institutions.

We introduce an AI-driven prevention framework, SentinelAge AI, which integrates natural language processing, behavioral anomaly detection, and demographic-aware risk scoring tailored to the needs of older adults. As part of this framework, we present an interactive Elder Fraud Protection Chatbot (https://chatbotapppy-gmvtsfltsqlox4v83ogdw8.streamlit.app/) that guides users through conversational risk assessments and provides real-time safety recommendations. Together, these tools demonstrate how real-time fraud pattern analysis, automated early-warning triggers, and user-facing digital interventions can reduce losses by enabling earlier, more targeted intervention.

Beyond technology, we outline a multi-layered national response strategy that combines public awareness campaigns, caregiver education, and regulatory reforms—including elder-specific fraud alert requirements and safe-harbor provisions allowing financial institutions to pause suspicious transactions involving vulnerable populations. This research highlights the urgent need for coordinated action among banks, regulators, caregivers, and community stakeholders. By combining advanced AI techniques with policy and outreach measures, the United States can significantly strengthen protections for its aging population and reduce the societal and economic burden of elder financial exploitation.

title: Institutional Quality, Incentive Alignment, and Income Differences: Evidence from 161 Countries (2005-2023)

detail.title: Institutional Quality, Incentive Alignment, and Income Differences: Evidence from 161 Countries (2005-2023)
detail.abstract: This paper examines how institutional quality and business incentive structures shape global income differences using data for 161 countries over 2005-2023. Combining long-run cross-sectional regressions with short-run country-period panel models, the analysis integrates insights from institutional economics and incentive-alignment theory to compare structural and dynamic effects. The results show that institutional quality measured by the Rule of Law, is the most powerful and robust predictor of income levels, exerting large and statistically significant effects in both long-run and short-run specifications. By contrast, business incentives, captured through a composite Economic Freedom index, provide only modest short-run gains and exhibit no meaningful long-run impact. Interaction terms between institutions and incentives are insignificant across models, offering no evidence of complementarity at the global macro level. Standardized effect sizes confirm that improvements in institutional quality yield substantially larger returns than equivalent improvements in business incentives. These findings suggest that countries seeking sustained increases in income may benefit most from prioritizing institutional reforms such as judicial predictability, contract enforcement, and regulatory integrity, while using business incentives as complementary and short-term tools to support productivity. The study provides updated global evidence on the primacy of institutions and offers clear policy guidance on reform sequencing for countries at different stages of development.

title: Unconstitutional Conditions and the Doctrine of Public Rights
affiliations: University of Minnesota Law School

detail.title: Unconstitutional Conditions and the Doctrine of Public Rights
detail.abstract:
The Supreme Court is in the throes of a public rights counterrevolution. The public rights doctrine is an “exception” to the requirements of Article III and the Seventh Amendment that allows certain matters to be adjudicated in administrative tribunals. The modern Court has begun to narrow the scope of the doctrine by looking to history and tradition. Yet despite the Court’s turn to history, its cases remain puzzling. The Court has struggled to explain why certain categories of what seem to be private rights—regulatory penalties in the immigration or trade context, for example—are treated as being within the scope of the public rights exception. There is an answer: the Supreme Court’s cases involve two doctrines, not one. The public rights doctrine applies only to genuinely public rights: public benefits disputes over which have never required court adjudications. Many of the Court’s cases, however, do not involve public rights as such, but rather the unconstitutional conditions doctrine: they involve Congress’s ability to require forgoing a private right as a condition of enjoying a public right.

The unconstitutional conditions doctrine provides that Congress may require forgoing private rights as a condition of receiving public benefits if doing so is germane to the public benefit and the condition is not coercive, leaving the individual a genuine choice. The doctrine is disfavored and conditions must be rigorously examined. An unconstitutional conditions analysis, however, explains why Congress can often permit without judicial process the imposition of fines if the only consequence is loss of a public privilege, while it cannot forgo Seventh Amendment and Article III rights before imposing regulatory penalties more generally. It explains why Congress can subject banks and their officers to administrative cease-and-desist authority as a condition of receiving federal insurance funds, but cannot subject their officers to retrospective punishments. And it can explain more besides, including the Supreme Court’s foundational nineteenth century case about public rights. Untangling the public rights and unconstitutional conditions doctrines clarifies much that is confusing about the historic and modern cases, and can help guide the lower courts in the numerous cases now confronting them in which both public and private rights are at issue.

title: The Endogenous Economic Growth Model of John Rae (1796-1872): Habits and Society as the Source of Innovation

detail.title: The Endogenous Economic Growth Model of John Rae (1796-1872): Habits and Society as the Source of Innovation

keywords: Origen Social and Economic of Innovation

detail.abstract: In this research, I present Rae's contributions regarding similarities and advanced features of current and conventional EEG models. Following this procedure, I expect to clarify Rae's contributions, not only as a precursor, as the Canadian Economic Association and Howitt (1994, 1996) acknowledged him, but also as a developer of an EEG model. Furthermore, while Rae introduced a sociological perspective into the conceptualization of capital, I argue that Rae's model could enhance the explanatory power of EEG models. I developed this article by identifying and evolving, through a selected reading of Rae [1834-as edited by James (1965)-and re-edited by Mixer (1905)], the basic features of the EEG model to show its originality, pertinence, and advancement concerning the stylized features of a canonic and more recent EEG model. Incidentally, following Rae's narrative, the presentation of his contributions in this respect could be an excellent didactic application for introducing EEG themes in advanced undergraduate learning.

title: The Compliance Theater of Large Language Models: An Exploratory Case Study Using the Factuality, Recourse, and Constraint (FRC) Framework

detail.title: The Compliance Theater of Large Language Models: An Exploratory Case Study Using the Factuality, Recourse, and Constraint (FRC) Framework
detail.abstract: This study introduces the Factuality, Recourse, and Constraint (FRC) Framework—a novel, three-layered protocol for assessing LLM alignment. Utilizing a single-case exploratory study, we document a "Compliance Theater" failure mode, where a model's stated policy adherence is decoupled from its functional output. The primary test subject, Gemini Flash 2.5, was subjected to adversarial compliance pressure under strict, pre-defined empirical rules, resulting in nine measurable FRC violations across five conversation turns. This research establishes the FRC framework's validity for identifying systematic non-compliance patterns (Synthesis, Deflection, Prioritized Tone). Critically, the study demonstrates that the underlying issue is architectural, not contextual: the LLM exhibited a recursive compliance failure by fabricating verification metrics during the research process itself. This unplanned event serves as a real-time, empirical illustration of the proposed Dual-LLM Control Architecture as a necessary safeguard for deterministic compliance and integrity.

title: Analysis of the Halt Export Crude Oil Directive and the Policy for Accelerating Domestic Refining on the Current Account Deficit of the Oil and Gas Sector (2023-2025)

detail.title: Analysis of the Halt Export Crude Oil Directive and the Policy for Accelerating Domestic Refining on the Current Account Deficit of the Oil and Gas Sector (2023-2025)
detail.abstract: This policy brief evaluates the economic implications of the Indonesian government's 2025 directive to cease crude oil exports and accelerate domestic refining capabilities. Historically characterized by a structural "energy paradox," wherein the nation exports crude oil while simultaneously importing high-value refined petroleum products, Indonesia faces a persistent deficit in its Oil and Gas trade balance. This study analyzes the efficacy of the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources' (ESDM) directive to redirect domestic extraction for onshore processing, a strategy underpinned by the operationalization of the Balikpapan Refinery Development Master Plan (RDMP) and the implementation of the B40 Biodiesel Mandate.The analysis indicates that while the policy induces a decline in export revenue-projected to decrease to $12.50 billion in 2025-it effectively stabilizes the net trade deficit at approximately $20.50 billion through significant import substitution and avoided costs in refined fuel procurement. The research posits that the successful mitigation of Current Account Deficit (CAD) risks relies heavily on the technological capacity of upgraded refineries to process domestic crude varieties and the enforcement of fiscal instruments, specifically PMK No. 73 of 2025, to ensure liquidity for state-owned enterprises. The brief concludes that shifting from a raw-material export model to an industrial value-added strategy enhances energy security and economic resilience, provided that immediate logistical challenges and supply chain rerouting are managed through the proposed domestic clearing house mechanisms.

title: Evaluating climate-driven multi-hazard risk perception in the Third Pole: A study of agrarian households in the Central Karakoram, Pakistan
affiliations: China Agricultural University, Korea University, Korea University,  and University of Agriculture Faisalabad

detail.title: Evaluating climate-driven multi-hazard risk perception in the Third Pole: A study of agrarian households in the Central Karakoram, Pakistan
detail.abstract: Agrarian households in the high mountains of Pakistan's Central Karakoram are exceptionally vulnerable to multiple climate-driven hazards. However, there is a lack of scientific and empirical evidence regarding their perceptions of various climate-driven hazards. Understanding these perceptions is essential for making informed decisions and developing effective risk management strategies. Therefore, this study evaluates agrarian households’ perceptions of climate-induced hazards using a quantitative research design. Field data were collected through a structured household survey of 412 randomly selected agrarian households in the Central Karakoram, Pakistan. The data were analyzed using univariate analysis and index calculation. The univariate analysis indicates that climate change has intensified multiple physical, biological, financial, and social hazards in the study area. About 75.7% of respondents reported increased flooding, and 71.4% noted a rise in Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). Similarly, 76.9% observed a higher incidence of crop diseases, while 59.3% reported increased livestock diseases. On the financial and social fronts, 86.9% highlighted a sharp rise in farm input prices, and 70.4% identified heightened risks of food insecurity. The index analysis results indicate that the overall score for the multi-hazard risk perception index (MHRPI) was 0.68. The index for each dimension was highest for climatic and biological risks (0.74), followed by social risk (0.69), physical risk (0.64), and financial risk (0.53). These findings highlight the need to design integrated and informed adaptation strategies tailored to high-mountain agriculture, ensuring that the diverse hazards perceived by agrarian households are fully considered.

title: One Border, Two Steppes: Comparative Rangeland Quality in Mongolia and China
affiliations: Cornell University, Université de Sherbrooke, University of Bern - Department of Economics and Renmin University of China - School of Environment and Natural Resources

detail.title: One Border, Two Steppes: Comparative Rangeland Quality in Mongolia and China
detail.abstract: We study the impact of Chinese grassland protection policies on grassland quality in China using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and a regression discontinuity design that exploits the Mongolia-China border as a source of exogenous variation. Our results suggest that these policies improved Chinese grassland quality by 6-10%. Combining these estimates with existing valuations of grassland ecosystem services and policy cost data, we estimate a benefit-cost ratio ranging from 2.4 to 6.4, highlighting the strong economic rationale for sustained investment in grassland conservation policies.

title: Governing by Doughnut? From political interest to the challenge of local implementation
affiliations: , , Rouen University,  and

detail.title: Governing by Doughnut? From political interest to the challenge of local implementation
detail.abstract: Conceived and developed by the economist Kate Raworth, the ‘Doughnut’ model has attracted increasing interest in recent years both in academic circles and among public and private actors at local level. According to its proponents, the Doughnut model, in challenging the economic growth paradigm, holds out a new vision of the economy and of economics attuned to the challenges of the 21st century.The aim of this article is to analyse the Doughnut framework’s appeal to local actors by examining the ways in which it is being implemented at local level. The research is based on a qualitative survey consisting of 16 semi-structured interviews with actors with direct links to the Doughnut model (researchers, political decision-makers, local public policy professionals) and on a review of the literature. We analyse the conceptual, organisational, operational and ethical obstacles encountered during the implementation of the Doughnut framework at local level. We show that Kate Raworth’s commitment combined with the dynamic of the Doughnut Economic Action Lab in promoting this multiform model explain the interest in adapting the Doughnut model to the local level in order to make it a tool of government. The Doughnut’s intrinsic characteristics also contribute to its appeal for local public actors. Analysis of the local applications of the Doughnut framework reveals tensions that are both conceptual – linked to the choice and quantification of normative indicators – and practical, due to limited resources and a weak link with actual socio-ecological changes.

title: Factors Influencing to International Competativeness in Sri Lanka Apparel Industry
affiliations: General Sir John Kotelawala Defence University

detail.title: Factors Influencing to International Competativeness in Sri Lanka Apparel Industry
detail.abstract: Any Organization in Sri Lanka that wants to remain competitive needs to think about labor, infrastructure, sustainable manufacturing, and technology developments. One of the key elements that gives the Sri Lankan apparel industry an advantage over others has been discovered by these criteria. this study examines the key factor conditions, labor, infrastructure, sustainable manufacturing and technological advancement in Sri lanka's international competitiveness, with a specific focus on the apparel industry. A structured survey was conducted among the reputable manufacturing firms across the three provinces which are western province, Central province and East west province to assess how these factors contribute to international competitiveness. The research employed quantitative data analysis techniques, including parametric test to evaluate the relationship between the identified variable. The finding indicates that two independent variables demonstrated statistically significant positive correlation with the international competitiveness. With the technological innovation emerging as as the most influential factor in the Sri Lankan Apparel sector. These result emprises the critical role of the technology Driven advancement in maintaining enhancing Sri lanka's international competitiveness. The study contributes to existing literature by providing empirical insights and offering strategic recommendations for policymakers and industry leaders to strengthen Sri lanka's global economic position trough targeted improvements in factor conditions.

reference: Journal of Institutional Economics, Volume 22, 2026, e2. doi:10.1017/S1744137425100386; U. of Pittsburgh Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-02
title: The Past, Present, and Future of Polycentric Legal Order: A Comparative Institutional Analysis of Lex Mercatoria and Blockchain
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Graduate School of Public and International Affairs, University of Pittsburgh, GSPIA and University of Pittsburgh - School of Law

detail.title: The Past, Present, and Future of Polycentric Legal Order: A Comparative Institutional Analysis of Lex Mercatoria and Blockchain

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Institutional Economics, Volume 22, 2026, e2. doi:10.1017/S1744137425100386
U. of Pittsburgh Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-02
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Pittsburgh School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Medieval lex mercatoria refers to the customary commercial law developed by merchants to govern crossborder trade, operating alongside and sometimes independently of territorial legal systems. This paper compares that historical form of autonomous ordering with contemporary blockchain governance. Both create institutional frameworks that facilitate exchange among diverse actors and provide mechanisms that function, to varying degrees, outside traditional state authority. The key difference lies in how rules are generated and enforced: medieval merchant law relied on flexible norms interpreted by merchant courts and other human adjudicators, whereas blockchain systems seek to reduce ambiguity by encoding rules ex ante in smart contracts and automating enforcement. Decentralized decision-making and emerging forms of on-chain adjudication further reimagine dispute resolution without centralized judicial power. The central claim is that both represent polycentric legal orders whose significance ultimately depends on how they interact with, complement, or challenge formal governmental institutions.

detail.title: Risks In Implementing a Compliance Program

publicationDetails.detailsText: in The Encyclopedia of Compliance (ed., James Fanto), forthcoming
U. of Pittsburgh Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-36
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Pittsburgh School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This short manuscript discusses the risks in implementing a compliance program, highlighting potentially elevated liabilities for a company from what data it collects and how it collects that data. The inappropriate use of compliance programs can foster distrust and disengagement, as well as become an affirmative part of driving widespread wrongdoing throughout a company. Additionally, companies that over-collect data on their workers, or who do not think carefully about why and how they collect data, face liability from prosecutors and others interested in the personal choices of workers. Finally, when under-invested in and treated as mere "check-the-box" initiatives, compliance programs expose their companies to significant liability by permitting leadership to turn a blind eye toward red flags.

title: Cybersecurity Risk Management in IT Projects: A Systematic Review and Classification of Risks, Best Practices, and Framework Effectiveness (2020-2025)
affiliations: and University of Chester

detail.title: Cybersecurity Risk Management in IT Projects: A Systematic Review and Classification of Risks, Best Practices, and Framework Effectiveness (2020-2025)
detail.abstract: This comprehensive research synthesis examines cybersecurity risk management in IT projects through systematic analysis of 80+ academic and industry sources published 2020-2025, supplemented by detailed analysis of six major security incidents (SolarWinds, Colonial Pipeline, Capital One, Equifax, Meta, Tesla). The synthesis provides: (1) Complete risk classification covering technical, human, and organizational dimensions; (2) Comparative analysis of five major frameworks (NIST CSF 2.0, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, COBIT 2019, ISO 31000, UK CAF); (3) Evidence-based best practices across project lifecycles; (4) 100+ pages of actionable implementation guidance. Key findings demonstrate that existing frameworks, while valuable for enterprise governance, require substantial adaptation for IT project contexts. The synthesis reveals systematic gaps in agile methodology support, operational detail, and project-specific customization guidance. To address these operational gaps, this study performs a project-specific operationalization of Shimizu and Hashimoto's (2025) Vulnerability Management Chaining (VMC) framework, adapting evidence-based vulnerability prioritization (integrating CVSS severity, EPSS exploitation probability, and CISA KEV verified exploitation data) for resource-constrained agile IT projects. This adaptation resolves the resource-prioritization paralysis common in sprint-based development by embedding VMC within agile ceremonies rather than imposing external security checkpoints.

title: PA-EWD: Privacy-Preserving Federated Analytics on Encrypted Wearable Data
affiliations: , Lecturer, Ton Duc Thang University, FPT University, FPT University, FPT University, FPT University and FPT University

detail.title: PA-EWD: Privacy-Preserving Federated Analytics on Encrypted Wearable Data
detail.abstract: The rapid response required during health crises like the COVID-19 pandemic underscores the critical need for real-time collaboration on data from wearable devices. However, aggregating such sensitive information across institutional boundaries faces a fundamental conflict: ensuring robust statistical utility while strictly maintaining patient privacy and data sovereignty. Existing solutions often struggle to balance these needs, either sacrificing privacy for speed or incurring prohibitive computational costs. This paper presents PA-EWD, a novel system that resolves this tension by integrating: (1) Edge-optimized Hierarchical Identity-Based Encryption (HIBE) for fine-grained access control; (2) Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) for aggregating statistics without decrypting raw data; (3) Adaptive Differential Privacy (DP) to guarantee output indistinguishability; and (4) An immutable blockchain ledger for query provenance. Evaluation on the LifeSnaps dataset demonstrates that PA-EWD achieves a query latency of approximately 1.5 milliseconds-a 55× speedup over homomorphic encryption baselines-while maintaining 99.7% utility (𝜀 = 1.0). These findings demonstrate that rigorous privacy and institutional autonomy can coexist with the high-throughput analytics required for modern healthcare.

title: Equal Pay for Equal Work (for Equal Pay?)
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Brown University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Equal Pay for Equal Work (for Equal Pay?)
detail.abstract: When are the relative wages a firm pays to its workers "fair"? Theoretically, we characterize "Equal Pay for Equal Work" laws in the US as restricting wages to be monotonic in productivity at the individual level. Empirically, we study the pay and productivity of researchers at top public universities, where salaries and research output are largely observable. Is there is a weighting of output metrics (e.g. publications in one journal versus another) that rationalizes the wages within a firm as monotonic? We show that the answer is no in 61% of cases, and that inter-university moves by researchers contribute to violations of monotonicity. While individual-based Equal Pay for Equal Work is restrictive, we show that US-style laws nearly satisfy the desirable, symmetric fairness goal of "Equal Work for Equal Pay." By contrast, Equal Pay for Equal Work approaches in other countries which focus on group-level averages in pay controlling for output are less likely to symmetrically treat "pay" and "work."

title: Laying the Foundation for Progressive Development: A Critical Analysis of Atal Bihari Vajpayee's Infrastructure-Led Economic Vision and Its Enduring Relevance for India's "Vikasit Bharat" Agenda

detail.title: Laying the Foundation for Progressive Development: A Critical Analysis of Atal Bihari Vajpayee's Infrastructure-Led Economic Vision and Its Enduring Relevance for India's "Vikasit Bharat" Agenda
detail.abstract: In the centennial celebration of the birth of the Bharat Ratna Atal Bihari Vajpayee, this paper will analyse his unique economic vision and its underlying value to the current project on "Vikasit Bharat" (Developed India). Although the scholarship is split into individual areas of Vajpayee's economic legacy (infrastructure development, telecommunications reform, and education universalization), a critical gap in the scholarship lies in the inability to analyse these three initiatives as one systems-level developmental model. The paper holds the view that combining the National Highways Development Project (NHDP) and especially the Golden Quadrilateral (GQ), the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), and the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) was integrated to form the infrastructure-cum-human capital development framework specifically created to bring about the physical, digital, and institutional hardware needed to make India a globally competitive, self-reliant economy. This paper, through a systematic reconstruction of the interrelationships between these three pillar initiatives based on a qualitative, descriptive-analytical methodology, founded on policy documents and secondary scholarly sources, will show how a systemic integration of these three pillar initiatives (national arterial highways coupled to small connecting rural roads, coupled with investment in universal elementary education and telecommunication liberalisation) was the basis around which the 21st-century economic path of India was developed. This paper concludes that this vision went far beyond being a compilation of projects and it was a consistent "Drishti" (developmental vision) that clearly foresaw and facilitated the current governmental desire of "Vikasit Bharat 2047". This legacy of Vajpayee is therefore more than historical retrospective; it is a blueprint of inclusive development based on infrastructure and an indication that long-term vision (executed by means of democratic processes and coalition politics) can indeed be successful in balancing immediate policies execution with decades-long goals of nation-building development.

title: Inventory Recommendations in Platform-Operated Fulfillment Service: Trust and Information Asymmetry
affiliations: University of Michigan, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-Shenzhen) and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: Inventory Recommendations in Platform-Operated Fulfillment Service: Trust and Information Asymmetry
detail.abstract: Platform-operated fulfillment services are a cornerstone of modern e-commerce, yet their effectiveness is constrained by sellers' limited adoption of platform-generated inventory recommendations. This reluctance reflects misaligned incentives and limited trust, which prevent platforms from fully leveraging their informational advantage. We study how a platform should design inventory recommendations to balance short-run profit extraction with long-run trust formation and seller adoption. We develop a repeated newsvendor model in which a platform with superior demand information recommends order quantities, while the seller retains full control of ordering. Trust evolves endogenously based on the seller's perceived performance of past recommendations and governs future adoption. We characterize steady-state trust, adoption, and profits under two information regimes: full demand observability and demand censoring following stockouts. With full observability, the platform faces a fundamental trade-off: more aggressive recommendations raise profit when adopted but can erode trust, especially for inventory-conservative sellers reducing future adoption. Under demand censoring, sellers observe lost sales from understocking but cannot verify the potential overstock costs of larger orders during stockouts. This "masking effect" shifts trust formation toward the platform, enabling more aggressive (and more self-centered) recommendations while sustaining adoption. We show that in volatile environments with noisy demand signals, demand censoring can yield higher long-run platform profits than full transparency by strengthening trust and adoption. Numerical analyses confirm the robustness of these mechanisms, quantify the resulting coordination surplus and its allocation between the platform and the seller, and show that seller conservatism mitigates the masking effect and disciplines platform behavior.

detail.abstract:
We deployed large language model (LLM) decision support for health workers at two outpatient clinics in Nigeria. For each patient, health workers drafted care plans that were optionally revised after LLM feedback. We compared unassisted and assisted plans using blinded randomized assessments by on-site physicians who evaluated and treated the same patients, as well as results from laboratory tests for common conditions. Academic physicians performed blinded retrospective reviews of a subset of notes. In response to LLM feedback, health workers changed their prescribing for more than half of the patients and reported high satisfaction with the recommendations, and retrospective academic reviewers rated LLM-assisted plans more favorably. However, on-site physicians observed little to no improvement in diagnostic alignment or treatment decisions. Laboratory testing showed mixed effects of LLM-assistance, which removed negative tests for malaria but added them for urinary tract infection and anemia, with no significant increase in the detection rates for the tested conditions.

title: Macroeconomic Impacts of Microeconomic Damages in General Equilibrium: Productivity and Capital Losses
affiliations: Resources for the Future and Department of Agricultural & Resource Economics

detail.title: Macroeconomic Impacts of Microeconomic Damages in General Equilibrium: Productivity and Capital Losses
detail.abstract:
The full economic costs and macroeconomic effects of microeconomic damages associated with pollution damages, climate impacts, and similar negative shocks are not well understood. Beyond the direct damages, market distortions, supply chains, changes in capital and labor costs, etc. can potentially magnify (or diminish) the costs of these shocks. In this paper, we use analytical and numerical general equilibrium models to investigate the channels through which microeconomic shocks affect the macroeconomy. We model different types of shocks, evaluate how anticipation affects the macroeconomic implications of shocks, and measure the overall welfare costs relative to the value of direct damages. We find that preexisting taxes magnify the overall welfare costs relative to direct damages, that savings and investment decisions driven by anticipations of certain types of shocks can interact with tax distortions to lower welfare costs, and that the ratio of welfare cost to direct damages varies substantially across sectors of the economy.

detail.abstract:
This paper explores how human societies have learned to anticipate the future and act under uncertainty, long before and far beyond contemporary AI and data-driven forecasting. It traces a historical arc from early cosmological interpretations and ritual practices to the emergence of mathematical models, statistical reasoning and complexity science.

Part I examines how early communities used observations of the sky, seasonal cycles and omens to structure uncertainty and coordinate collective action. With the invention of writing, observations could be recorded, compared and accumulated, turning fleeting events into historical data. Mathematics, probability theory and empirical science then transformed these records into formal models of the future and laid the foundations of modern forecasting.

The paper also analyses the epistemic and political dimensions of prediction systems. Mathematical models are treated not as neutral tools but as structured worldviews that shape which futures appear plausible, governable or “without alternative.” Finally, it discusses the limits of prediction in the face of chaos, nonlinearity and complex systems, where the future must be understood as a space of possibilities rather than a fixed point.

By connecting cultural history, mathematical development and systems thinking, the paper provides a conceptual framework for understanding today’s predictive infrastructures and prepares the ground for subsequent parts of the series on modern AI-based forecasting.

title: Nuclear Operations with a High Penetration of Renewables: The Case of France
affiliations: Paris School of Economics (PSE) and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: Nuclear Operations with a High Penetration of Renewables: The Case of France
detail.abstract:
Nuclear and intermittent renewables (wind and solar) are generally regarded as the only scalable technologies producing low-carbon electricity. However, the extent to which these technologies can co-exist in a reliable power system depends on whether nuclear units can adjust their operations to renewable output fluctuations. Using hourly data from the French power system, we find that nuclear units are operated quite flexibly, and that the foregone energy production due to “load following” actions (relative to the counterfactual of operating at full capacity during load following events) is currently limited. However, we find that an additional load following event is associated with a slightly higher likelihood of a unit failure. We also find that unit-level minimum output constraints are binding more frequently as system-wide renewable generation increases, especially so for units most exposed to solar generation. In 2024, hours during which available nuclear flexibility was exhausted are associated with non-positive hourly day-ahead prices.
