title: Brexit and UK Migration: Germany-Benchmarked Evidence on Structural and Reallocation Shifts
affiliations: Tel Aviv University - Eitan Berglas School of Economics

detail.title: Brexit and UK Migration: Germany-Benchmarked Evidence on Structural and Reallocation Shifts
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how Brexit reshaped the volume and composition of UK migration flows. To address the inherent endogeneity of migration responses to political change, the study employs a Difference-in-Differences design that benchmarks the United Kingdom against Germany, a stable EU member unaffected by Brexit-related institutional shocks. Treating the 2016 referendum and the 2021 end of free movement as sequential shocks, the results show that migration volume increased after both shocks, but through different channels: the referendum reduced emigration relative to Germany, while the post-2021 points-based system triggered a reallocation of inflows away from EU free-movement migrants toward non-EU migrants from the rest of the world, with a markedly stronger skill-selective profile. The paper analyzes how Brexit reshaped migration flows into and out of the United Kingdom by exploiting the 2016 referendum and the 2021 termination of free movement as sequential institutional shocks. Using a Difference-in-Differences design with Germany as a stable EU benchmark, the results show that Brexit acted as a structural regime shock, not a border-tightening event. Net migration into the UK rose after both shocks—first due to a sharp post-referendum decline in emigration relative to Germany, and later due to a substantial expansion of non-EU immigration under the new points-based system. Immigration patterns exhibit a clear regime shift, with EU inflows contracting sharply after 2016 and globally sourced, skill-selective inflows rising after 2021. In the later period, a modest but notable increase in UK-born emigration relative to Germany also emerges, reflecting frictions in post-Brexit mobility. Overall, Brexit reoriented—rather than reduced—UK migration flows, transforming both their scale and composition.

title: Global Stratification Economics (GSE): A Primer - Definitions and Research Implications
affiliations: City University of New York, Colorado State University, Fort Collins and Occidental College

detail.title: Global Stratification Economics (GSE): A Primer - Definitions and Research Implications
detail.abstract:
We coin the term Global Stratification Economics (GSE) to extend Stratification Economics (SE) to international contexts where mechanisms emerge that can be identified as (1) universal but matched to positioning along a country’s development path or (2) context-specific and historically dependent in ways different from the United States and other international environments. Building on SE’s core insight that groups compete over scarce resources and that dominant groups shape rules to preserve advantage, we define GSE as an approach that foregrounds historical genesis (e.g., settler colonialism, slavery, caste, extractive governance, military intervention), local institutions that structure dominance and resistance, and transnational mechanisms (e.g., imported stratification and the lateral mobility hypothesis) that link origin- and destination-country hierarchies. Drawing on evidence from Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and the global macroeconomy, we synthesize research on intergenerational mobility, wealth and asset inequality, labor-market segmentation, colorism, caste and ethnicity, gendered and intersectional constraints, spatial inequality and property regimes, and global value chains. We conclude by outlining how GSE reshapes measurement and international policy evaluation by centering group-differentiated outcomes, institutional transformation, and pillars of recognition, redistribution, and repair and by offering a checklist for researchers to apply GSE.

title: The Impacts of Parole Supervision
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis, Washington University in St. Louis and University of Chicago

detail.title: The Impacts of Parole Supervision
detail.abstract:
We study the impacts of a reform to parole supervision in Illinois. The reform reduced the term of supervision for some parolees from 12 months to 6 months while many similar parolees continued to receive 12 months of supervision. We evaluate the impact of the reform using a standard difference-in-differences estimator, and we find clear evidence that the reform reduced prison re-entry rates. Sharp drops in rates of technical revocations drove these reductions. Rates of prison re-admissions linked to new crimes did not change. We merge data from Cook County Courts with our data on state prison admissions and releases, and we find no evidence that the reform increased crime rates among parolees. The reform reduced both the cost of incarceration and the cost of parolee supervision without creating harms to public safety.

title: Automation Experiments and Inequality
affiliations: Chapman University and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Automation Experiments and Inequality
detail.abstract:
Many experiments study the productivity effects of automation technologies such as generative algorithms. A key test in these experiments relates to inequality: does the technology increase output more for high- or low-skill workers? However, the theoretical content of this empirical test has been unclear. Here, we formalize a theory that describes the experimental effect of automation technologies on worker-level output and, therefore, inequality. Worker-level output depends on a task-level production function, and workers are heterogeneous in their task-level skills. Workers perform a task themselves or delegate it to the automation technology. The inequality effect of improved automation depends on the interaction of two factors: (i) the correlation in task-level skills across workers, and (ii) workers' skills relative to the technology's effective skill. In many cases we study, the inequality effect is non-monotonic --- as technologies improve, inequality decreases then increases. The model and descriptive statistics of skill correlations generally suggest that the diversity of automation technologies will play an important role in the evolution of inequality.

title: State and Time-Dependent Pricing
affiliations: Bank of England, Stanford University - Department of Economics, Bank of England, King’s College London - King's Business School, University of Nottingham and Bank of England

detail.title: State and Time-Dependent Pricing
detail.abstract:
We present new evidence on how firms set prices using direct questions from a large, economy-wide survey of UK firms. Since 2023, 54% of firms report setting prices in a state-dependent manner, as opposed to changing prices at fixed intervals. In contrast, 44% of firms used state-dependent pricing in 2019. Smaller firms, those with a higher share of non-labour costs, and those reporting higher subjective uncertainty around sales and prices are more likely to be state-dependent. We then analyse the implications of price-setting behaviour for inflation dynamics. State-dependent firms experienced a sharper increase in price growth over 2022-2023, and also a faster subsequent decline. Using evidence from a randomised survey experiment, firm-level forecast errors, and local projections, we show that prices of state-dependent firms respond faster to cost shocks. The difference between state-dependent and time-dependent firms is furthermore larger for bigger shocks, consistent with theoretical predictions.

detail.abstract:
The arrival of GLP-1 medications has been described as one of the most important health care innovations in recent years. We provide large-scale quasi-experimental evidence on their real-world impacts by exploiting variation in the eventual prescribing propensities of patients’ pre-existing primary care providers. Using a panel intent-to-treat design, we compare outcomes for 1.4 million diabetic or obese veterans based on their 2018 provider’s eventual propensity to adopt GLP-1s, leveraging comprehensive electronic health records and biomarker data from the Veterans Health Administration, a setting with minimal insurance attrition and low-cost access to these drugs. Patients whose providers become higher propensity adopters experience substantial improvements in glycemic control and clinically meaningful weight loss; our treatment-on-the-treated estimates closely match estimates from clinical trials. Despite these metabolic benefits, we find no statistically significant effects on emergency department utilization, mental health and substance use outcomes, or non–GLP-1 medical spending through 2024.

title: Effective Protection with Global Value Chains
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business, University of Notre Dame and University of Notre Dame - Department of Economics

detail.title: Effective Protection with Global Value Chains
detail.abstract:
The effective rate of protection (ERP) is a widely-used tool to evaluate the joint impact of input and output tariffs on the net protection offered to individual sectors. Nonetheless, the theoretical foundations underlying the traditional ERP are decades out of date. In this paper, we provide fresh guidance for policy analysts that seek to measure effective protection, with two core elements. First, we develop a new ERP concept, which measures how much tariffs shift the derived demand for real value added at the sector level. The ERP then has an intuitive interpretation: it is the effective subsidy to buyers of sectoral value added that replicates the impact of the tariff structure on demand. Second, we demonstrate how to compute our ERP index accounting for global value chain linkages. The result is an ERP for the GVC age, in which effective protection depends on the structure of value chains across countries and sectors, and the structure of all tariffs applied globally. We demonstrate the usefulness of our approach by analyzing how recent tariff changes have altered effective protection in the United States and the rest of the world.

title: With or Without U? Binning Bias and the Causal Effects of Temperature Extremes
affiliations: Northwestern University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: With or Without U? Binning Bias and the Causal Effects of Temperature Extremes
detail.abstract:
Estimates of climate impacts show that extreme temperatures have large and wide-spread effects. To estimate these effects, a common approach counts days in different temperature ranges and considers how exposure to these distinct 'bins' affects outcomes. This often produces non-linear, U-shaped results, in which high and low temperatures have the largest effects. We show that non-linear approaches like these can generate spurious findings. Specifically, global warming induces trends in extreme temperature exposure that correlate mechanically with a location's baseline temperature. Substantial bias emerges if trends in the outcome variable also correlate with baseline temperature for any reason. We demonstrate this problem theoretically, in simulations, and with real outcomes. We then develop solutions. In applications using US data, some results in the literature are unaffected by these corrections, while other results change substantially.

title: How Globalization Unravels: A Ricardian Model of Endogenous Trade Policy
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: How Globalization Unravels: A Ricardian Model of Endogenous Trade Policy
detail.abstract:
We study how uneven gains from globalization can endogenously generate protectionism as a political equilibrium. Using U.S. data, we document that regions more exposed to import competition display stronger opposition to globalization, especially among households with little financial wealth, and that firms in trade-exposed sectors sharply increase lobbying expenditures. To interpret these patterns, we develop and quantify a general equilibrium Ricardian model with heterogeneous households, input-output linkages, and endogenous trade policy shaped by voting and lobbying. Distributional shocks reallocate political support among voters, while lobbying propagates through production networks, generating strategic complementarities that sustain protectionism. Calibrated to U.S.-China sectoral data from 1991--2019, the model accounts for rising inequality, declining support for globalization, and key aggregate trends in consumption and trade.

title: Price Discrimination with Costless Resale
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Price Discrimination with Costless Resale
detail.abstract:
This paper shows that income effects create an endogenous barrier to arbitrage, allowing price discrimination to survive costless resale. A monopolist sells an indivisible good to consumers with heterogeneous incomes who can freely resell. When the good is strictly normal, a consumer's reservation price to resell increases as the purchase price decreases—lower prices leave buyers wealthier and raise their valuation of the good. The monopolist exploits this by subsidising low-income consumers to raise their reservation prices to a target that high-income consumers must also pay. The optimal schedule increases dollar-for-dollar with income in the subsidised segment, weakly dominates uniform pricing, and achieves the first-best allocation when the entire market is served. We show the mechanism extends beyond income effects: low substitutability with market alternatives generates large reservation-price responses even when income sensitivity is modest. Sustaining discrimination requires market power at the individual level—consumer-specific quantity limits—not merely aggregate output restrictions. Extensions examine multiple monopolists and endogenous privacy choices.

title: Banks, Financial Education and Digitalization in Highly Informal Economies: A Micro–Macro Model of Endogenous Screening

detail.title: Banks, Financial Education and Digitalization in Highly Informal Economies: A Micro–Macro Model of Endogenous Screening
detail.abstract: In many developing economies, informal firms account for a major share of employment and market activity, but remain largely excluded from bank credit. Classical models of credit rationing emphasize adverse selection and moral hazard, and focus on interest rates, collateral, or capital-intensive monitoring as ways to deal with imperfect information. However, a large fraction of informal firms are not intrinsically unprofitable: they mainly suffer from organizational deficits (no cash register, no bookkeeping, approximate inventory management) and a quasi-absence of data that can be exploited by banks and tax authorities. This paper proposes a micro-macro model in which a bank invests in a financial education and digitalisation program, denoted E, combining practical training, point-of-sale and payment tools, and a structured banking relationship. This investment reduces the adoption cost for high-potential firms, improves the traceability of their flows and generates a mechanism of endogenous screening: for a given effort level E, productive types adopt and become bankable, while subsistence activities self-select out. At the micro level, the adoption of E increases the survival probability and the customer lifetime value of large informal firms. At the macro-financial level, E reduces the preference for cash, raises the level and stability of deposits, lowers portfolio risk and increases the lending capacity of the banking system. We show that the bank's private optimum satisfies E >0 , but that the social optimum is higher (E soc > E) due to positive externalities on money creation, macro-financial stability and tax revenues, which justifies the intervention of public development banks.

title: The Economics of Scaling Early Childhood Programs: Lessons from The Chicago School
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Economics of Scaling Early Childhood Programs: Lessons from The Chicago School
detail.abstract:
Many ideas show remarkable returns in small-scale trials but often disappoint when scaled to broader populations and contexts. Using early childhood investment as a case study, this study develops a dynamic human capital formation model that integrates complementary skill investment with “Option C thinking” on scaling challenges. The model is stylized in the Chicago tradition: micro-founded with optimizing agents, dynamic skill production, and a policymaker evaluating scaling decisions. It formalizes how naive extrapolation from pilot studies systematically overestimates policy efficacy by ignoring “voltage drops,” declining treatment effects due to unrepresentativeness at scale. The model demonstrates that optimal scaling policy requires mechanism-based design that anticipates these failures through backward induction from implementation realities. The scientific insights from a set of recent studies provide valuable perspectives on the model.

title: Experiences, Expectations, and Asset Prices
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Experiences, Expectations, and Asset Prices
detail.abstract:
In models with subjective beliefs, the dynamics of investor beliefs are central to explaining asset price movements. Allowing subjective beliefs to deviate from full-information rational expectations requires a model of how investors form beliefs. I review recent research that explores experience-based belief formation. The experience-based model closely resembles Bayesian updating but allows individuals to overweight data observed during their own lifetimes when forming beliefs about the parameters of the data-generating process. Because individuals of different age learn from different histories, the model predicts heterogeneity between age groups that evolves over time with the path of realized data individuals have experienced, closely mirroring the age-related variation observed in survey microdata. At the aggregate level, experience-based expectations formation can explain asset price dynamics. In the stock market, learning from experience about long-run cash flow growth generates valuation cycles and return predictability. Experience-based formation of long-term inflation expectations can explain secular changes of real interest rates. I conclude by outlining directions for future research.

title: Corporate Intent
affiliations: HEC, University of Pennsylvania and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Corporate Intent
detail.abstract:
Do investors care about why a firm behaves responsibly, over and above what the firm does and how much cash it earns? In our main experiment, participants value shares in companies that reduce pollution relative to peers, while CEOs articulate the company’s intentions: prosocial or for-profit. Investors are willing to pay more for shares in a company that takes a given prosocial action if it is motivated by social concern rather than profit maximization. This "intention premium" is distinct from the valuation effects of cash flows and environmental externalities. Respondents who are deontological, politically liberal, female, or less individualistic value the company’s intent the most. Additionally, and somewhat surprisingly, respondents view favorably firms that embrace both profit and social objectives, without ranking them. Overall, our findings temper claims that when there is no financial trade-off between doing good and doing well, shareholder value and stakeholder value maximization are equivalent.

detail.abstract: We find that preschools facilitate early diagnosis and treatment of conditions that can hinder learning. Low-income children born shortly before their state's school-entry cutoff date are 16.9, 9.3, and 14.8 percent more likely to be diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, a speech or language disorder, and a hearing or vision condition at ages three and four, compared to children born after the cutoff. title: Transformed Intermediation:  Credit Risk to NBFIs, Liquidity Risk to Banks
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Transformed Intermediation:  Credit Risk to NBFIs, Liquidity Risk to Banks
detail.abstract:
We argue that the rapid asset growth of nonbank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) relative to banks is the outcome of transformations of risks between banks and NBFIs that increase the interconnectedness of the two sectors. These transformations are consistent with avoiding tighter, post-GFC bank regulation while harnessing the funding and liquidity advantages of bank deposit franchises and access to safety nets. Specifically, we show that banks fund NBFIs through senior loans and credit lines, which NBFIs use for acquiring junior credit claims, warehouse financing, and liquidity management. We empirically demonstrate that shocks experienced by NBFIs spillover to the banks that provide them with credit lines, particularly in times of stress. We then describe a number of policy approaches that are consistent with our transformation view and conclude with suggestions for future research.

title: Do GLP-1 Medications Pay for Themselves?
affiliations: Indiana University, Indiana University, University of Wisconsin-Madison and Indiana University

detail.title: Do GLP-1 Medications Pay for Themselves?
detail.abstract:
Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) represent a major improvement in treatment of diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular risk reduction, but they are also among the most expensive drugs in widespread use and the subject of significant policy debate. The high price of these drugs may overstate their net cost if the health improvements they produce lead to reduced downstream health care use and medical spending, that is, cost offsets. We estimate such offsets using insurance claims data, examining the effects of GLP-1 initiation on subsequent GLP-1 use and spending, and on other non-GLP-1 spending. We use a stacked difference-in-differences design, comparing patients initiating GLP-1 medication to not-yet-treated controls who initiate GLP-1s several months or years later, allowing us to control for underlying time trends and baseline characteristics. Overall, we do not find a reduction in downstream medical spending. Although GLP-1 initiation reduces spending on other diabetes medications, total non-GLP-1 spending increases, driven by higher outpatient health care use; GLP- 1 drug spending rises mechanically. For health care payers, the relevant cost of GLP-1 initiation therefore extends beyond the sticker price of the drug. We find similar results across subgroups of GLP1 initiators including those with prior cardiovascular disease and those without diabetes (consistent with obesity indication). Our main results examine spending responses over the first year after initiation. However, we also estimate longer run effects in a smaller sample and find no cost offsets even five years after GLP-1 initiation. Taken together, these results suggest that payers facing the costs of GLP-1 coverage are unlikely to see large savings from reduced spending on other care. If GLP-1 therapies ultimately yield cost savings, they are likely to occur only over longer horizons or through non-medical channels.

title: Platform Work: Evidence from Drivers in India, Indonesia, and Kenya
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD), IDinsight, IDinsight, IDinsight, Independent Researcher, Independent Researcher and IDinsight

detail.title: Platform Work: Evidence from Drivers in India, Indonesia, and Kenya
detail.abstract:
Using surveys and administrative data from representative samples of drivers working on three leading gig platforms in India, Indonesia, and Kenya, we document the composition, economic experiences, and labor market trajectories of platform workers. Combining platform-based earnings with operating cost data, we estimate earnings net of costs (in PPP-adjusted terms) in each context. We find that the flexible nature of platform work enables drivers to work substantially more than the full-time equivalent, generating higher monthly net earnings than low-skill or casual employment, despite comparable or lower hourly net earnings relative to these outside options. Drivers who exit platform work in India and Indonesia do so to take up better-paying full-time positions. In contrast, Kenyan drivers often exit involuntarily, returning to offline driving with adverse financial consequences. One-third of drivers across countries rely on platform work to supplement earnings during emergencies or slow work periods, suggesting that platform work may play an important role as a financial safety net.

detail.title: Price Risk Management through NCDEX Futures: Evidence from the Indian Coriander Market
detail.abstract: Aim: This study explores the effectiveness of NCDEX futures contracts in reducing price risks for coriander crops (stakeholders). NCDEX (National Commodity and Derivatives Exchange) offers futures contracts to manage risks, hedging practices, and price discovery mechanisms. Study Design: Non-probability and purposive sampling techniques are used for the study area, sample size selection, and selection of stakeholders as they are selected based on language, time duration, some telephonic interviews, etc, and convenience sampling is used for the preparation of the questionnaire through Google form .Analysis the all phases using technical indicators like Candle stick chart, Bollinger bands, %B, ADX-Average Directional Index, Moving Average Exponential (EMA) and Relative Strength Index (RSI),MACD- Moving Average Convergence and Divergence, CCI-Commodity Channel Index, and Stochastic RSI provides more valuable insights for anticipating future trends. Econometric models like VAR (Vector Auto-Regression) was used especially in monthly prices of Coriander crop. Methodology: In this study, data was collected from primary and secondary sources such as farmers in major coriander cultivating areas, and NCDEX data respectively. The research is conducted incoriander-producing regions such as Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, and Assam. Hence, purposively the regions have been selected to know their perception towards coriander crop, some important information gathered for my research. The total sample size is 300. Findings and Results: Price volatility is a significant challenge for coriander farmers and traders due to seasonal production patterns, unpredictable weather, and fluctuations in demand. The study found key barriers, along with scarce resources like awareness, infrastructure, and less number of participants in cultivation. This research includes suggestions to improve the adoption of future contracts, focus on policy support, quality education, and enhanced market access. Over the last 10 years, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan have remained the top producers of coriander, with consistent growth in both area and production because of favorable conditions and better farming practices. India consistently contributes over 60% of the global coriander production, Turkey remains the 2nd largest producer. The ‘r’ value is 0.924428969, ‘p’ value is 0.00013, so there is a significant relation between Area’ (thousand hectares) and ‘Production’ (thousand metric tons). ‘tvalue’ is 6.856, which indicates that the observed correlation is very far from expected under the null hypothesis. The F- value is 0.0000529183 so there is a significant impact of the Production in thousand metric tons and Productivity in kg/ha. The adjusted R-square value is 86.892; therefore, 87 % of this variance of the dependent variable is explained by the independent variable, it has a positive impact on output. So there is a linear relationship between Production in thousand metric tons and Productivity in kg/ha. title: Firm Emissions and Credit Allocation
affiliations: University of California, Santa Cruz - Department of Economics, University of California, Santa Cruz, University of California, Santa Cruz and

detail.title: Firm Emissions and Credit Allocation
detail.abstract:
Do banks help or hamper green transition? To answer this question, we analyze the dynamics of bank lending to firms in the US, EU, and separately Denmark in relation to the borrowers' emissions of CO2. We evaluate the allocation of bank loans across industries and within industries across firms, allowing for heterogeneity of firm emissions and changes in these emissions. To facilitate green transition, bank lending needs to flow to greener and greening firms, but not out of high-emission industries that need funding to transition to cleaner production methods. Using syndicated loan data, we find that for US borrowers, bank lending was likely hampering green transition, while in the EU bank lending is more likely to facilitate it. Zooming in on Denmark, for which we have data on the full universe of firms and banks, we find more significant credit reallocation to greener firms, especially within industries. However, the reallocation of funds to green firms is, to a large extent, a byproduct of green firms becoming bigger. We do not find any evidence consistent with banks active stewardship of green transition.

title: The End of the Blank Check: Strategic Decoupling of the United States and Israel, 2035 ± 2 Years

detail.title: The End of the Blank Check: Strategic Decoupling of the United States and Israel, 2035 ± 2 Years

declarations.funderStatement: I funded it myself. It was independent research. All that was required was my time and a laptop.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a calibrated hierarchical system of differential equations, coupled with 15,000 Monte Carlo simulations, to examine the conditions under which unconditional U.S. strategic support for Israel might terminate. Under baseline assumptions and wide parameter variation, the model generates a sharply peaked collapse of annual aid below USD 0.8 billion (real 2025 dollars) between 2032 and 2038, with a median date of 2035.4. The primary drivers are the interaction of rising U.S. debt-servicing costs with generational turnover in the electorate and the subsequent rise of domestic political restraint on foreign-aid appropriations. A concurrent 60-75 % decline in Tel Aviv prime residential property values emerges endogenously as markets reprice the loss of perceived U.S. security guarantees. The projected termination window is robust to plausible variation in behavioural and macroeconomic parameters and does not require exogenous war or diplomatic rupture. To the author's knowledge, this is the first quantitative forecast of a specific termination interval for a major post-1945 unconditional security relationship.

title: How In-School Supervised Ed-Tech Support Produces Massive Learning Gains: A Khan Academy Field Experiment in India
affiliations: University of Toronto - Department of Economics, University of Toronto and

detail.title: How In-School Supervised Ed-Tech Support Produces Massive Learning Gains: A Khan Academy Field Experiment in India
detail.abstract:
Computer-assisted learning (CAL) platforms frequently underperform at scale not because the technology is ineffective, but because schools face substantial implementation frictions: teachers and administrators must overcome initial technical hurdles, reorganize instructional routines, manage competing scheduling pressures, and do so while uncertain about the technology’s effectiveness—conditions that often lead to low and unproductive student engagement. This study explores whether strengthening implementation structure can raise both the quantity and quality of CAL usage in 83 residential government middle schools in Uttar Pradesh, India and, in turn, learning gains. All schools had access to Khan Academy, but randomly selected treatment schools received on-the-ground lab-in-charges whose sole responsibility was to ensure high-fidelity implementation by securing reliable connectivity, simplifying student rostering, protecting weekly practice time, supervising in-class use, coordinating content with teachers, and monitoring progress. The intervention increased platform usage from 7.2 to 47.4 minutes per week. Mathematics achievement rose by almost half a standard deviation over 31 weeks, with gains broad-based across achievement levels and question difficulty. These results show that the central constraint on effective and scalable CAL is not technology or content, but the presence of organizational structures that ensure sustained, productive instructional use.

title: The dynamic relationship between Anglo-American monetary policy and financial markets: Empirical evidence
affiliations: University of Birmingham and University of Birmingham

detail.title: The dynamic relationship between Anglo-American monetary policy and financial markets: Empirical evidence
detail.abstract: We employ a dynamic time-varying parameter vector autoregression (TVP-VAR) model to investigate the transmission channels and impacts of US monetary policy shocks, particularly through the effects of inflation, exchange rates, interest rates, and money supply on the global financial market, focusing on the UK as a highly interdependent financial partner. By analyzing data from the early 2000s to recent years, we examine whether the unprecedented monetary expansions following the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic have altered the global transmission mechanisms of US monetary policy and diminished its influence. Our findings clearly reveal asymmetric impacts on the UK financial market. In particular, we find that US expansionary policies often stimulate UK financial activity, while contractionary policies exert downward pressure. Our results also suggest that over the past two decades, the independence of the UK currency has gradually increased, and the UK’s foreign exchange and capital markets have responded more strongly to domestic monetary policy than the US. Overall, we contribute to understanding how macroeconomic policy changes affect financial markets over time, providing a framework for predicting the effects of future policy changes.

title: China-Tajikistan Economic Cooperation Plan a Geoeconomic Closed Door on the Belt and Road

detail.title: China-Tajikistan Economic Cooperation Plan a Geoeconomic Closed Door on the Belt and Road
detail.abstract: The bilateral China-Tajikistan Economic Cooperation Plan remains classified. It is an important document outlining the geoeconomic, geoindustrial, and trade relationship between China and Tajikistan. While the core agreement is classified, several surrounding documents are in the public domain. This article presents primary-source research from China's public administration side of the bilateral economic relationship focusing on Party-state policy, foreign policy, the Belt and Road and International Capacity Cooperation policies, and external industrial policy-arguing for a parallax viewing. It details some of the key areas of policy cooperation, demonstrates the spatial planning and public administrative architecture that Tajikistan is expected to dock with on the China side, and places China-Tajikistan foreign policy in relation to other regional economies in China's developing international relations hierarchy. The article is framed within China's International Capacity Cooperation outward FDI policy and details some key areas of industrial, science and technology and agroindustrial cooperation. It concludes that the geoindustrial policy deployed by China in Tajikistan and wider Central Asia is as yet malformed, but that a geoeconomic approach to future geoindustrial policy analysis is essential.

detail.abstract:
he Barina Money Mindset Framework (BMMF) is an evidence-
informed, non-clinical behavioural education model designed to
strengthen adult financial decision-making competence. The
framework integrates behavioural economics, adult development
theory, cognitive-behavioural principles, and awareness-based
practices to bridge the gap between financial knowledge and
consistent behavioural execution.
BMMF provides a structured pathway for improving decision-making
stability, reducing impulsive financial behaviour, strengthening
reflective evaluation, and supporting long-term behavioural change.
The model does not involve therapy, trauma processing, clinical
intervention, or psychological treatment. Instead, it establishes a clear
behavioural-education methodology with defined ethical boundaries
and instructional standards.
This paper outlines the conceptual foundations of BMMF, describes
its pedagogical architecture, explains the multi-level competency
structure, and presents the applied mechanisms through which
participants develop conscious, stable, and integrated financial
behaviours. The purpose of the paper is to articulate a
comprehensive conceptual model that can be reviewed, critiqued,
replicated, or extended by professionals in behavioural science, adult
learning, financial literacy, and applied psychology.

title: The Fight for Queer Black Dignity

detail.title: The Fight for Queer Black Dignity
detail.abstract: Bayard Rustin stated: 'When an individual is protesting society's refusal to acknowledge his dignity as a human being, his very act of protest confers dignity on him'. 1 As the quote suggests, dignity is often actively sought, and this is especially the case with black dignity, more specifically among black queer individuals like Rustin. Black individuals have frequently faced violence and degradation, and queer Black individuals have been disproportionately affected, particularly in Africa, where there is often a refusal to acknowledge their dignity. FannyAnn Eddy, a Sierra Leonian lesbian LGBTQ activist, was raped and stabbed, resulting in her death. 2 Almost twenty years later, Edwin Chiloba was murdered in Nairobi. 3 Millions of queer people are denied their rights, and a disproportionate number of them are black and brown individuals on a global scale. 4 This undignified reality is the reason for this research paper. The basis of this article lies in the challenges facing the LGBTQ community within Africa and the British Caribbean. It aims to provide a comprehensive picture of the indignities these communities face and how the legal concept of dignity is ingeniously used by courts to advance LGBT rights through judicial challenges.

title: Residential Relocation, and Commuting Distance under Hybrid Work in Paris and London
affiliations: Université de Bourgogne and PSB Paris School of Business

detail.title: Residential Relocation, and Commuting Distance under Hybrid Work in Paris and London
detail.abstract: SummaryHybrid work has raised concerns that telework may encourage residential decentralisation and longer commuting distances, with negative implications for transport demand and emissions. This study examines whether telework independently drives residential relocation and commuting expansion within metropolitan areas, or whether observed patterns reflect spatial selection. Using original 2023 survey data from Paris and London (N = 726), structural equation modelling jointly accounts for pre-pandemic residential location, workplace location, telework frequency, residential relocation, and commuting distance. Results show that telework frequency has no independent effect on residential distance to the CBD or commuting distance once initial spatial configurations are controlled for. Longer commutes among teleworkers reflect selection into telework rather than telework-induced sprawl. For policy, the findings suggest that hybrid work can reduce transport demand by lowering the frequency of long-distance commuting.

title: The Return Signal: A Method for Measuring Genuine Cognitive Integration Through Unprompted Re-Engagement

detail.title: The Return Signal: A Method for Measuring Genuine Cognitive Integration Through Unprompted Re-Engagement
detail.abstract: How can we tell if an idea has been learned rather than merely performed? Behavioral science has relied for a century on two flawed signals: immediate compliance (doing what is asked, when asked) and silence (no observable response). Immediate compliance reflects performance under observation-not genuine integration. Silence is uninterpretable because it can be produced by many distinct internal processes that standard methods cannot distinguish. This paper introduces the Return Signal, a measurable indicator of genuine cognitive integration: a delayed, voluntary, unprompted re-engagement with a concept or behavior in a naturalistic context. Unlike compliance or silence, the Return Signal provides unambiguous evidence that an idea has been internalized. We define the construct, provide operational criteria, specify an implementable protocol for identifying Return Signals in digital interaction environments, and outline the implications for measurement, intervention research, and theories of cognitive integration. The Return Signal corrects a foundational flaw in how behavioral change has been assessed and provides a practical method for detecting real learning in the wild.

title: Optimal Monetary and Fiscal Policy: Implications of Government Debt Portfolio Choice

detail.title: Optimal Monetary and Fiscal Policy: Implications of Government Debt Portfolio Choice
detail.abstract: This paper studies government debt portfolio choice in a Ramsey model with distortionary taxation and nominal rigidities. We show that there is a fundamental trade-off that governs optimal portfolio composition, a tradeoff between smoothing inflation and the output gap over time vs smoothing across states of the world. We find that risk alone can explain several key features of government debt maturity, including why governments issue both long-and short-term bonds, and the positive maturity-debt relation. We also estimate the model and quantify the welfare gains from optimal debt policy. Methodologically, we develop a tractable solution approach that characterizes both the steady state and the dynamics of optimal debt portfolios.

title: Time is Money: The Role of Reallocation Speed Under Capital Constraints

detail.title: Time is Money: The Role of Reallocation Speed Under Capital Constraints

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Austin Bennett is a Software Engineer on the Research team of Circle Internet Financial

detail.abstract: Capital-constrained businesses often decide between supporting additional blockchains or maintaining higher liquidity for their protocols across existing blockchains. This paper develops a general model to quantify how the speed and cost of cross-chain capital allocation affect capital efficiency gains. We introduce a conservative estimate for per-period gains that can be constructed with two inputs: the cost differential between reallocation options and the incremental revenue unlocked by faster allocation at potentially less capital. Under this model, businesses obtain capital efficiency gains when the value of newly accessible opportunities from faster cross-chain speeds outweighs the additional costs of reallocation.

title: Systemic Financial Risk in a Late-Cycle Global Monetary Regime
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Systemic Financial Risk in a Late-Cycle Global Monetary Regime
detail.abstract: Advanced economies are currently experiencing a late-cycle monetary environment characterized by monetary tightening, elevated public debt, and highly integrated financial markets. Although recent discussions of financial instability frequently emphasize isolated risk factors such as asset price cycles, leverage, or sovereign debt, these compartmentalized approaches may fail to capture the systemic interactions through which monetary conditions transmit across borders and balance sheets. This study introduces a global and symmetric monetary framework to examine systemic financial risk as a configurational outcome arising from interacting transmission channels, rather than as the result of independent vulnerabilities. The analysis draws on foundational concepts from monetary economics, financial cycle theory, and research on fiscal dominance, with a particular focus on credibility, expectations, and policy constraints. Empirically, the study employs a theory-guided, indicator-based methodology and structured case analysis across six domains: global interest-rate asymmetries, credit-financed asset price inflation, leverage concentration in corporate networks, real estate wealth effects, monetary policy credibility under fiscal and political constraints, and fiscal stress in integrated monetary systems. The findings indicate that systemic financial vulnerability increases nonlinearly when these channels interact under late-cycle conditions that limit monetary policy flexibility. Notably, this study does not attempt to forecast the timing of crises. Instead, it identifies structural configurations that elevate the probability and potential severity of systemic financial disruptions, thereby complementing formal debt sustainability and stress-testing frameworks.

title: Risk Selection Scenario for Decision Making in the Sustainable Climate Village Program in Jambi City
affiliations: , Universitas Andalas, Universitas Andalas, Universitas Andalas and Nurdin Hamzah University

detail.abstract: This study aims to develop a collaborative decision-making scenario to strengthen the sustainability of the Climate Village Program (Proklim) in Jambi City. The research was conducted through socio-demographic observations and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with five expert groups representing local governments, technical agencies, academics, civil society organizations, and farmer associations. The analysis was conducted using an Interpretive approach. Structural Modeling (ISM) to identify interrelationships between elements, determine hierarchical levels, and formulate alternative adaptive decision-making scenarios. The research results identified eight main elements: access to information, participation, actor roles, coordination, funding, regulation, monitoring, and risk management. All elements are in the linkage quadrant, indicating the system is interdependent and sensitive to change. The funding element occupies the position of the main driver, while coordination, regulation, monitoring, and risk management function as synergistic nodes that determine the effectiveness of the actor's role at the outcome layer. Based on this hierarchical structure, a decision-making scenario was developed that emphasizes the provision of sustainable funding, strengthening cross-sectoral coordination, and data-based monitoring as the basis for policy interventions. This scenario is expected to become a climate action roadmap that encourages inclusive, adaptive, and sustainable climate governance at the city level.

detail.abstract: This study examined the micro-level factors influencing the adoption and market viability of chickencow compost for sustainable household food production in urban and peri-urban backyard farms. By decoupling the goal into two broad aims, which involved identifying the household-level determinants of compost adoption and its influence on urban backyard food production dynamics and investigating the factors determining the willingness of cultivators to buy and pastoralists to supply chicken-cow compost, this research addressed four relevant research questions corresponding to four specific objectives. Employing an observational cross-sectional design, the methodology integrated Saunders’ Research Onion across three phases: Research Designs and Methods, Data Collection and Sampling Design, and Data Preparation and Modelling. With a mixed-method design, primary data were collected by five field assistants through a structured Urban Household Compost Survey (UHCS) questionnaire uploaded via Google Form and through direct observations. Using a stratified sampling technique and Cochran’s formula (𝑍∝ #$ = 1.96, p = 0.5, e = 0.07) for sample size determination, 400 participants comprising 200 backyard crop farmers and 200 pastoral farmers (150 poultry and 50 cattle farmers) in ten areas (5 municipal areas and 5 peri-urban areas) of Abuja were selected. Preliminary analysis involving Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) for variable reduction, preference matrices and descriptive statistics was conducted. Using R software, the study employs a multi-method quantitative analysis approach to estimate the objectives with Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) and Ordered Logistic Regression. By expectation, the findings of this study will provide evidence and policy insights for institutionalising a new product in homestead urban organic farming, consequently informing the firm-level or micromarket translation. This working paper outlines the conceptual framework and analysis plan, which contributes to sustainable agriculture discourses in developing settings.

title: The Folahan Mechanism: From Redistribution to Initial Distribution – Overcoming Fiscal and Policy Limits for Sustainable Equity

detail.title: The Folahan Mechanism: From Redistribution to Initial Distribution – Overcoming Fiscal and Policy Limits for Sustainable Equity
detail.abstract: The Folahan Mechanism: From Redistribution to Initial Distribution. This document presents the Folahan Mechanism, an innovative model designed to overcome the structural limitations in the fight against inequality and poverty. Classic redistribution is capped by fiscal, political, and administrative constraints, particularly the weak tax base in many countries. It fails to sustainably bridge the wealth gap. The Folahan enacts a paradigm shift, moving from redistribution (fixing retroactively) to initial distribution (building upstream). It integrates every individual into the value creation dynamic from the start and uses seigniorage as a distributive instrument. The Folahan thus transforms disposable income into active wealth, offering a scalable solution capable of self-financing economic equity, independent of public budget cycles. The objective is to demonstrate the model's effectiveness through pilot projects supported by the World Bank.

title: Financial markets, monetary transmission and psychological spreads: A theoretical monetary VAR-APS with empirical evidence from U.S
affiliations: University of Douala - Faculty of Economics and Applied Management

detail.title: Financial markets, monetary transmission and psychological spreads: A theoretical monetary VAR-APS with empirical evidence from U.S

keywords: monetary transmission and psychological spreads: A theoretical monetary VAR-APS with empirical evidence from U.S

detail.abstract: The transmission of monetary policy to financial markets remains plagued by four persistent puzzles : the price puzzle, the exchange rate disconnect, overshooting, and incomplete transmission. Despite methodological refinements, standard SVAR models fail to explain these anomalies, suggesting structural myopia. We propose the monetary VAR-APS model (Vector Autoregressive with anticipated psychological spreads), which micro-founds chartist expectations through APS. Our central theoretical contribution introduces a unifying analytical condition : the ratio between the speed of psychological forces Δ and the speed of fundamental reversion Δ* as the determinant of three transmission regimes. When fundamentals dominate (Δ < Δ*), transmission is normal. In the amplification regime (Δ ≈ Δ*), the monetary multiplier explodes, generating overshooting. In the inversion regime (Δ > Δ*), the multiplier changes sign, explaining the price puzzle or incomplete transmission. Empirically, using U.S. data (2000–2025), the SVAR-APS outperforms the standard SVAR in predictive accuracy, endogenously detecting an inversion regime during 2016–2019 of the incomplete transmission type for EURUSD quotations and of the price puzzle type for JPYUSD and CNYUSD quotations. Furthermore, it produces IRFs showing significant modulation of APS. Normatively, the optimal Taylor rule integrates technical thresholds.

title: Operationalizing Curiosity: A Non-Threatening Framework for Human Cognitive Engagement

detail.title: Operationalizing Curiosity: A Non-Threatening Framework for Human Cognitive Engagement
detail.abstract: Human beings respond to unfamiliar information in one of two directions: curiosity or threat. This is not a choice but a structural property of the nervous system. Most communication fails because it attempts persuasion—an act the brain interprets as threat. This paper formalizes an alternative: designing conditions under which the nervous system naturally shifts into curiosity mode, initiating voluntary investigation rather than defensive contraction. The framework is mechanistic, falsifiable, and applicable from education to diplomacy.

detail.abstract: This paper presents an applied behavioural-education model for developing financial decision-making competence in adults. The model is based on structured behavioural training, scenario practice, reflective analysis, and non-clinical emotional stabilisation methods adapted for adult learning environments. It outlines the methodological foundations, instructional principles, assessment structure, and behavioural mechanisms used to support the development of conscious, stable, and responsible financial behaviour. The framework prioritises behavioural awareness, decision-making clarity, and action consistency rather than financial advice or clinical emotional processing. It is designed for professional development contexts and adheres to strict non-clinical boundaries. The purpose of this paper is to articulate the applied methodology of financial decision-making education, bridging the gap between theoretical understanding and real-world behavioural execution.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence hyperscale deployments are driving unprecedented localized electricity demand, from 100-500 MW baseloads at the campus level to rack-level densities above 60-100 kW. This trajectory creates constraints not only in systemwide generation but also in localized power quality, thermal management, and reliability metrics that traditional grid extension and fossil baseload cannot sustainably meet. This paper examines the technical, operational, and governance implications of colocating microreactors with advanced AI compute facilities in cold-region, fully automated configurations. It assesses microreactor-microgrid integration for load buffering, fault isolation, and thermal efficiency, emphasizing remote supervisory control, segmentation of nuclear safety systems, and safeguards-compliant fuel-cycle stewardship. The analysis proposes a long-term architecture wherein baseload microreactors enable high-density, carbon-free AI compute without reliance on the expansion of fossildependent grid infrastructure. In turn, the resultant model underlines a structured pathway toward autonomy, safety, and regulatory adaptation, while preserving norms on nonproliferation and maintaining defensible standards of reliability for critical digital infrastructure.

title: Spatial Modeling of Air Pollution Exposure and Health Risk in Metropolitan Areas

detail.title: Spatial Modeling of Air Pollution Exposure and Health Risk in Metropolitan Areas
detail.abstract: Urban air pollution poses significant health risks, particularly in rapidly growing metropolitan areas. Understanding fine-scale spatial patterns of pollutants is essential for effective public health interventions and urban planning. This study aims to assess the distribution of air pollutants and associated health risks at high spatial resolution in major metropolitan regions. We combined high-resolution air quality monitoring with GIS-based spatial modeling and machine-learning approaches to predict pollutant concentrations across urban landscapes. Population exposure was quantified, and health risk assessments were conducted to identify vulnerable groups and potential environmental justice concerns. Our findings reveal distinct pollution hotspots, with elevated concentrations of particulate matter and nitrogen oxides near high-traffic zones and industrial areas. Vulnerable populations, including children, the elderly, and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, were disproportionately exposed to elevated pollutant levels. Statistical analyses show significant correlations between pollutant exposure and increased risks of respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes. These results highlight the critical need for targeted mitigation strategies, such as traffic management, urban green infrastructure, and localized pollution control measures. The integration of spatial modeling with health risk assessment provides actionable insights for policymakers and urban planners, enabling interventions that are both data-driven and equitable. This study demonstrates the value of combining high-resolution environmental data with predictive modeling to inform public health strategies and reduce the burden of urban air pollution.

detail.abstract: This paper outlines the ethical boundaries that define non-clinical behavioural education in the context of adult financial decisionmaking development. As behavioural training becomes more widely used in adult learning and professional development settings, clear distinctions between educational methodologies and clinical interventions are essential. This paper establishes the conceptual, ethical, and procedural boundaries necessary for safe and responsible delivery of non-clinical behavioural education. Drawing on adult learning theory, behavioural science, professional ethics, and non-clinical practice standards, the paper clarifies the limits of instructor responsibility, the appropriate handling of emotional content, referral pathways, and the necessary conditions for maintaining participant safety. The purpose of the paper is to articulate a comprehensive ethical framework that can guide practitioners delivering behavioural education programmes and ensure that the distinction between educational and clinical domains remains clear, consistent, and professionally grounded.

title: From Impossible Trinity to Stablecoin: A Resource-Capital-Information (RCI) Framework for Monetary Anchors
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: From Impossible Trinity to Stablecoin: A Resource-Capital-Information (RCI) Framework for Monetary Anchors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: nil
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: nil

detail.abstract: This study revisits the classic theory of the "impossible trinity" by extending its analytical logic from international monetary regimes to blockchain governance and stablecoin design. It develops the Resource-Capital-Information (RCI) framework, distinguishing between ideal anchors (R, C, I) and their degraded forms (r, c, i), and demonstrates how these anchors shape the stability, independence, and transparency of monetary institutions. Through historical cases-including the gold standard, Bretton Woods, Argentina's currency board, the euro, and SDRs-and contemporary cases such as USDT, USDC, DAI, Terra-LUNA, Bitcoin, and CBDCs, the study shows that single anchors offer strength but rigidity, composite anchors provide complementarity but amplify fragility in crises, and stablecoins embody a "three-anchor paradox": stable but not independent, independent but not transparent, transparent but not stable. To address these systemic dilemmas, the paper proposes the RCI triple-anchor model, which integrates resource scarcity, institutional independence, and informational transparency as complementary dimensions. This model not only clarifies the structural isomorphism of monetary and technological governance but also offers policy guidance for stablecoin regulation, CBDC design, and global monetary coordination. The RCI triple-anchor model offers a systemic pathway for stablecoin regulation, resilient CBDC design, and multipolar global monetary governance.

title: Credit Risk Evaluation of Small, Medium, and Micro-Enterprises Based on Recurrent Neural Networks
affiliations: University of the Punjab

detail.title: Credit Risk Evaluation of Small, Medium, and Micro-Enterprises Based on Recurrent Neural Networks
detail.abstract: Small, medium, and micro-enterprises (SMMEs) are vital to China's economy but face high credit risks due to limited assets and volatile revenues. This study proposes a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) model to assess SMME credit risk using time-series financial and operational indicators. Principal component analysis (PCA) refines indicators, followed by RNN training to predict risk levels (low, medium, high). Applied to 500 SMMEs' data (2019-2021), the model achieves 85.3% accuracy, outperforming logistic regression (78.6%). The approach captures sequential patterns, aiding banks in lending decisions. Limitations include data availability and computational demands. Results offer insights for policymakers and financial institutions.

detail.title: Anatomy of AI-Driven Socioeconomic Strain: Modeling the Nation-State as an Energy-Flow System (Part 1: United States)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author has no financial, personal or business interaction with any of the specific institutions and organizations that may have been mentioned.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Author has solely self-funded this paper.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces an energy-flow framework for analyzing the macroeconomic implications of rapid software-AI substitution in advanced economies. Conceptualizing the nation-state as a thermodynamic-like system—where physically grounded labor (CAT1) generates primary value, cognitive information-processing labor (CAT2) amplifies and converts it, and dependent populations (CAT3 + CAT4) represent expanding sinks—we model the contraction of operable economic surplus under converging technological, demographic, and fiscal pressures.

Using the United States as the initial case, detailed occupational demarcation and conservative assumptions about AI capability scaling (∼100× effective improvement in relevant tasks by the mid-2030s) yield baseline projections of substantial socioeconomic strain. The largest acceleration of timelines occurs when the replaceability ratio (REP%) exceeds 20%—a level even below the predicted rates of some major mainstream models such as CBO and McKinsey—while this paper's model calculates replaceability to approach 41%. Sensitivity analyses varying replacement intensity, immigration flows, deficit financing, and entitlement growth reveal material probabilistic risks of critical threshold crossings—defined by the Contraction Scale Metric (CSM) and Effective Burden Rate (EBR) approaching depletion—within a 12–36-year horizon. Traditional policy levers provide only marginal and transient mitigation.

The framework highlights structural vulnerabilities: as AI erodes the convertible labor layer at near-zero marginal cost, demographic aging and statutory commitments amplify surplus contraction.

This study establishes the methodological foundation for this analysis, with the U.S. serving as the initial case; subsequent papers in this series will extend the framework to all G20 nations, which face analogous converging demographic, fiscal, and technological pressures but with unique factors and influences.

title: Policy Learning for Payment Compliance: Out-of Time Evidence on the Value-and Limits-of ML Targeting at a Brazilian Water Utility
affiliations: Lehigh University, , Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information & Systems Management, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Management & Organization and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Policy Learning for Payment Compliance: Out-of Time Evidence on the Value-and Limits-of ML Targeting at a Brazilian Water Utility

declarations.ethicsApproval: Exempt status was granted by Lehigh University's IRB.

detail.abstract: Water utilities in emerging markets face a finance problem disguised as an operations problem: chronic late payments reduce cash flow, raise financing needs, and ultimately threaten service provision. We partner with a large Brazilian water and sewer utility and run a preregistered randomized controlled trial with approximately 160,000 customers to test behaviorally informed SMS reminders delivered one day before the bill due date. We compare four theory-based message frames-personal benefit (credit building), personal cost (credit harm), collective benefit (public good provision), and social norm (injunctive). In the first month, the credit-focused frames perform best on average, increasing on-time payment by about one percentage point relative to the utility's standard reminder (a 3.7% increase over a 27% baseline). We also find that responses vary with prior payment behavior. Customers with strong payment histories respond most to the credit-building appeal, while chronically delinquent customers respond more to collective and norm-based messages. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we train machine learning models on administrative billing data to target customers with one of the messages and experimentally evaluate the resulting decision policy in an out-of-time, on-policy holdout field test five months later. In this test, personalized messaging increases on-time payment by 2.4 percentage points relative to control, but we observe no statistically significant gain relative to the best-on-average message (2.1 percentage points). Together, the results show the value of behaviorally informed text messages and the limits of ML-based targeting for personalization.

title: Predicting Heatwave Vulnerability Using Spatial Analytics and Demographic Data

detail.title: Predicting Heatwave Vulnerability Using Spatial Analytics and Demographic Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare sole authorship of the article
declarations.ethicsApproval: I declare sole authorship of the article
declarations.funderStatement: I declare sole authorship of the article
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: I declare sole authorship of the article

detail.abstract: Heatwaves pose increasing risks to urban populations, particularly in the context of climate change and rapid urbanization. This study aims to predict heatwave vulnerability by integrating spatial analytics with demographic and socioeconomic data to identify populations and areas at greatest risk. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) were employed to map urban heat intensity and overlay demographic variables, including age, income, and population density. Statistical modeling techniques, including Geographically Weighted Principal Component Analysis (GWPCA) and multi-criteria analysis, were applied to quantify vulnerability scores across different neighborhoods. The findings reveal distinct geographic hotspots where high exposure intersects with socioeconomic disadvantage, highlighting communities with heightened susceptibility to heat-related hazards. Vulnerable populations, such as the elderly and low-income households, were disproportionately concentrated in these areas, suggesting systemic disparities in adaptive capacity. These results underscore the importance of targeted intervention strategies, such as heat-health early warning systems, urban greening initiatives, and resource allocation for emergency services. By providing spatially explicit vulnerability assessments, the study offers actionable insights for policymakers, urban planners, and public health officials to enhance resilience and prioritize at-risk communities in heatwave preparedness and response efforts. Overall, the integration of spatial and demographic analyses demonstrates a robust framework for anticipating climate-related risks and supports evidence-based decision-making for climate adaptation planning (D'Ambrosio et al., 2023; Bhattarai et al., 2024).

title: Expectation Setting with Machine Learning
affiliations: Complex Systems Research Group

detail.title: Expectation Setting with Machine Learning
detail.abstract: The formation of expectations lies at the heart of economic behaviour and hence agentbased modelling of that behaviour. Though many observations and relationships about which expectations are formed could be represented as functions, not all can be specified as such. In these cases, machine learning algorithms, specifically non-parametric nonlinear regressions known as neural networks, can help us model expectations with functional forms is are unknown, heterogenous, or untidy. We present two machine learning implementations of expectation settings. In the first, a firm form expectations about household demand, and in the second, a firm forms expectations about workers' effort responses to wages. The results are evaluated against the revealed relationships for heterogenous agents in both static and dynamic conditions.

title: Reducing Transport Externalities through Nudging: Results from a GPS-Tracked Experiment
affiliations: University of Basel, University of Basel, Swiss National Bank and

detail.title: Reducing Transport Externalities through Nudging: Results from a GPS-Tracked Experiment
detail.abstract: This study presents a randomized controlled trial in Switzerland to investigate the effects of a non-monetary intervention on transport choices. A GPS-based tracking app records the movements of 814 participants for several months, and automatically detects their travel modes. The treatment consists of sending personalized transport reports to a randomly selected subgroup. These reports contain personalized descriptive and prescriptive information on participants' transport-related external costs. The treatment reduces the climate-related external costs by 5.1% (p=0.05). We find that the treatment effects increase with age and the level of education, and that they decrease with income. Reports with positive prescriptive feedback were correlated with further reductions in external costs, whereas the opposite is true for negative feedback, thus suggesting a ``boomerang effect''. Based on participants' travel response and their willingness-to-pay for future reports, we compute average gross welfare gains of 3.09 Swiss francs per participant and report from a targeted intervention.

title: Oil & Gas Transactions in Nigeria: Navigating Compliance, Innovation and Continuity for National Development

detail.title: Oil & Gas Transactions in Nigeria: Navigating Compliance, Innovation and Continuity for National Development
detail.abstract: Nigeria’s oil and gas sector remains the cornerstone of the nation’s economy, contributing over 80% of export revenue and substantial government income in 2025. The Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) 2021, together with its implementing regulations and ongoing amendments, has created a modern regulatory framework that emphasizes transparency, local content, environmental responsibility, and commercial viability. While strict compliance requirements, evolving fiscal terms, and host-community obligations present real challenges, rapid innovation through initiatives such as digital field management, floating LNG, landmark domestic refining, and the rise of capable indigenous operators has begun to reverse years of production decline. Major asset divestments by international oil companies into Nigerian hands, combined with multibillion-dollar field development plans and improved security measures, signal a new phase of growth. This article examines the current legal and operational landscape, highlights practical pathways through the compliance maze, showcases transformative innovations, and identifies the critical steps needed to ensure long-term continuity. It concludes that disciplined adherence to the PIA, sustained technological adoption, and equitable benefit-sharing can convert Nigeria’s vast hydrocarbon resources into lasting national development.

title: Symbolic Representation, Moral Value Congruence, and Coproduction
affiliations: , University of Pittsburgh and Seattle University

detail.title: Symbolic Representation, Moral Value Congruence, and Coproduction
detail.abstract: Symbolic representation (SR) theory holds that the demographic makeup of public agencies can shape state-citizen interactions, yet empirical evidence on whether representation increases citizens' willingness to coproduce with government remains mixed. We argue that part of this ambiguity stems from under-specifying the interpretive process through which citizens draw inferences from representation when deciding whether to coproduce. We theorize that citizens interpret representation as a cue about an agency's underlying moral commitments, and that representation increases coproduction willingness in part by increasing perceived moral value congruence between citizen and agency, especially among marginalized groups. We test this account in the critical case of American policing. Our pre-registered survey experiment shows that racial representation increases both coproduction willingness and perceived moral value congruence among Black respondents, and that moral value congruence mediates roughly one-third of the SR effects. Counterintuitively, White respondents report lower willingness to coproduce under racial match, and White representation is not associated with perceived moral value congruence, although moral value congruence itself positively predict coproduction intentions. We contribute to the literature by specifying and testing a value-based mediation mechanism and by showing that its strength is conditional on group position. In doing so, we move SR theory toward a more process-oriented account of when and through what interpretive pathway SR shapes state-citizen interactions.

title: Beyond Financial Dominance: A Multi Ledger Architecture for Modern Organizational Performance

detail.title: Beyond Financial Dominance: A Multi Ledger Architecture for Modern Organizational Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not require ethics approval because it involved no human participants, identifiable data, or experimental procedures.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary organizations operate in environments characterized by complexity, interdependence, and rapid information flows, yet most continue to rely on accounting architectures developed for industrial-era production systems. Traditional financial accounting was designed to satisfy external reporting requirements and gradually evolved into an internal performance regime that favors financial indicators over other forms of organizational value. Research across management accounting, organizational behavior, and financialization demonstrates that this single-ledger architecture produces systematic distortions, including the concentration of decision rights, the marginalization of cross-functional expertise, and the underinvestment in capacity, learning, and long-term organizational health. These distortions are not isolated but structural, emerging predictably from the dominance of financial metrics in internal governance systems. 

This white paper introduces Integrated Value Architecture (IVA), a multi-ledger accounting and performance framework that addresses these structural limitations. IVA expands the accounting architecture to include five ledgers capturing financial performance, operational quality, organizational capacity, externalities and equity, and learning and innovation. The framework integrates these ledgers into a coherent performance system supported by a governance model that distributes interpretive authority across functions. IVA contributes to ongoing debates in accounting and governance by offering a structural mechanism for reducing financial dominance, improving decision quality, and aligning performance systems with traditional organizational demands. The framework provides leaders with a more comprehensive representation of value creation and supports the development of resilient, equitable, and strategically coherent organizations.

title: The Lender of Last Resort and Moral Hazard Reassessing the Legal Basis of Central Bank Liquidity Support
affiliations: University of Zurich - Rechtswissenschaftliches Institut (School of Law)

detail.title: The Lender of Last Resort and Moral Hazard Reassessing the Legal Basis of Central Bank Liquidity Support
detail.abstract: The modern formulation of the lender of last resort (LOLR) was coined by Walter Bagehot in 1873 in his work Lombard Street (Bagehot, 1873). Bagehot argued that one of the main functions of a central bank was to maintain financial stability during times of market distress by providing emergency liquidity assistance in the form of loans to solvent but illiquid banks that are no longer able to refinance their operations on the markets. To limit moral hazard, central bank lending should be at a penalty interest rate and based on good collateral. In the twentieth century, many central banks began to follow a policy of 'constructive ambiguity', which means that the LOLR would have the right to intervene in a crisis but will not promise in advance to do so. During the banking crisis of the 1980s and again during the global financial crisis (GFC) of 2007-2008, however, central bank lending to financial institutions was done at artificially low interest rates that did not reflect the credit risk of those institutions. These moves depart from the traditional principle established by Bagehot and mirror the strong interdependence between governments and central banks, on the one hand, and commercial banks, on the other. Following these crises, central banks have been following an alternative version of the LOLR principle in which lending to ailing institutions and markets would be automatically triggered if the values of bank and market assets suddenly dropped or became volatile. This paper analyzes what types of moral hazard these evolving central bank practices have created and the related legal framework and what this means for the "lender of last resort" principle and the credibility of central banks and governments.

title: Modelling the Fiscal Implications of Alternative Minimum Support Price (MSP) Policy Scenarios in Indian Agriculture
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University and  ICAR- National Institute of Biotic Stress Management

detail.title: Modelling the Fiscal Implications of Alternative Minimum Support Price (MSP) Policy Scenarios in Indian Agriculture
detail.abstract: The Minimum Support Price (MSP) policy is central to farm income stabilisation and food security in India, but extending assured procurement beyond paddy and wheat to all 23 notified crops raises significant fiscal and operational concerns.
