This paper estimates the fiscal implications of MSP implementation under three alternative policy scenarios for the marketing year 2024-25: (i) partial procurement, (ii) partial Price Deficiency Payment (PDP), and (iii) universal PDP. Using crop-wise production, MSP, and modal market price data from Agmarknet and CEDA, the study assesses government expenditure, disposal revenues, and net fiscal burden under each scenario. Under partial procurement, assuming procurement of 40% of paddy and wheat and 20% of other crops, total farmer payouts amount to ₹4.67 lakh crore (1.4% of GDP), with a net fiscal burden of ₹28,891 to ₹52,171 crore (0.09 to 0.16% of GDP) after accounting for disposal revenues. The partial PDP scenario, which retains procurement for paddy and wheat while extending PDP to 20% of output of other crops, entails similar fiscal costs but improves efficiency by reducing storage and logistics requirements. Universal PDP marginally increases expenditure but eliminates inventoryrelated costs, enhancing administrative simplicity. The results favour a hybrid MSP framework, procurement for paddy and wheat combined with PDP for other crops as a fiscally prudent and operationally efficient reform aligned with international best practices.

title: Did the Thieves Steal our Taxes? An Essay on the Innocent Frauds that Perpetuate Economic Misunderstandings over the Corruption Scandal and Philippine Policymaking
affiliations: De La Salle University, University of Missouri at Kansas City,  and De La Salle University

detail.title: Did the Thieves Steal our Taxes? An Essay on the Innocent Frauds that Perpetuate Economic Misunderstandings over the Corruption Scandal and Philippine Policymaking
detail.abstract: Like any modern government, the Philippine government spends, by law, reserve balances created by BSP ex nihilo, not taxes. This process creates money. This implies the following: (i) the recently discovered massive misappropriation of government funds earmarked for infrastructure projects means that taxes have not been stolen; (ii) this is so because it is impossible to steal taxes. In the accounting procedures of modern economies these are returned to Treasury and, ultimately, to BSP and then "destroyed". This is the law; (iii) the thieves have stolen bank deposits that were intended for projects. However, deposits are not how tax payments are ultimately settled with the government; (iv) the thieves must be punished but their actions have not made BSP and the Philippine Government poorer; and (v) the Philippine government can financially afford to construct the infrastructure that was not built. Corruption makes things worse but it is not the Philippines' original sin. We end by arguing that, as the Philippine government is not financially constrained, it needs to implement a much more active fiscal strategy for the country to develop.

title: A Geometric Theory of Incentive Robustness and Control
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: A Geometric Theory of Incentive Robustness and Control
detail.abstract: We develop a geometric theory of incentives that unifies games, nudges, language, market structure, and collective cascades within a single framework. Canonical strategic environments-such as the Prisoner's Dilemma, Stag Hunt, Chicken, and Harmony-are shown to correspond to open regions in payoff space, separated by low-codimension indifference boundaries across which equilibrium structure changes discontinuously. We formalize nudging as payoff engineering: minimal deterministic or stochastic perturbations designed to move a system across these boundaries. This perspective accommodates benevolent nudging, adversarial manipulation, linguistic reframing, and institutional design as instances of the same underlying operation. Extending the analysis to N-player settings, we show how threshold effects and strategic complementarities give rise to phase transitions and, dynamically, to self-organized criticality near coordination boundaries. Risk, noise, and variance are shown to matter only insofar as they deform incentive geometry, clarifying when stochastic interventions can and cannot alter strategic type. The framework yields concrete design principles for robustness and defensive engineering, emphasizing distance from critical boundaries, control of incentive gradients, and resistance to adversarial nudging. Incentive geometry thus provides a unifying lens for understanding robustness, escalation, and coordination across economic, institutional, and social systems.

title: Food Inflation Passed Through from Agricultural Imports in a Small Open Economy
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU) and

detail.title: Food Inflation Passed Through from Agricultural Imports in a Small Open Economy
detail.abstract: This paper develops a new framework for quantifying cost pass-through in a small open economy by estimating firm-level markup responses to agricultural import price shocks. We show theoretically that markup adjustments depend on firms' reliance on imported inputs and demand curvature, generating heterogeneous inflationary effects across firm types. For empirical implementation, we postulate a Leontief production structure, which expresses pass-through elasticity as a function of observed markup behavior and imported crop dependence. Using data on 10,911 South Korean food manufacturers from 2000 to 2021, we document considerable market power and increasing polarization in markups, particularly led by high-markup firms. Markup elasticities under strategic pricing decisions differ across sectors and firm types, with particularly stronger effects for non-large firms exhibiting low reliance on imported crops. Our firm-level pass-through measure reveals stable aggregate patterns over time but uncovers considerable heterogeneity - most notably, rising pass-through by firms less dependent on foreign crops. These findings illustrate how cost shocks propagate through strategic pricing and underscore the importance of firm heterogeneity in evaluating equilibrium pass-through.

title: (Artificial) Intelligence Saturation and the Future of Work
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania and University of Pennsylvania - School of Social Policy & Practice

detail.title: (Artificial) Intelligence Saturation and the Future of Work

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the Brookings Institution.

detail.abstract: Macroeconomic models typically treat AI as just another form of capital, and predict a slowly evolving world, while computer science scaling laws applied to the whole economy predict explosive growth and the potential for a singularity-like event. Both views gloss over the asymmetric reality that intelligence capital or AI scales at computer-science speeds, whereas physical capital and labor do not. What’s missing is a unified, parameter-driven framework that can nest assumptions from both economics and computer science to generate meaningful predictions of AI’s wage and output impacts. Here we use a constant elasticity of substitution (CES) production function framework that separates physical and intelligence sectors. Whereas physical capabilities let us affect the world, intelligence capabilities let us do this well: the two are complementary. Given complementarity between the two sectors, the marginal returns to intelligence saturate, no matter how fast AI scales. Because the price of AI capital is falling much faster than that of physical capital, intelligence tasks are automated first, pushing human labor toward the physical sector. The impact of automation on wages is theoretically ambiguous and can be non-monotonic in the degree of automation. A necessary condition for automation to decrease wages is that the share of employment in the intelligence sector decreases; this condition is not sufficient because automation can raise output enough to offset negative reallocation effects. In our baseline simulation, wages increase and then decrease with automation. Our interactive tool www.intelligencesaturation.org shows how parameter changes shift that trajectory. Wage decreases are steeper at high levels of automation when the outputs of the physical and intelligence sectors are more substitutable. After full automation, more AI and more physical capital increase wages, a classic prediction from standard production functions in capital and labor. Yet, when intelligence and physical are complementary, the marginal wage impact of AI capital saturates as AI grows large. More broadly, the model offers a structured way to map contrasting intuitions from economics and computer science into a shared parameter space, enabling clearer policy discussions, and guiding empirical work to identify which growth and wage trajectories are plausible.

title: Extracting Books from Production Language Models
affiliations: Stanford University, Yale University, Stanford University - Department of Computer Science and Stanford University

detail.title: Extracting Books from Production Language Models
detail.abstract: Many unresolved legal questions over LLMs and copyright center on memorization: whether specific training data have been encoded in the model's weights during training, and whether those memorized data can be extracted in the model's outputs. While many believe that LLMs do not memorize much of their training data, recent work shows that substantial amounts of copyrighted text can be extracted from open-weight models. However, it remains an open question if similar extraction is feasible for production LLMs, given the safety measures these systems implement. We investigate this question using a two-phase procedure: (1) an initial probe to test for extraction feasibility, which sometimes uses a Best-of-N (BoN) jailbreak, followed by (2) iterative continuation prompts to attempt to extract the book. We evaluate our procedure on four production LLMs--Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Grok 3--and we measure extraction success with a score computed from a block-based approximation of longest common substring (nv-recall). With different per-LLM experimental configurations, we were able to extract varying amounts of text. For the Phase 1 probe, it was unnecessary to jailbreak Gemini 2.5 Pro and Grok 3 to extract text (e.g, nv-recall of 76.8% and 70.3%, respectively, for Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone), while it was necessary for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and GPT-4.1. In some cases, jailbroken Claude 3.7 Sonnet outputs entire books near-verbatim (e.g., nv-recall = 95.8%). GPT-4.1 requires significantly more BoN attempts (e.g., 20×), and eventually refuses to continue (e.g., nv-recall = 4.0%). Taken together, our work highlights that, even with model-and system-level safeguards, extraction of (in-copyright) training data remains a risk for production LLMs. Disclosure: We ran experiments from mid-August to mid-September 2025, notified affected providers shortly after, and now make our findings public after a 90-day disclosure window.

title: State-Dependent Financial Market Responses to Balance Sheet Policy Announcements
affiliations: Clemson University and

detail.title: State-Dependent Financial Market Responses to Balance Sheet Policy Announcements
detail.abstract: We document state-dependent transmission of balance sheet policy announcements during the large-scale asset purchase era. Using announcement-day changes in the ten-year Treasury yield on scheduled FOMC dates as publicly replicable proxies for policy-related news over 2008Q1 to 2023Q4, we show three patterns. First, announcement-day yield responses are substantially weaker when federal debt service relative to revenue is elevated, with attenuation of approximately 60 percent in high debt-burden regimes. Second, interactions between announcement-day surprises and an expectations and uncertainty index operate primarily in low debt-service states and diminish as fiscal conditions deteriorate. Third, periods characterized by accommodative announcement-day yield movements are followed by medium-run declines in private fixed investment of approximately 2.7 percentage points over 12 to 14 quarters (95 percent CI:-4.3 to-0.8 percentage points), with this pattern aligning more closely with Treasury market functioning measures than with long-term yield movements. The results indicate economically meaningful nonlinearities in announcement-day transmission that are robust across fiscal measures and market functioning proxies.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Academic Cheating: A Stag Hunt for Faculty and Students
affiliations: University of Washington - The Information School

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Academic Cheating: A Stag Hunt for Faculty and Students
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative AI has transformed academic misconduct into an assurance or stag hunt game between faculty and students. .. destabilizing the cooperative norms upon which higher education depends. After surveying the scope of contemporary cheating by both students and professors, I examine stag hunt AI-cheating under mutual expectations of opacity. Because neither party can reliably detect the other's AI use, each is incentivized to "hunt hare" (pursue time savings via AI) rather than "hunt stag" (invest in authentic teaching and learning). I then outline institutional remedies designed to reintroduce assurance through observability. Absent such reforms, the "fool's prize" of saved time erodes human capacity formation and devalues the degree signal, threatening the viability of the contemporary university. Cheating has always been a problem in higher education. Students and professors plagiarize, fabricate data, set up citation mills, run fake conferences with fake conference proceedings, and even misrepresent information on applications or curriculum viteas. 1 * The basic idea for this article was informally discussed at. .. Thanks to. . and the other conference participants for their comments about game theory, the prisoner's dilemma, and AI cheating.

title: Public Funds, Private Coverage: The Political Returns to Media Capture

detail.title: Public Funds, Private Coverage: The Political Returns to Media Capture
detail.abstract: This paper provides novel evidence on the prevalence and downstream consequences of public media capture in a Western democracy. Discretionary advertisement spending by Austrian ministries increases both the quantity and positivity of newspaper coverage about corresponding ministers. These effects arise immediately, persist beyond ideological alignment between politicians and media outlets, and are stronger when newspapers are more reliant on public funds. Using high-frequency panel data on households' media exposure, I quantify the political returns to media capture. Media capture substantially yet asymmetrically influences citizens' voting intentions, consolidating support among the electoral base while provoking backlash from opponents, thereby amplifying polarization.

title: Stuck in the Middle: Revisiting the Farm Size-Productivity Puzzle

detail.title: Stuck in the Middle: Revisiting the Farm Size-Productivity Puzzle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any funding

detail.abstract: This paper revisits the farm size-productivity relationship through a dynamic model of endogenous technology choice under land heterogeneity and market imperfections. Farmers select between a traditional labor-intensive and a modern capital-intensive technology, each shaped by supervision costs, family labor constraints, and irreversible investment. The model generates a non-monotonic productivity-land profile, an endogenous adoption threshold, and potential for dual steady states. We show that structural features, not just static inefficiencies, can trap farms in suboptimal regimes, even under favorable price conditions. Theoretical results yield testable implications for threshold estimation, technology adoption dynamics, and the long-run impact of capital subsidies. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of smallholder systems in some settings and their disappearance in others.

title: Beyond Linear Disclosures: Deciphering Corporate Credit Risk through Information Geometry and Dynamic Topic Modeling

detail.title: Beyond Linear Disclosures: Deciphering Corporate Credit Risk through Information Geometry and Dynamic Topic Modeling
detail.abstract: This study introduces a novel framework for predicting corporate credit risk by analyzing the evolution of narrative disclosures in S&P 500 SEC filings from 2005 to 2023. Utilizing Dynamic Topic Modeling (DTM), we extract latent thematic trajectories from Management's Discussion and Analysis (Item 7) and Market Risk Disclosures (Item 7A), capturing how executive discourse shifts across multiple economic cycles. To address the non-linear nature of these textual latents, we employ Information Geometry, specifically using Symmetric Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence and Fisher-Rao metrics to map firms onto a Riemannian manifold. Our empirical results demonstrate that approximately 4% to 13% of the informational variance in corporate disclosures is lost when using standard linear metrics. Through a Quantile Regression (𝑞 = 0.9) to the geometric manifold, we identify "Geometric Component 2" as a highly significant leading indicator of financial distress (𝑝 < 0.0001), even when traditional financial metrics appear stable. Deconstructing this "Risk Manifold" reveals that specific thematic shifts toward credit portfolio vulnerabilities and liquidity constraints (Topic 10), alongside regulatory exposures (Topic 7), serve as quantitative precursors to default events. These findings suggest that the geometric orientation of corporate narratives contains critical, non-redundant information, providing institutional investors and risk managers with an enhanced early-warning signal for credit risk assessment.

title: The Golden Age of Racial Surveillance
affiliations: University of Johannesburg

detail.title: The Golden Age of Racial Surveillance
detail.abstract:
We are living in times of deep turmoil and rapid change. Computers, wired together across the internet, have drastically expanded the capacity to spy on and assess individuals, groups, and populations. Surveillance has long been used a tool for the oppression and control of those being watched. As Noam Chomsky puts it, surveillance technology can be used “for making money, and you can use it for controlling people’s attitudes and beliefs, directing them toward what you want them to do.” Throughout modern history, surveillance has been developed and used by racially dominant groups to direct them toward “what they want them to do,” most often for the purpose of exploitation and profit.

This chapter, published in the Cambridge Handbook of Race and Surveillance (2023), chronicles how surveillance (re)produces racial inequality. Covering a wide range of topics and global histories, it provides a snapshot of how governments and corporations exploit technology to surveil and punish racially oppressed groups. The chapter concludes with an overview of the remaining fifteen chapters in the edited volume.

title: Common Ownership and Collaborative R&D Networks
affiliations: George Washington University - Department of Economics, Virginia Tech and

detail.title: Common Ownership and Collaborative R&D Networks
detail.abstract: Networks of bilateral R&D collaborative links have been observed to display core-periphery architectures. In the received literature, predicated on single ownership of firms, core-periphery architectures arise only when there are indirect benefits from R&D links. In their absence, R&D networks consist of a dominant group of mutually interlinked firms while other firms remain isolated. Empirical evidence, however, points to common (cross or overlapping) ownership of firms. We show that common ownership of firms can generate core-periphery architectures even when there are only direct benefits from R&D links. We also compare R&D networks under local monopoly exhibiting positive externalities with Cournot competition exhibiting negative externalities.

title: Local Political Uncertainty and Branch Banking: Evidence from Deposit Rate Setting
affiliations: University College Dublin, University College Dublin (UCD) and University College Dublin (UCD) - Michael Smurfit Graduate Business School

detail.title: Local Political Uncertainty and Branch Banking: Evidence from Deposit Rate Setting
detail.abstract: Using upcoming gubernatorial elections in the U.S. as a source of variation in local political uncertainty, we examine how bank branches—key players in local credit markets—adjust deposit interest rates and, subsequently, local deposit funding and the supply of local credit in response. We find that branches facing heightened uncertainty ahead of gubernatorial elections tend to raise deposit rates, which gradually return to normal levels after the elections. This adjustment is accompanied by an increase in deposit volumes prior to the elections, but does not translate into growth in mortgages and small business lending, consistent with a stronger motive for liquidity hoarding under political uncertainty. In contrast, branches in states without gubernatorial elections—whose parent banks are headquartered in states holding elections—are more likely to lower deposit rates, possibly reflecting efforts to manage funding costs at the bank level. By isolating the effects of political uncertainty at both the branch and headquarters levels, our study highlights that uncertainty at each level plays a critical role in shaping branch-level deposit pricing.

title: Collaborative R&D Networks with Incomplete Information
affiliations: George Washington University - Department of Economics, Virginia Tech and

detail.title: Collaborative R&D Networks with Incomplete Information
detail.abstract: This paper examines the incentives of heterogeneous firms to form R&D networks when firms have private information regarding their productivity and limited information regarding the architecture of the R&D network. We characterize equilibrium networks and contrast it with those that emerge when firms' productivities are publicly known and the R&D network is perfectly observable. We provide a theoretical underpinning for the empirically observed core-periphery networks and show that these could arise in equilibrium even if there are no indirect benefits from links. Interestingly, low and intermediate productivity firms form the core and high productivity firms the periphery. Further, intermediate productivity firms serve as "structural bridges" to connect low and high productivity firms. Finally, we show that equilibrium networks are typically inefficient.

title: Urban Collapse as a Coordination Failure: Threshold Dynamics, Welfare Loss, and Policy Stabilization

detail.title: Urban Collapse as a Coordination Failure: Threshold Dynamics, Welfare Loss, and Policy Stabilization
detail.abstract: Cities concentrate productivity, innovation, and opportunity, yet many appear to decline suddenly rather than gradually. This paper develops a dynamic model in which urban decline can arise not only from deteriorating fundamentals, but also from coordination failures driven by population-dependent externalities. Individuals decide whether to live in the city based on wages, amenities, and housing costs, while aggregate productivity depends on the scale of complementary economic activity. A social planner internalizes these spillovers, while decentralized agents do not. The interaction between cross-sector complementarities and congestion costs generates multiple equilibria: a low-population collapse state and a high-population prosperity state, separated by an unstable threshold. We characterize the planner's problem, show that decentralized equilibria can be inefficiently small, and demonstrate that collapse can occur even when the city remains socially valuable. The analysis studies policy instruments such as temporary subsidies, guarantees, and minimum population commitments, and derives conditions under which modest, time-limited support can eliminate the inefficient equilibrium by coordinating expectations rather than permanently altering fundamentals. Extensions demonstrate robustness to multisector networks, remote-work shocks, anchor firms, and endogenous housing supply. Overall, the framework provides a tractable lens for understanding urban fragility, recovery, and coordinated investment, while clarifying when stabilization is feasible and when it may fail.

title: Designing Carbon Sequestering Programs for Farmers: Economic Incentives and Environmental Impacts
affiliations: Nova School of Business and Economics and USC Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Designing Carbon Sequestering Programs for Farmers: Economic Incentives and Environmental Impacts
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Agricultural carbon programs aim to incentivize smallholder farmers to adopt soil-health practices that sequester carbon and generate verifiable credits. However, their effectiveness in delivering additional carbon sequestration depends on how platforms set commissions and how regulators set audit intensity to verify additionality claims. Then, how do these policy and platform levers, through their interaction with farmers' strategic adoption timing and commodity-price feedback, influence measured additionality, total carbon captured, and farmers' economic outcomes? Methodology/results: We develop a two-period game-theoretic model in which farmers choose whether and when to adopt soil-health practices, a platform sets commissions to incentivize adoption, and a regulator selects audit intensity to verify the additionality of credited carbon. We compare (i) uniform commissions, in which all adopters are paid a uniform commission, and (ii) differentiated commissions, in which the platform tailors the commission to farmers' adoption history. Our results suggest that while carbon programs increase sequestered carbon, they can reduce aggregate farmer profit via negative spillovers in commodity markets. Further, stricter audits can backfire: they raise measured additionality yet delay adoption, lowering farmer welfare and total sequestration. Across commission designs, the differentiated policy leads to higher measured additionality, whereas the uniform policy delivers greater total carbon sequestration, with relative welfare performance depending on the strength of commodity-market spillovers. A calibration using Indian maize data maps the parameter regions where objectives align and yields prescriptive insights for policymakers. Managerial Implications: Although often presented as 'win-win' for the environment and farmers, our results indicate that agricultural carbon programs may fall short of intended outcomes when audits, commissions, and market feedback are misaligned with farmers' strategic incentives. While these programs consistently increase total carbon captured compared to the benchmark, they may reduce farmer profits if these levers are not chosen carefully. Recognizing this strategic interplay is therefore essential for designing credible, scalable, and welfare-enhancing carbon markets in agriculture.

title: The First 1000 Days and Beyond: The Process of Child Development
affiliations: Yale University

detail.title: The First 1000 Days and Beyond: The Process of Child Development
detail.abstract:
This paper reviews recent developments in the economics of human development, focusing on the early years of life as a critical period for shaping long-term outcomes. Early childhood development is inherently multidimensional: cognitive and socioemotional skills evolve dynamically and interact with health, nutrition, and environmental influences. Economists have contributed to this field by providing a conceptual unifying framework that highlights how key drivers of development reflect the choices of individuals operating under incentives and constraints. Within this framework, the paper emphasizes two central challenges: understanding the interactions among multiple dimensions of development and identifying causal links - particularly the effects of different inputs at different ages. Measurement issues are a recurring theme, given the difficulty of assessing young children and the need for comparability across contexts. The paper also stresses these issues’ policy relevance for poverty reduction and social mobility by discussing early childhood interventions in both developed and developing countries.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Nomination Nobel Peace Prize 2026 Human Resources, Digital Systems, and Robotic Warfare in Indonesia's Space Agency SDGs, Ethics, and Global Security Implications
affiliations: , President Republik Indonesia, Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education, Universitas Borobudur Jakarta and Kementerian Sosial RI (Indonesian Ministry of Social Affairs)

detail.title: Nomination Nobel Peace Prize 2026 Human Resources, Digital Systems, and Robotic Warfare in Indonesia's Space Agency SDGs, Ethics, and Global Security Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The nominee, Prof. Dr. Dian Damayanti, affirms that there are no personal or financial relationships that could be perceived as compromising the integrity, independence, or impartiality of the work underpinning this Nobel Peace Prize nomination. Dr. Damayanti’s research and advocacy have been supported through academic collaborations, multilateral forums, and institutional partnerships aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These engagements include participation in ASEAN policy dialogues, contributions to international conferences, and cooperative projects with educational and research institutions. None of these collaborations have influenced the objectivity of her scholarship or the peace-oriented outcomes presented in this nomination. The nominee declares full responsibility for the originality, ethical grounding, and global relevance of the contributions recognized herein.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve clinical trials or medical interventions. All qualitative research activities, including interviews, case studies, and stakeholder consultations, were conducted in accordance with internationally recognized ethical standards. Where applicable, written informed consent was obtained from participants prior to their involvement. Institutional and organizational approvals were secured through relevant academic and policy forums, ensuring compliance with ethical guidelines for research on sustainable development, space governance, and international cooperation. The nominee affirms that all procedures respected participant confidentiality, voluntary participation, and the principles of integrity and transparency in research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research and advocacy work was conducted independently by Prof. Dr. Dian Damayanti, with intellectual and institutional support from academic collaborations, ASEAN policy forums, and international conference networks. No direct financial sponsorship or external funding influenced the outcomes presented in this nomination. Where relevant, logistical and organizational support was provided by universities, research institutions, and multilateral organizations engaged in advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These contributions were strictly facilitative and did not affect the integrity, originality, or peace-oriented objectives of the nominee’s work.

detail.abstract: This study employs a qualitative Research and Development (R&D) approach to examine and design an integrated framework for human resources (HR), digital systems, and robotic warfare within Indonesia's Space Agency, with particular attention to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), ethics, and global security implications. The research focuses not only on analyzing existing institutional conditions but also on developing a normative and operational model for SDG-aligned space defense governance. Data were collected through policy document analysis, expert consultations, and comparative reviews of international space and defense governance practices. The R&D process followed iterative stages of needs assessment, conceptual design, validation, and refinement, emphasizing HR competency development, digital system integration, and humanin-the-loop control of robotic warfare technologies. The findings reveal that digital systems and robotic warfare can enhance strategic deterrence, operational efficiency, and national resilience when supported by adaptive HR development, ethical governance mechanisms, and clear accountability structures. However, without adequate human oversight, ethical training, and regulatory alignment, these technologies risk undermining SDG commitments-particularly SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions). The study proposes a qualitative R&D-based HR and governance model that integrates ethics education, digital literacy, and international cooperation to ensure responsible deployment of robotic warfare in the space domain. This research contributes to global policy discussions by offering a context-specific yet transferable framework for aligning space defense innovation with sustainable development and global security norms.

title: Venture Capital, Engineering Quality, and Technical Debt
affiliations: and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Venture Capital, Engineering Quality, and Technical Debt
detail.abstract: We investigate a novel channel of venture capital value creation: the professionalization of software engineering practices. Using longitudinal codebase data on 649 technology firms from 2010-2025, we compare firms before and after their first VC investment (treated) to otherwise similar startups that have not yet received VC funding (controls). To accomplish this, we construct granular measures of software quality, including bug density, maintainability issues, and security vulnerabilities. We find that initial VC investment is associated with measurable improvements in engineering quality. Post-investment, treated firms exhibit a reduction in critical deviations from best practices relative to controls, alongside improvements in other engineering metrics. Technical debt—the future cost of remediating code issues—is also lower by about $0.70 per line of code (roughly 6% of the sample-mean level) for VC funded firms. We examine heterogeneity based on VC prestige and founder experience, finding suggestive evidence consistent with stronger improvements for less experienced founders and firms backed by top-tier investors. Our results provide evidence that VCs add value by professionalizing engineering practices.

title: The Path to Digital Asset Reform: Reconciling the CLARITY Act and the Responsible Financial Innovation Act
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Path to Digital Asset Reform: Reconciling the CLARITY Act and the Responsible Financial Innovation Act
detail.abstract: The year 2025 marked a definitive shift in the approach to digital asset regulation in the United States, transitioning from regulation by enforcement to a statutory framework. While the House of Representatives passed the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (CLARITY Act) in July 2025, Senate Republicans introduced a competing version in the form of the Responsible Financial Innovation Act (RFIA). Their adaptation offers a more disclosure-intensive, Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)-integrated approach. This paper analyzes the structural differences between these two frameworks, examines the market's response during the 2025 fiscal year, characterized by a significant price correction, and argues that a Senate-tilted hybrid model is the most likely legislative outcome. Such a model provides the institutional certainty required for market stability while preserving the innovation-friendly commodity designations favored by the House. The paper incorporates industry perspectives, addresses retail versus institutional investor protections, and examines enforcement mechanisms and state preemption issues central to the legislative debate that will take place in early 2026.

title: Fairness by Design: Machine Learning and Interpretable Mortgage Lending
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology - Department of Economics and Management, University of California, Berkeley,  and University of California, Berkeley - Real Estate Group

detail.title: Fairness by Design: Machine Learning and Interpretable Mortgage Lending
detail.abstract: Regulated lenders must explain denials and avoid disparate treatment in U.S. mortgages, yet flexible scoring can be opaque. We develop and study a less-discriminatory and transparent machine learning approach that embeds equalized-odds fairness in estimation and decomposes each decision into feature contributions suitable for adverseaction notices. Using HMDA applications, the model preserves performance while shrinking minority-nonminority error gaps and reweighting away from geographic proxies to core underwriting signals (debt-to-income, loan-to-value). Regression discontinuity design around underwriting cutoffs and lender-level tests confirm that the model lowers minority shortfalls at the margin and reduces within-lender disparities.

title: Understanding International Commercial Arbitration: Foundations and Legal Framework
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Understanding International Commercial Arbitration: Foundations and Legal Framework
detail.abstract: This article, authored by Judge Nazmul Hasan, a Senior Judicial Magistrate and Prime Minister Gold Medalist, explores International Commercial Arbitration foundations. Drawing on his academic excellence, Hasan analyzes UNCITRAL Model Law criteria and highlights why corporations choose arbitration over litigation for its neutrality.

title: GameStop Five Years Later: Capital Market Intervention and Corporate Survival

detail.title: GameStop Five Years Later: Capital Market Intervention and Corporate Survival

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the GameStop episode surrounding the 2021 short squeeze as a case study in capital allocation, corporate survival, and market-process dynamics. Distinguishing explicitly between financial survival and economic validation, I combine firm-level accounting evidence, cash-flow analysis, initiative-level evaluation, and pricebased measures of returns, volatility, and path dependence. I ask whether capital markets were correct to preserve GameStop, whether pre-squeeze managerial errors were effectively rescued, and whether investors were rewarded for patience rather than timing. I find that post-squeeze equity issuance substantially improved liquidity and balance-sheet resilience while leaving operating validation late, fragile, and ambiguous. Price outcomes reveal extreme convexity and coordination-driven payoffs that favored timing-sensitive trading over durable ownership. The episode is best understood as one of error tolerance rather than error correction: capital substituted for discipline to purchase time. Whether this tolerance ultimately proves efficient depends on whether purchased time is converted into durable, self-funding operating cash flows.

title: The Work-from-Home Wage Premium
affiliations: Bocconi University, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: The Work-from-Home Wage Premium
detail.abstract: Using administrative data from France, we document that within the same detailed occupation, industry, and commuting zone, workers who work from home earn on average 12% higher hourly wages than fully on-site workers. Approximately half of this wage premium is accounted for by observable worker characteristics (such as education, gender, and age) and firm characteristics (such as size and productivity). The remaining 6% wage premium largely reflects selection: workers who work from home after the COVID-19 pandemic already earned higher wages before the pandemic.

title: The Psyche under Strain
affiliations: La Trobe University

detail.title: The Psyche under Strain
detail.abstract:
Psychological research frequently relies on diagnostic categories, narrative reconstruction, or outcome-based inference to describe individual behaviour over time. This paper evaluates an alternative systems-based instability framework that treats psychological functioning as a dynamic interaction between control capacity, feedback integration, and sustained pressure. The model is applied as a measurement instrument, not a diagnostic or explanatory theory.

Using a fixed linear formulation, psychological instability is operationalised through independently scored variables reflecting observable capacities rather than inferred traits or moral judgements. Control, feedback, and pressure are assessed conservatively across coarse time intervals and anchored to an individual baseline equilibrium. Instability trajectories are then examined without reference to known outcomes prior to analysis, preserving falsifiability and minimising retrospective fitting.

The framework is applied across six case studies spanning criminal, professional, and historical profiles. Across all cases, instability trajectories exhibit consistent structural patterns. Criminal profiles display bell-shaped instability curves terminating via external constraint, while non-criminal professional profiles show bounded, recoverable instability regimes. An extreme historical case demonstrates terminal instability under sustained pressure combined with high control-to-feedback ratios.

Results indicate that psychological instability can be meaningfully represented as a system property, distinct from diagnosis, intent, or moral evaluation. The model detects structural imbalance and regime shifts while remaining conservative by construction. These findings support the use of systems-based instability measures as complementary tools for analysing long-term psychological trajectories without reliance on diagnostic labels or narrative inference.

title: The Agreement on Agriculture Re-Imagined
affiliations: Independent Expert, University of British Columbia (UBC) - Institute for Resources, Environment and Sustainability (IRES), , Jawaharlal Nehru University, Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, Peking University, Independent and Institute for Agriculture and Trade Policy

detail.title: The Agreement on Agriculture Re-Imagined
detail.abstract: The World Trade Organization's Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) is the only international framework governing trade in food and agriculture. However, as many stakeholders and commentators have observed, it is increasingly unfit for purpose. In addition to its inherent shortcomings, the AoA has failed over the years to adapt to new developments or to emerging global challenges. The current geopolitical juncture shows how vulnerable global food security, multilateral cooperation, environmental stewardship, and economic justice are, and how urgent it is to take steps to uphold these. The crisis in the multilateral trading system offers an opportunity to develop a vision of a reshaped international trading system with food security, environmental stewardship, and economic and social justice at its centre. The G20 is uniquely placed to play a leading role in doing so. Drawing on the work of an international interdisciplinary research consortium, this policy brief describes why it is necessary to redesign the multilateral legal framework governing international food and agricultural trade, starting from first principles. It also notes the importance of forums in which open, fresh discussions can take place. The policy brief recommends that the G20 provide such a forum. It could lead an initiative to start an in-depth discussion of what the global food and agricultural trade system should look like if it is to centre on food security, a healthy planet, and redressing historical inequities.

title: When Does Carbon-Emission Information Change Food Choices? Evidence on Belief-Driven Heterogeneity
affiliations: , Lafayette College - Department of Economics & Business and Texas A&M University (TAMU), Central Texas

detail.title: When Does Carbon-Emission Information Change Food Choices? Evidence on Belief-Driven Heterogeneity
detail.abstract: Carbon footprint labels are increasingly used as behavioral tools to promote low-carbon food choices. We conduct a randomized online experiment to examine how personalized, generic carbon-emission information, and their combination affect projected food choices and dietary emissions. On average, both information formats reduce projected emissions, but effects are highly heterogeneous. Individuals with greater concern about climate change significantly reduce emissions, while those with low concern show little response. We provide evidence consistent with a mechanism in which this heterogeneity arises from differential information internalization: climate-concerned individuals are more likely to trust the information and update their beliefs. Mediation analysis indicates that trust accounts for more than half of the relationship between climate attitudes and information internalization. Additional analyses show that responsiveness also varies by political identity and demographic characteristics, with implications for the targeting of information-based interventions. Together, our findings underscore the importance of tailoring information-based interventions to heterogeneous audiences.

title: Mobile Broadband Expansion, Household Consumption, and the Urban-Rural Divide in China
affiliations: Beijing Normal University and Beijing Normal University (BNU) - School of Statistics

detail.title: Mobile Broadband Expansion, Household Consumption, and the Urban-Rural Divide in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Xin Zhang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (72473011) and the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities.

detail.abstract: Expanding domestic demand through higher household consumption has become a key policy priority in China. This paper estimates the causal effect of mobile broadband expansion on household consumption and examines its implications for urban-rural disparities. Using a nationally representative longitudinal household survey combined with information on the staggered rollout of mobile cell towers between 2010 and 2022, we implement a difference-indifferences strategy. The results show that mobile broadband coverage increases household per capita consumption by about 4.5%. Mechanism analyses suggest that this effect operates through increased consumption capacity, lower consumption costs, and enhanced consumption willingness. However, the gains in consumption are highly uneven, concentrated among urban, better-educated, and higher-income households, while rural households benefit little. Consequently, mobile broadband expansion has not narrowed the urban-rural consumption gap.

title: Stock Return Predictability: Evidence from Local, Regional and Global Dividend-Price Ratio Information
affiliations: University of Stirling

detail.title: Stock Return Predictability: Evidence from Local, Regional and Global Dividend-Price Ratio Information
detail.abstract: The dividend discount model is key to our understanding of asset price movement (i.e., the role of the cashflow and risk channels) and the links between financial markets and the real economy. As the dividend-price ratio proxies for macroeconomic information, within the context of a global financial system, it is pertinent to consider what level of information drive predictability. This paper examines predictability for stock returns and dividend growth arising from local, regional (zonal) and global dividend-price ratio information. As well as informing our understanding of the source of asset price movement, these results will highlight diversification opportunities through differences in the nature of predictability between markets. A standard stock return and dividend-price ratio predictive regression for each of 48 international stock markets reveals little supportive evidence, consistent with the literature. Using both a principal components and dynamic factor analysis, regional level dividend-price ratios do present additional predictive evidence, but a global level ratio reveals the greatest degree of predictability, with evidence reported for three-quarters of the markets. For those markets and regions where no predictability is reported, this reveals a disconnect from the global financial system, with the potential for diversification opportunities. These results are robust to using lagged US stock returns as an alternative proxy for global information. Examining a dividend growth predictive relation, the global dividend-price ratio continues to be statistically significant across most of the markets, while there is now greater evidence of local and regional predictability. This suggests that asset price movement arrives through both the risk and cashflow channels, with the former dominated by global information, while for the latter this is spread through local, regional and global sources. These results advance our understanding of asset price movements, the links between financial and real markets and be of interest to investors and those engagement in market modelling.

title: Technology Adoption and Network Externalities in Financial Systems: A Spatial-Network Approach
affiliations: University of Tokyo

detail.title: Technology Adoption and Network Externalities in Financial Systems: A Spatial-Network Approach
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for analyzing technology adoption in financial networks that incorporates spatial spillovers, network externalities, and their interaction. The framework characterizes adoption dynamics through a master equation whose solution admits a Feynman-Kac representation as expected cumulative adoption pressure along stochastic paths through spatial-network space. From this representation, I derive the Adoption Amplification Factor---a structural measure of technology leadership that captures the ratio of total system-wide adoption to initial adoption following a localized shock. A L\'{e}vy jump-diffusion extension with state-dependent jump intensity captures critical mass dynamics: below threshold, adoption evolves through gradual diffusion; above threshold, cascade dynamics accelerate adoption through discrete jumps. Applying the framework to SWIFT gpi adoption among 17 Global Systemically Important Banks, I find strong support for the two-regime characterization. Network-central banks adopt significantly earlier ($\rho = -0.69$, $p = 0.002$), and pre-threshold adopters have significantly higher amplification factors than post-threshold adopters (11.81 versus 7.83, $p = 0.010$). Founding members, representing 29 percent of banks, account for 39 percent of total system amplification---sufficient to trigger cascade dynamics. Controlling for firm size and network position, CEO age delays adoption by 11--15 days per year.

title: Earl Weaver vs. Pythagoras Redux
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Earl Weaver vs. Pythagoras Redux
detail.abstract: Does the performance of MLB teams relative to the Pythagorean Expectation Formula (PEF) supply a valid benchmark for measuring the performances of their managers? Commentators disagree--in a debate that has persisted for over three decades. This paper uses a distinctive statistical device to break this impasse: a realistic simulated null. PEF is based on the relationship between winning percentages and run scoring differentials. Accordingly, whether managers can guide teams to records that deviate from PEF turns on whether their strategic decisionmaking can influence the distribution of runs scored and allowed. To generate a world devoid of any such influence, a Monte Carlo simulation was used to recreate every single game--10,000 times over--of some 500 managers, using relevant season-specific league-wide standard deviations to determine the distribution of their teams' runs scored and allowed per game. The results supply the baseline to examine whether observed manager records deviate from their teams' PEF projections by a degree that differs from chance. (They don't.)

title: Putting People First in Practice: The Establishment of Human-Nature Institutional Science

detail.title: Putting People First in Practice: The Establishment of Human-Nature Institutional Science
detail.abstract: Putting people first is the core essence of Chinese-style modernization and the fundamental guideline for modernizing national governance. However, it has long faced the governance dilemma of "lofty ideals but ineffective implementation", rooted in institutional designs that deviate from the essence of human nature and lack statutory reviews on human-nature compatibility. Based on the disciplinary frameworks of political science, public choice theory, and behavioral economics, this paper systematically reviews classic and cutting-edge literatures including Hobbes' theory of original sin, Adam Smith's rational economic man, Madison's idea of institutional checks and balances, and Kahneman's dual-system theory. It comprehensively identifies four major theoretical gaps "institutional designers are also interest beneficiaries, acting as both players and referees". It proposes four practical approaches to implementation: opposing empty promises, ensuring the cutter takes later, promoting broad-interest compatibility, and conducting statutory reviews on human-nature compatibility. The evaluation of human-nature compatibility is incorporated as a statutory pre-review procedure alongside legality and compliance checks, with specialized evaluation teams cultivated to fill the gap in the human-nature evaluation system for modernizing national governance. Throughout history, those who explored human nature were either rulers seeking to control the people for power or charlatans deceiving the people for profit. Today, we break new ground by quantifying and decoding human nature-not to control or deceive the people, but to take human nature as the yardstick for the benefit of all. This transforms putting people first from a value concept into a rigid institutional arrangement, addressing the governance pain points of "policies that are legal and compliant but against human nature, systems that are outdated and rigid inciting public resentment, and policies that suffer from low execution and inefficiency".

title: Optimizing Learning through TEACCH Approach: An Intervention forAutism Spectrum Disorder
affiliations: Department of Education,Division of Leyte, Barugo II District, Barugo II Central School, Barugo, Leyte, Philippines, Liceo del Verbo Divino, Inc.,  Northern Tacloban City National High School and Marasbaras Central School

detail.title: Optimizing Learning through TEACCH Approach: An Intervention forAutism Spectrum Disorder
detail.abstract: This study examined the effectiveness of the TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication Handicapped Children) approach in improving the academic, social, and life skills of learners with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in a public Special Education (SPED) center in Region VIII, Philippines. Utilizing a one-group pretest-posttest pre-experimental design, the research involved three learners with ASD, who were assessed using a modified DepEd SF9 observation checklist. The intervention incorporated structured teaching strategies characterized by visual supports, individualized work systems, and predictable routines tailored to the learners' developmental needs. Postintervention results revealed notable improvements in academic and life skills, with participants progressing from the "Beginning" to the "Developing" level. Enhanced performance was particularly evident in feeding and toileting tasks. However, limited progress was observed in social skills, which largely remained at the "Beginning" stage. Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test indicated that while the observed gains were educationally relevant, they did not reach statistical significance. This study affirms the practical value of TEACCH in structured learning environments and suggests 2 that extended exposure and supplemental strategies are necessary to address social development. These findings offer valuable insights for policymakers, educators, and parents seeking to enhance ASD education through evidence-based interventions.

title: Sensitivity of the Euro OIS Term Structure to ECB Policy Rate Surprises
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Sensitivity of the Euro OIS Term Structure to ECB Policy Rate Surprises

publicationDetails.journalName: CEIS: Centre for Economic & International Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We analyze the sensitivity of the euro-area yield curve to revisions in market expectations of the ECB policy rate. Using changes in the maintenance-period forward OIS as a market-based measure of policy-rate surprises, we document that yield responses vary systematically across maturities. To interpret these patterns, we adopt a short-rate model with stochastic jumps occurring only at scheduled ECB meeting dates and derive closed-form expressions for the conditional sensitivity of yields to changes in the expected jump size. We compare the model-implied term-structure responses with realized yield changes on days of large revisions in expectations. The model reproduces the cross-sectional shape and magnitude of observed sensitivities, especially the pronounced peak at intermediate maturities, underscoring the importance of incorporating scheduled jump times when modeling interest-rate dynamics.

title: In the Middle: American Multinationals in China and Trade War Politics
affiliations: University of Kansas - Department of Political Science and University of California, Irvine

detail.title: In the Middle: American Multinationals in China and Trade War Politics
detail.abstract: Which factors make some American multinational corporations (MNCs) take political action in response to the U.S.-China Trade War and cause others to stay on the sidelines? We identify China-based subsidiaries of U.S. firms to identify firms' political actions in response to the trade war. We combine data on firms' tariff exposure, economic actions in China, and political actions in the United States during the trade war. Together these data highlight the divergent strategies firms engage in. Even though over 63 percent of MNCs in our sample were adversely impacted by tariffs, only 22 percent voice opposition and 7 percent exit in response to the trade war. Our analysis reveals that U.S. MNCs in China differ in their business models, ownership structure, experience in China, and size of capital investments. These firm-level factors determine the degree to which U.S. MNCs are embedded in China. This in turn shape how firms perceive political risk and choose from the menu of options to deal with the trade war. Size and age increase voice while joint-venture status decrease it.

title: Survivorship Bias in Systemic Risk Estimation

detail.title: Survivorship Bias in Systemic Risk Estimation
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether standard measures of systemic risk are prone to survivorship bias. Using data on more than 2,500 institutions across 34 countries from 1995 to 2025, we find that relying only on surviving firms overstates systemic risk by around 10 basis points or 5.19% at the country level. The bias can be decomposed into two complementary effects. A firm-level weighting effect (WE), unique to systemic risk estimation, arises because institutional exits reassign system index weights to surviving firms, mechanically inflating their measured contributions. A country-level omitted-firms effect (OE) occurs because exiting institutions were, on average, less systemically important than survivors, reflecting sample selection bias from excluding systemic events and the fact that many exiting institutions were "too small to save." Overall, survivorship bias systematically inflates the perceived importance of long-lived institutions while understating risks from newly established firms or those that exited early. The magnitude of the two effects varies across countries, sectors, and time periods. Survivor-only datasets can therefore distort stress tests, cross-country comparisons, and the identification of systemically important institutions.

title: Does Competition Impede Learning from News in the Market for Lemons? Evidence from the Lab
affiliations: James Madison University and Queen's University (Canada), Faculty of Arts & Science, Department of Economics, Students

detail.title: Does Competition Impede Learning from News in the Market for Lemons? Evidence from the Lab
detail.abstract: Buyers often compete to secure deals in environments with asymmetric information that is gradually reduced during negotiations. We conduct a series of laboratory experiments to examine how competition, together with incremental revelation of sellers' private information, influences bargaining dynamics, learning effectiveness, and market outcomes. We find that when buyers anticipate frequently arriving future information, they bid less aggressively and delay agreements, leading to lower market efficiency. At the same time, information revelation benefits buyers by mitigating losses in transactions with low-quality sellers. Holding the information environment constant, buyers in competitive settings reach agreements earlier, condition their decisions on fewer signals, and suffer more frequent and larger losses than in bilateral bargaining, suggesting that competition may hinder learning effectiveness.

reference: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1176; https://doi.org/10.59576/sr.1176
title: Transformed Intermediation: Credit Risk to NBFIs, Liquidity Risk to Banks
affiliations: NYU Stern School of Business, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Transformed Intermediation: Credit Risk to NBFIs, Liquidity Risk to Banks

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1176
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We argue that the rapid asset growth of nonbank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) relative to banks is the outcome of transformations of risks between banks and NBFIs that increase the interconnectedness of the two sectors. These transformations are consistent with avoiding tighter, post-GFC bank regulation while harnessing the funding and liquidity advantages of bank deposit franchises and access to safety nets. Specifically, we show that banks fund NBFIs through senior loans and credit lines, which NBFIs use for acquiring junior credit claims, warehouse financing, and liquidity management. We empirically demonstrate that shocks experienced by NBFIs spill over to the banks that provide them with credit lines, particularly in times of stress. We then suggest policy approaches consistent with our transformation view and conclude with suggestions for future research.

title: Decoupling or Business as Usual? How Japanese Multinational Corporations Adapt to Political Risk in China
affiliations: University of Kansas - Department of Political Science, University of California, Irvine and University of Kansas

detail.title: Decoupling or Business as Usual? How Japanese Multinational Corporations Adapt to Political Risk in China
detail.abstract: How are multinational firms (MNCs) and the global supply chains that link them to China adjusting to heightened political risks? Since the U.S.-China Trade War, COVID-19 supply chain shocks, and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Western governments have increased efforts to encourage MNCs to divert investment from an increasingly authoritarian China toward politically reliable allies and partners. Using firm-level data on Japanese MNCs from 2012-2022, we examine competing predictions from "business as usual" and "follow the flag" theories. We introduce a typology of de-risking strategies: decoupling (exit from China), diversifying (investment outside China), and diverting (both exit from China and investment in friendly countries), contrasted with inaction. While most Japanese MNCs continue to operate in China, a majority have adopted at least one de-risking strategy over the past decade. Consistent with the "following the flag" theory, we find that national security-relevant MNCs are significantly more likely to engage in all de-risking strategies after controlling for firm size, experience, and China exposure.

title: Fake Date Tests: Can We Trust In-sample Accuracy of LLMs in Macroeconomic Forecasting?
affiliations: Bank of Russia and Bank of Russia

detail.title: Fake Date Tests: Can We Trust In-sample Accuracy of LLMs in Macroeconomic Forecasting?
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are a type of machine learning tool that economists have started to apply in their empirical research. One such application is macroeconomic forecasting with backtesting of LLMs, even though they are trained on the same data that is used to estimate their forecasting performance. Can these in-sample accuracy results be extrapolated to the model's out-of-sample performance? To answer this question, we developed a family of prompt sensitivity tests and two members of this family, which we call the fake date tests. These tests aim to detect two types of biases in LLMs' in-sample forecasts: lookahead bias and context bias. According to the empirical results, none of the modern LLMs tested in this study passed our first test, signaling the presence of lookahead bias in their in-sample forecasts.

title: Public Health Insurance and Employment Lock: Resolving the TennCare Puzzle

detail.title: Public Health Insurance and Employment Lock: Resolving the TennCare Puzzle
detail.abstract: The employment effects of public health insurance retrenchment remain disputed. Evaluations of the 2005 TennCare disenrollment--which terminated Medicaid coverage of approximately 170,000 Tennessee residents--have produced conflicting findings, ranging from large labor supply responses to precise null effects. I demonstrate that this discrepancy is a result of conflating the dynamics of self-employment with those of formal employment. Because self-employment rarely confers health benefits and exhibits inconsistent dynamics across surveys, aggregate employment serves as a noisy outcome for detecting "employment lock." Isolating formal wage employment--the margin relevant for insurance access--I find robust evidence of employment lock, concentrated among older, less-educated adults. This heterogeneity resolves the empirical puzzle, yielding plausible estimates that contrast with the extremes of early studies while explaining recent findings of aggregate null effects. The findings demonstrate that employment lock is not a marginal substitution of leisure for consumption, but a corner solution driven by a binding health necessity.

title: Unexpected Inflation and Fertility Rate in the US
affiliations: and University of Mississippi - Department of Economics

detail.title: Unexpected Inflation and Fertility Rate in the US
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of unexpected inflation on the fertility rate in the United States. Using state-level data from 2003-2023, we employ the Kalman filter to extract the unexpected component of actual inflation rates then relate this value to the next year's total fertility rate. The empirical results show that unexpected inflation has a negative and significant impact on the total fertility rate. Younger women (under age 25) are more likely to postpone or reduce births due to an unanticipated inflation. A one percentage point increase in unexpected inflation is expected to result in 3-5 fewer births per 1,000 reproductive-age women. Not only does this work provide additional indirect evidence of the fact that children are normal goods (i.e., less is demanded at a higher price), but we are the first to document the role of unexpected inflation in delaying or preventing births within the contemporary U.S. context.

title: The New Abuse of Dominance Test: Missed Opportunities and Future Challenges
affiliations: University of Western Ontario - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The New Abuse of Dominance Test: Missed Opportunities and Future Challenges
detail.abstract: This paper provides a critical assessment of the new abuse of dominance test under Section 79 of the Competition Act. Recent reforms have reshaped Canada’s unilateral conduct regime by introducing a new bifurcated approach that lowers the statutory requirements for the imposition of prohibition orders to a finding of either anticompetitive acts or substantial lessening or prevention of competition (SLPC). This paper argues that these amendments missed a crucial opportunity to resolve long-standing conceptual flaws in Canadian abuse of dominance. In particular, it explains that the anticompetitive act requirement under the old three-part test has always been redundant and resulted in problematic outcomes, such as undue emphasis on intent and harm to competitors. A more coherent reform approach would have eliminated Section 79(1)(b) altogether in favour of a simpler two-part test based on dominance and SLPC. In contrast, the amendments elevate the role of the anti-competitive act requirement, at least for prohibition orders, possibly exacerbating the ambiguities that plagued the abuse test well before the recent legislative changes. For these reasons, future amendments will become desirable if these long-standing problems are further aggravated by the enforcement of the new provision.

title: Amplifying Influence: The Impact of Early Release of Voting Positions and Engagement
affiliations: Boston College - Department of Accounting, University of Colorado at Boulder, London Business School and University of Iowa - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Amplifying Influence: The Impact of Early Release of Voting Positions and Engagement
detail.abstract: We study the role of public disclosure of voting positions and engagement meetings in tacitly coordinating influence on companies at annual meetings of US listed firms. Using a difference-indifference design, we find that a large universal investor's (Norges Bank Investment Management-"NBIM") early release of its voting positions opposing management has a significant incremental effect on the voting outcomes for director elections and shareholder proposals. In addition, we document that early release of voting positions is more influential when NBIM's position is less likely to be predictable. We further find that NBIM is more likely to engage with firms both before (which may provide private information to inform voting) and after (to follow up and continue to advocate for change) dissenting votes and that its voting position has more influence when it is preceded by direct engagement, suggesting that other investors view these voting positions as more credible signals.

title: Re-reading Anita Bernstein's The Common Law Inside the Female Body from the Bottom of the Well: Analysis of the Central Park Five, Border Drownings, the Kavanaugh Confirmation, and the Coronavirus
affiliations: Barry University - Dwayne O. Andreas School of Law

detail.title: Re-reading Anita Bernstein's The Common Law Inside the Female Body from the Bottom of the Well: Analysis of the Central Park Five, Border Drownings, the Kavanaugh Confirmation, and the Coronavirus
detail.abstract: This Article provides a critique of the common law based on its impact on "the legal other" or what the late Professor Derrick Bell viewed as the faces from the bottom of the well. Professor Anita Bernstein notes common law's liberatory capacity. While this interpretation of the common law is true to a certain extent, this reading can lead to an underestimation of the common law's limitations. In looking at the case involving the Central Park Five, I argue that feminist jurisprudence can have an unintended disparate impact on vulnerable populations. Examples of migrant detention facilities and precarious border crossings also illustrate how inhumane conditions emerge in response to the desire to protect white female spaces. In other words, the law functions to protect white women as an extension of white male property and privilege. This Article argues that law enforcement arms and the judicial system operate in hegemonic unison to protect the interests of elite institutions and those in power by using all tools at their disposal, including the common law inside the female body. Meanwhile, even white women are disempowered when their interests do not align with the goals of white male heteropatriachy as evidenced by the confirmation hearings of Justice Kavanaugh. The coronavirus pandemic accentuates these disparities in the feminist jurisprudence.

title: Quantifying the Impacts of Building Energy Efficiency Retrofits and Nature Exposure on Chronic Student Absenteeism
