detail.abstract: Chronic absenteeism—defined as missing 10% or more of school days—affects over 14 million United States students, with rates nearly doubling since the COVID-19 pandemic and disproportionately impacting disadvantaged communities. Schools function as socioeconomic hubs where compounding barriers related to housing, transportation, health, and environmental conditions converge to shape attendance outcomes. While socioeconomic and demographic factors are established risk factors, the role of equitable infrastructure investments in addressing these interconnected barriers remains underexplored. This study provides the first large-scale evidence linking school energy efficiency retrofits funded through California's Proposition 39 Clean Energy Jobs Act to attendance outcomes. We quantified the impact of retrofits and nature exposure on chronic absenteeism across 2,686 K-12 schools (2020–2024) using Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations with Bayesian inference and optimal propensity score matching, controlling for 16 equity and sustainability covariates. Nature exposure demonstrated the largest standalone effect, with schools exhibiting 6.88% lower chronic absenteeism (d = 0.44, p < .001; n = 2,035). Combined lighting, pumps, motors, and drives retrofits with nature exposure were associated with 5.49% lower chronic absenteeism (d = 0.41, p < .001; AUC = 0.716). Preliminary evidence suggests pumps, motors, and drives retrofits alone were associated with 5.58% lower chronic absenteeism with medium effect size (d = 0.60, p < .05; n = 18), though limited sample size necessitates replication before definitive conclusions. Nature exposure achieved the highest return on investment (16.1%, 6.2-year payback), with estimated annual savings of $37,525 and 3,191 recovered instructional days annually—the only intervention meeting the 10-year policy benchmark. These findings position K-12 schools as strategic socioeconomic hubs where equitable infrastructure investments simultaneously reduce chronic absenteeism, improve indoor environmental quality through enhanced ventilation and thermal comfort, and advance SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 7 (Clean Energy), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities), and SDG 13 (Climate Action) while supporting Paris Agreement commitments, particularly in disadvantaged communities.

title: Market for Lemons in Academia: Adverse Selection with Dynamic Human Capital Formation and Policy Lock-in
affiliations: International School of Economics

detail.title: Market for Lemons in Academia: Adverse Selection with Dynamic Human Capital Formation and Policy Lock-in
detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic theory of academic publishing in which evaluation metrics interact with researchers' skill formation. Building on classic models of adverse selection and signaling, the analysis introduces endogenous human capital dynamics: researchers' skills evolve as a function of their publication choices. Engagement with high-scrutiny journals enhances skills through learning-by-doing and referee feedback, while repeated publication in low-scrutiny outlets leads to skill depreciation. The model shows that when governing bodies fail to differentiate between high-and lowscrutiny publication outlets-treating all indexed outputs as equivalent-researchers optimally exert minimal effort, triggering a decline in aggregate research skills. Crucially, this process generates hysteresis: even if evaluation policies are later corrected, accumulated skill depreciation may prevent the re-emergence of a separating equilibrium. The theory is empirically motivated by a comparison of two research funding regimes in Kazakhstan-one imposing strict publication targets tied to indexed journals, and another without publication requirements-which generate markedly different publication patterns despite operating within the same academic environment. The framework highlights a previously unexplored channel through which metric-based evaluation systems can cause persistent damage to research capacity. It delivers clear policy implications: delayed reforms are costly, stronger differentiation across publication outlets may be required to restore quality, and increasing the cost of low-scrutiny publication can be as important as raising rewards for high-quality output. While grounded in a specific institutional setting, the model provides a general framework for understanding durable quality failure in research systems reliant on targeted publication metrics.

title: Action-Inferred Vicarious Learning Networks: Evidence from Insurance Price Filings
affiliations: University of Mississippi, Florida State University and University of Iowa - Department of Finance

detail.title: Action-Inferred Vicarious Learning Networks: Evidence from Insurance Price Filings
detail.abstract: Organizations often learn vicariously from competitors to navigate uncertainty, yet who learns from whom is typically presumed from static firm characteristics rather than from observed learning behaviors. We introduce an action-inferred vicarious learning framework that applies a network inference algorithm to detect persistent learning ties from the timing of firms' repeated strategic decisions. Using over 57,000 auto insurance price filings, we uncover state-specific learning networks that reveal consistent leader-follower patterns in insurers' price-changing decisions. These network structures vary across states, highlighting the localized nature of vicarious learning. Contrary to conventional views, the most influential learning targets in the network are often not market share leaders but smaller insurers or third-party data aggregators. We further demonstrate that regulation and market conditions shape the intensity of vicarious learning: it is stronger in states with more stringent price regulation and during periods of heightened market uncertainty, such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Capitalization of Environmental Change: Road Noise Trajectories and Housing Prices
affiliations: Poznan University of Economics and Business and University of Connecticut - School of Business

detail.title: Capitalization of Environmental Change: Road Noise Trajectories and Housing Prices

detail.abstract: Transportation noise is a disamenity that is often capitalized into home prices. Standard hedonic models condition on disamenity levels at a particular point in time, but housing markets may also be absorbing information about the noise trajectory that leads to those levels. Spatial heterogeneity is also often a concern in noise studies. We propose an innovative two-dimensional classification framework that separately distinguishes net outcome (improvement vs. deterioration) and temporal pattern (permanent, late, non-permanent), as well as controls for spatial effects. We leverage this framework to analyze three distinct versions of Warsaw's Noise Maps (2012, 2017, 2022) linked to more than 147,000 apartment sales. Noise improvements are capitalized into significant home price premia that are systematically moderated by trajectory type. Permanent Improvements are associated with 2.6-3.9% home price premia, and Non-permanent Improvements (net reductions achieved by non-monotonic paths) experience intermediate price effects of 1.5-1.7%. The resulting per-decibel capitalization rate is nearly twice as large for permanent vs. late-arriving improvements (0.49%/dB vs. 0.26%/dB), suggesting that markets value demonstrated persistence above and beyond current conditions. Deterioration effects are statistically significant but less robust than improvement effects, with relatively small sample sizes reducing statistical power. These results show trajectory characteristics can offer information that can be capitalized above and beyond disamenity levels, and that standard hedonic estimates may substantially overstate deterioration effects when spatial dependence is ignored.

title: Robust Factor Estimation and Determination in Large-Dimensional Time Series
affiliations: Shandong University, Shandong University and University of Illinois at Chicago - Department of Information and Decision Sciences

detail.title: Robust Factor Estimation and Determination in Large-Dimensional Time Series

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2023YFA1008701)

detail.abstract: Large-dimensional factor models are powerful dimension-reduction tools for analyzing large-dimensional time series and have been extensively studied in the literature. However, many existing methods lack robustness to heavy-tailed distributions and outliers, which are pervasive in financial and macroeconomic data. Inspired by the median-of-means principle, we propose a new robust estimation procedure, Averaged Projection with Series Segmentation (APSS), that achieves robustness through segment-wise estimation and projection averaging. In addition, we develop an auxiliary Averaged Projection with Eigenvalue Gap (APEG) method for consistent estimation of the number of factors. Our theoretical analysis shows that the proposed estimators attain the same convergence rates as those by conventional principal component analysis, and we establish their asymptotic distributions under mild regularity conditions. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that APSS outperforms several existing competitors across a wide range of settings, highlighting its superior robustness and finite-sample performance. We further illustrate the practical relevance of our approach through an empirical application to the FRED-MD macroeconomic dataset.

title: Measuring Housing Market Slack
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee

detail.title: Measuring Housing Market Slack
detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework to estimate U.S. housing market slack-the deviation of inventory from equilibrium levels needed for stability. We measure slack as a common cyclical component of existing and new home inventories that drives house prices through a housing Phillips curve. Results show a statistically significant inverse relationship between slack and price growth, with persistent negative slack since 2010 and extreme tightness during the pandemic. A shock to the estimated housing market slack generates substantial, lasting effects on house prices and rents, with rental impacts peaking 24 months after initial shocks.

title: Regime-Dependent Housing Valuations: Price-Rent Ratios, Volatility, and Structural Breaks in U.S. Markets
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee

detail.title: Regime-Dependent Housing Valuations: Price-Rent Ratios, Volatility, and Structural Breaks in U.S. Markets
detail.abstract: We propose a present value model with structural breaks to explain why U.S. house prices remain persistently high relative to rents-a pattern that standard time-invariant models struggle to capture. Our model uses quarterly data from 1975 to 2023 and incorporates the time-varying volatility of the net discount factor as a key priced risk factor. We find five distinct periods with very different pricing patterns. During the Great Moderation (1981-2001), the usual textbook logic held: higher expected rent growth pushed valuations up, while higher discount rates pulled them down. But in the stagflation era of the late 1970s and again in the recent period (2016-2023), these relationships reversed-higher expected rent growth actually lowered valuations. The two big housing booms of the 2000s and the recent period arose through different forces: the 2000s boom saw prices break free from rents, while the recent period showed an unusually strong reaction to discount rates and a new positive role for volatility, suggesting that uncertainty itself made housing more attractive. These shifting patterns show that what once looked like model failures are better understood as signs of changing market regimes.

title: Single-Factor Augmenting Growth Models: The Sources of Steady-State Instability
affiliations: Brandeis University - International Business School

detail.title: Single-Factor Augmenting Growth Models: The Sources of Steady-State Instability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper posits that single-factor technology augmenting models are intrinsically steady-state inconsistent. Functioning in the steady-state, whether the model of Malthus or Solow, a twofactor production technology in which only one factor continuously augments, while the other lies technologically dormant, creates a technology divide that diminishes the ability of the augmenting factor to be technologically effective. Taking the now axiomatic representation of technical change as purely labor-augmenting Harrod neutral, this paper models the implications of a growing technological divide for the stability of labor augmenting's marginal product. As MPA → 0, the output elasticity and unaugmented capital-augmented labor substitution elasticity also become unstable, thereby overturning the steady state and functioning a a trap for technical change and economic growth.

title: City of Shame: Crime Signaling and Inverse Deterrence in a Weak State
affiliations: and Saint Olaf College - Department of Economics

detail.title: City of Shame: Crime Signaling and Inverse Deterrence in a Weak State
detail.abstract: Do high-profile crimes deter future offending or signal weak enforcement? We study the effects of the highly publicized rape and murder of a seven-year-old girl in Kasur, Pakistan, in 2018 on child sexual abuse. Using district-month data from 2015-2024 and a synthetic difference-indifferences design, we compare Kasur to a constructed counterfactual from other districts. We find a large, persistent increase in reported child abuse-about ten additional cases per monthconcentrated in opportunistic offenses and weakly supervised settings. The increase coincides with judicial congestion, consistent with inverse deterrence driven by institutional strain rather than transient reporting effects.

title: A Survey on Mechanism Design Meets Large Language Models
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers University and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: A Survey on Mechanism Design Meets Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in interactive and strategic settings such as negotiation, preference elicitation, evaluation, alignment, and multi-agent coordination. These settings are inherently incentive-driven, yet most existing approaches rely on heuristic designs with limited guarantees against manipulation or misalignment. This survey develops a unified, bidirectional view of the relationship between mechanism design and LLMs. We discuss (i) LLMs for mechanism design, where language models are used as strategic agent proxies, simulators, and natural-language interfaces for economic mechanisms, and (ii) mechanism design for LLMs, where incentive-aware principles are applied to LLM evaluation, alignment, and training. We conclude by identifying challenges in incentive-compatible evaluation, human-LLM interaction protocols, and emerging markets for LLM services.

title: Forecast of Mining Fatalities using Machine Learning Algorithms
affiliations: Michigan Technological University

detail.title: Forecast of Mining Fatalities using Machine Learning Algorithms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: Mining industry plays a crucial role in economic development but is often accompanied by notable occupational hazards, including fatalities. This research investigates the application of machine learning techniques to predict mining fatalities in the United States using historical data from 1983 to 2023, sourced from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) and FRED Economic Data. Predictive models including Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), Decision Tree (DT), Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), and Linear Regression (LR), were employed to assess relationships between operational parameters and annual fatality counts. The dataset was thoroughly preprocessed, addressing missing values and deriving a fatality rate metric to improve predictive accuracy. Model performance was evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and the Coefficient of Determination (R²). Among the models, GB achieved the highest predictive accuracy, with an MAE of 7.85, RMSE of 10.04, and R² of 0.903, followed closely by RF and LR approaches. These findings highlight the effectiveness of machine learning, especially ensemble methods, in modeling complex patterns and offering valuable insights for improving safety outcomes in the mining sector. To support interpretability, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was employed to explain feature contributions, providing insights into how key variables influenced model predictions.

title: Training Intensity in European Firms: Organisational Characteristics and Institutional Contexts
affiliations: University of Warwick and

detail.title: Training Intensity in European Firms: Organisational Characteristics and Institutional Contexts
detail.abstract: This study examines the determinants of training intensity across European firms, focusing on the depth and scope of employer-provided training rather than its mere provision. Using three waves of the Continuing Vocational Training Survey (2010, 2015, 2020), we apply a three-level regression models to analyse how firm characteristics, sectoral patterns, and institutional contexts shape training hours and costs per employee. Contrary to conventional assumptions, larger firms deliver less intensive training per employee than smaller enterprises. Knowledge-intensive sectors demonstrate higher training intensity, reflecting continuous skill development needs in technology-driven industries. Technological investment at the country level significantly moderates the relationship between firm size and training intensity, with firms in high-investment contexts achieving greater cost efficiency while maintaining or increasing training volumes. Persistent country-level effects remain even after controlling for structural factors, suggesting the influence of unobservable institutional variables. These findings highlight the need to distinguish between training provision and intensity and emphasise the importance of organisational scale, sectoral demands, and institutional environments in shaping workforce development. The results offer policy-relevant insights for designing targeted interventions that enhance the quality and depth of training across diverse organisational and national contexts.

title: Incomplete Market Equilibrium under Social Comparisons
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Mathematics, London School of Economics and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Incomplete Market Equilibrium under Social Comparisons
detail.abstract: We study how social comparisons shape asset prices in an incomplete-market economy with uninsurable income risk. Agents are heterogeneous in preferences, endowments, and in the weights they place on the consumption of others. Using a mean-field game framework with a directed network described by a finite-rank kernel, we derive in closed form the equilibrium interest rate, stock price, and individual consumption and portfolio policies. A social multiplier matrix captures how network interactions reallocate risk across agents. Social comparisons reduce the market price of hedgeable risk by raising the effective risk tolerance of the economy, as consumption and social reference benchmarks co-move with common shocks. The network structure governing social comparisons determines whether the precautionary-savings motive induced by unhedgeable risk is amplified or mitigated. If all agents exert the same influence on others and are equally sensitive to the rest of the system, as in a doubly stochastic comparison network, the specific network topology does not affect equilibrium prices.

title: Eight Ideas for 2028
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Eight Ideas for 2028
detail.abstract: Whatever the party of the new president, elected in 2028, it would be worthwhile for the incoming administration to consider eight ideas, to be explicitly embodied in executive orders or presidential memoranda: (1) a clear commitment to the independence of the Federal Reserve Board, certainly with respect to monetary policy; (2) a broad commitment to freedom of speech and the press, building on constitutional requirements; (3) a firm commitment not to interfere with the prosecutorial decisions of the Department of Justice; (4) an insistence on the centrality of cost-benefit analysis, designed to work against both overregulation and underregulation; (5) new restrictions on the pardon power, designed to regularize relevant processes; (6) reasonable (not excessive or expressive) restrictions on conflicts of interest and self-dealing, applicable to executive branch officials and the president personally; (7) a presumption against suits brought by the president in his personal capacity (a voluntary presidential disability, meant to parallel and accompany presidential immunity); (8) perhaps most controversially, a presumption (not a rule) against prosecution, by the current administration, of members of the previous administration. All of these ideas would have to be specified, but they are worthy of serious consideration, no matter the political party of the new administration.

title: European Smart Grids: Legislation, Business Models and Social Aspects
affiliations: KAPSARC School of Public Policy

detail.title: European Smart Grids: Legislation, Business Models and Social Aspects

publicationDetails.detailsText: Queen Mary Law Research Paper No. 03/2026

detail.abstract: This technical report analyses the regulatory, energy security, social and ethical as well as business-model landscapes for the implementation of smart grids across the European Union (EU), with particular focus on the existing legislation both at the EU level and the national level of the pilot sites for the WiseGRID project. The report discusses among other things the impact that the project will have on energy security as well as social and ethical considerations that ought to underpin projects of this nature. It also analyses and proposes workable business models for the implantation of the project.

title: When Long-Run Trends Are Unknown: Bond Pricing Implications
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and McGill University, Desautels Faculty of Management, Students

detail.title: When Long-Run Trends Are Unknown: Bond Pricing Implications
detail.abstract: This paper assesses the informativeness of the Treasury yield curve about the longrun real interest rate, r-star, when bond investors are uncertain about its value. We propose a macro-finance model where inflation, growth, and the monetary policy rate are driven by a combination of persistent trends and transitory cycles. Investors only observe the aggregate macroeconomic variables but infers trends and cycles to price bonds. In spite of imperfect information, our model preserves the simplicity of standard affine term structure models. Our estimation reveals wide investors uncertainty about r-star that does not disappear over time, and an increasing r-star trend before the Volcker era, largely contrasting with perfect information estimates. Because investors confuse trends with cycles, the yield curve can under or overreact to structural monetary policy shocks.

title: The Growth and Consequences of Index Investing
affiliations: Independent, Independent, University of Bristol, University of Bristol - Department of Finance and Accounting and

detail.title: The Growth and Consequences of Index Investing
detail.abstract: This paper documents the significant rise in index investing in equity and other financial markets over the last thirty years and outlines key features of the investment management industry. We examine the consequences of this growth in passive investment strategies for stock market informational efficiency, volatilities, correlations, systemic risks, competition and corporate governance.

title: Visibility Projects and De-privatization: A Case of China's Urban Bus Sector (Working Paper)
affiliations: Georgetown University

detail.title: Visibility Projects and De-privatization: A Case of China's Urban Bus Sector (Working Paper)
detail.abstract: This article introduces the concept of visibility in infrastructure politics and explains how the emphasis of visibility can lead to de-privatization of a public service sector. Using China's urban bus sector as a case, I introduce what "visibility projects" are-distorted public projects aimed at increasing government officials' visibility in politics and career prospects. These projects are highly costly and often compromise business interests because political visibility does not often translate into business profits. When a sector is chosen for visibility projects, government officials often seek financial contributions and operational changes from business in the sector, creating an uneven playing field between private companies and state-owned enterprises. Private companies, facing hard budget constraints, are more likely to resist visibility projects than state-owned companies, which can ultimately lead to de-privatization by the state. I show these dynamics with a quantitative analysis based on an original dataset, a process-tracing case study, and in-depth interviews.

title: Optimizing Information Asset Investment Strategies in the Exploratory Phase of the Oil and Gas Industry: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
affiliations: Independent, University Institute of Lisbon (IUL) - ISCTE and

detail.title: Optimizing Information Asset Investment Strategies in the Exploratory Phase of the Oil and Gas Industry: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
detail.abstract: Our work investigates the economic efficiency of the prevailing "ladder-step" investment strategy in oil and gas exploration, which advocates for the incremental acquisition of geological information throughout the project lifecycle. By employing a multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework, we model an alternative strategy that prioritizes the early acquisition of high-quality information assets. We simulate the entire upstream value chain—comprising competitive bidding, exploration, and development phases—to evaluate the economic impact of this approach relative to traditional methods. Our results demonstrate that front-loading information investment significantly reduces the costs associated with redundant data acquisition and enhances the precision of reserve valuation. Specifically, we find that the alternative strategy outperforms traditional methods in highly competitive environments by mitigating the "winner’s curse" through more accurate bidding. Furthermore, the economic benefits are most pronounced during the development phase, where superior data quality minimizes capital misallocation. These findings suggest that optimal investment timing is structurally dependent on market competition rather than solely on price volatility, offering a new paradigm for capital allocation in extractive industries.

title: The Catholic Church in Times of Ecological Crisis: An "Unusual Suspect" in Advancing the Transition to Sustainability?
affiliations: The King’s University

detail.title: The Catholic Church in Times of Ecological Crisis: An "Unusual Suspect" in Advancing the Transition to Sustainability?

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Canada Research Chairs Program (Award ID: CRC-2020-00006)

detail.abstract: Religious traditions and institutions have historically played a significant role in shaping cultural scaffoldings and social practices. Can they also help reshape the unsustainable world humans have made for themselves, which is now undermining not only the actual and prospective minimum standards of dignified life for the many, but also the basic fabric of Earth's life support? From an approach critical of mainstream sustainability and looking to the example of the Catholic Church and Pope Francis' vision of an "integral ecology", this article argues that, in spite of being a latecomer to the global sustainability debate, the Church is structurally uniquely positioned to play the role of a global sustainability governance agent in the necessary transition to future-able way(s) of societal organization. It can, however, do so only if it proves capable of avoiding the risks of corporatist takeover, instrumentalisation for economic and political purposes, and assimilation of the integral ecology narrative used by the overall ineffective approaches of mainstream sustainable development.

title: An Empirical Analysis of the Conditional Variance of Farmland Prices

detail.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Conditional Variance of Farmland Prices
detail.abstract: The conditional variance of farmland prices measures price dispersion among comparable plots and can be used to quantify the range of likely sale prices for a plot with given characteristics. We develop three conditional variance models with a parametric and semiparametric specification each to quantify price dispersion and to construct prediction intervals that adapt to different levels of price uncertainty for given farmland characteristics. Our application to the farmland market in Brandenburg reveals that price dispersion varies substantially across space, increased steadily between 2009 and 2022, and tends to be higher at higher price levels. We find that conditional variance models based on the assumption that farmland prices, conditional on characteristics, are lognormally distributed, produce accurate prediction intervals for typical farmland transactions.

title: Shadow Futures: Why Verifiable Work Cannot Signal Value in Path-Dependent Economies
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Shadow Futures: Why Verifiable Work Cannot Signal Value in Path-Dependent Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, professional, or financial relationships that could reasonably be perceived as influencing the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is purely theoretical and does not involve human subjects, participants, personal data, or experiments. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether verifiable work can serve as a reliable signal of value in economies characterized by path dependence and increasing returns. We present a minimal model in which agents perform observable and perfectly verifiable effort, summarized by a public work transcript, while rewards are allocated through a reinforcing network process, and show that even under perfect transparency work is informationally non-identifying. As reinforcement compounds, the mutual information between work and reward can collapse asymptotically to zero, even under perfect measurement. We introduce the concept of shadow futures, defined as unrealized but observationally indistinguishable effort trajectories that fail due solely to unfavorable timing or network position. The existence of shadow futures implies that observed success cannot be causally attributed to work even ex post, because identical verified effort histories are compatible with both success and failure. This failure of attribution is structural and does not depend on noise, manipulation, or institutional weakness. Applications include labor markets, scientific publishing, digital platforms, and proof-of-work systems, where verification mechanisms persist despite the loss of causal and informational content.

title: Predictability and Drivers of Free-Price Events in Great Britain’s Electricity Market: A 2024 Price-Carbon Analysis
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Predictability and Drivers of Free-Price Events in Great Britain’s Electricity Market: A 2024 Price-Carbon Analysis
detail.abstract: Periods in which wholesale electricity prices fall to zero or below (here termed free-price events) are becoming increasingly common in decarbonising power systems. Understanding their drivers and predictability is essential for market design, demand response (DR) strategies, and investments in system flexibility. This study provides a full-year empirical assessment of free-price events in Great Britain (GB) for 2024, combining 17,534 half-hourly observations of wholesale Market Index Data (MID) prices [1] with national carbon-intensity measurements [2]. We document 498 free-price half-hours (2.84% of the year; 14,940 minutes), concentrated in spring and late summer. Correlation analysis shows only weak contemporaneous coupling between carbon intensity and price (|r|<0.20), indicating that carbon levels alone do not explain price collapses.To identify structural drivers, we engineer calendar, diurnal, and lagged features and train a logistic regression classifier to estimate the probability of free-price conditions. The model achieves high discriminative performance (ROC AUC = 0.995; PR AUC = 0.842; Brier score = 0.028), demonstrating that free-price events are highly predictable despite their low base rate, with all metrics computed on a stratified hold-out test set. Lagged prices, lagged carbon intensity, and hour-of-day emerge as the strongest predictors, while seasonal progression (day-of-year) captures broader patterns of renewable generation. An odds-ratio analysis corroborates these drivers and shows significant temporal asymmetries preceding price collapses. These findings indicate that free-price events in GB are neither random nor purely weather-driven; instead, they reflect systematic market and system conditions that follow consistent patterns over time.

title: Sustainable Printing: The Strategic Role of Outsourcing in Reducing Costs and Environmental Impacts

detail.title: Sustainable Printing: The Strategic Role of Outsourcing in Reducing Costs and Environmental Impacts
detail.abstract:
Certainly! Here is the summary of the article "Sustainable Printing: The Strategic Role of Outsourcing in Reducing Costs and Environmental Impacts," by Reginaldo Bailo, translated into English.

📝 Summary of the Article

The article "Sustainable Printing: The Strategic Role of Outsourcing in Reducing Costs and Environmental Impacts," by Reginaldo Bailo, CEO of Suprink Brasil, argues that printing outsourcing is a corporate sustainability strategy that delivers environmental, economic, and social benefits, aligned with the Triple Bottom Line concept (People, Planet, Profit).

1. Context and Objective

  • The urgency of climate change and the demand for operational efficiency make the corporate printing sector a key focus of the ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) agenda.

  • Printing outsourcing, especially with platforms like NDD Orbix, goes beyond cost containment, becoming a tool to achieve sustainability.

2. Outsourcing and Environmental Sustainability

The transition from a decentralized, in-house structure to a sustainable, outsourced model provides concrete environmental benefits:

  • Paper Reduction: Quota control systems and authenticated printing (follow me printing) can reduce paper volume by 20% to 40%.

  • Input Efficiency: Centralized monitoring optimizes the use of toners and cartridges, preventing premature disposal.

  • Energy Saving: Modern, energy-efficient equipment reduces electricity consumption by up to 35%.

  • Less E-Waste: The rental model ensures responsible maintenance and replacement, extending the equipment's lifespan and avoiding improper disposal.

3. Economic Sustainability

Sustainability is a path to profitability. Organizations adopting sustainable outsourcing report reductions of 20% to 30% in operating costs, resulting from:

  • Centralization of the printing fleet.

  • Automation of supply and maintenance orders.

  • Elimination of unnecessary prints (requiring authentication alone reduces printed volume by up to 25%).

  • Use of management reports (KPIs) for data-driven decisions.

4. Technology and Cultural Engagement

The NDD Orbix platform is highlighted as the technological solution for this transformation.

  • NDD Orbix Features: Real-time monitoring, individual and departmental quota control, customizable reports on carbon emission per print, and integration with information security policies.

  • Cultural Impact: Monitoring usage prompts employees to reflect before printing, fostering a culture of environmental responsibility in daily corporate life.

5. Case Study and Conclusion

  • A case study in a logistics company with 2,500 employees resulted in a 37% drop in print volume and a reduction of 2 tons of paper in 12 months (equivalent to 34 trees saved).

  • The article concludes that the Administration professional plays a strategic role, transforming the adoption of sustainable outsourcing from a simple operational change into a long-term political and economic decision crucial for the company's future and competitiveness.

title: The Joule Standard: A Thermodynamic Theory of Monetary Evolution and Civilizational Collapse

detail.title: The Joule Standard: A Thermodynamic Theory of Monetary Evolution and Civilizational Collapse

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently and was not funded by any corporation, financial institution, or government entity. The motivation for this work is purely intellectual and scientific.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research consists of a quantitative analysis and re-interpretation of publicly available historical and economic data. No human or animal subjects, patient data, or primary experimental ethics approval were required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was entirely self-funded by the author. No external grants or institutional support were utilized.

detail.abstract:
Standard economic models often treat money as a social construct independent of physical laws. This paper proposes a unified Thermodynamic Theory of Value, positing that monetary systems are information protocols evolved to maximize entropy production in dissipative structures. By integrating Eric Chaisson’s Energy Rate Density (Φm) with historical economic data, we identify the "Joule Standard": a universal power law governing the relationship between Energy Cost (E) and Information Granularity (G).

We demonstrate that the acceleration of complexity follows a strict log-linear trajectory (R² > 0.999) spanning geological, biological, and economic substrates. We argue that this regression line is the visible trace of the Second Law of Thermodynamics maximizing entropy production.

Crucially, we provide a variational proof that the emergence of "Intelligence"—from biological coding to monetary protocols—is a non-arbitrary phase transition in fluid dynamics. By identifying the universal acceleration constant (C_acc ≈ 2.5) as the inverse von Kármán constant (1/κ), we demonstrate that information "ignites" as a mechanistic necessity when the entropy cost of turbulent drag (ignorance) exceeds the entropy cost of informational regulation (bits).

This provides a fluid-dynamic proof for the timing of historical substrate transitions, treating civilizational evolution as a high-Reynolds-number flow. We demonstrate that as a system’s Structural Power (Ω) increases, its Information Granularity must refine to prevent a catastrophic rise in Systemic Viscosity (η > 1). This model predicts that the current "Monetary Era" is a finite phase transition that concludes when systemic viscosity reaches the zero-friction limit, suggesting that the "Great Filter" is a thermodynamic boundary mandated by the physics of flow.

title: The Effect of Paid Sick Leave on Healthcare Expenditures
affiliations: Yale University, Tulane University - Department of Global Health Systems and Development, University of Missouri - Department of Economics and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: The Effect of Paid Sick Leave on Healthcare Expenditures

declarations.funderStatement: Research reported in this publication was supported by the National Cancer Institute and the National Institute of Mental Health under Award Number 1R01CA237888 (PI: Kevin Callison) and R01MH132552 (PI: Johanna Catherine Maclean). The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health.

detail.abstract: As of 2025, 18 states (including Washington D.C.), 17 cities, and four counties have paid sick leave mandates that allow workers to use paid time off for healthcare utilization. Some groups have argued that paid sick leave mandates could reduce healthcare spending overall by increasing use of preventive care and reducing incidences of infectious disease. We evaluate these claims by studying the effect of paid sick leave mandates on private insurance and Medicaid spending data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services National Health Expenditure accounts, and household spending data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. We find evidence that paid sick leave mandates significantly increase per-capita private insurance and Medicaid spending as well as out-of-pocket spending on prescription drugs. We find a 7.5% increase in per-capita private health insurance spending overall and a 13% increase in total Medicaid spending. Additionally, we find a 24% increase in prescription drug spending among households most likely to newly gain paid sick leave. We conclude that paid sick leave mandates are unlikely to reduce healthcare spending, at least in the short term.

title: Negligent Poisoned Environments: How Cumulative Input Negligence Undermines Enterprise AI

detail.title: Negligent Poisoned Environments: How Cumulative Input Negligence Undermines Enterprise AI
detail.abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly rely on internal data sources for training, fine-tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). While adversarial data poisoning has been extensively studied as a cybersecurity threat, this paper introduces a novel and distinct failure mode: the Negligent Poisoned Environment (NPE). NPE describes the cumulative degradation of AI-relevant data assets through routine workforce behaviors-such as inconsistent documentation, poor labeling, and reflexive feedback-that unintentionally contaminate the informational substrate of enterprise AI. Drawing from legal theory, the paper applies the four elements of negligence-duty, breach, causation, and damages-to the enterprise context, arguing that organizations may bear liability for failing to implement reasonable governance and quality controls over data inputs. The paper further proposes the analogy of the "enterprise as data polluter," reframing internal data mismanagement as a systemic risk akin to environmental contamination. This contribution fills a critical gap in AI governance literature by elevating input quality from a technical concern to a legal and strategic imperative.

title: Reinventing the Wheel: Copyrighting the Self in the Era of Deepfakes

detail.title: Reinventing the Wheel: Copyrighting the Self in the Era of Deepfakes
detail.abstract: This article examines the emerging legal concept of "copyrighting the self," focusing on whether a person's face, body, and voice can and should be recognized as copyrightable elements in the digital age. It analyses Denmark's 2025 proposal to amend its Copyright Act, which would grant individuals exclusive rights over digital replicas of their identities, and compares this approach with existing frameworks in the European Union, United Kingdom, and United States. The article explores how such rights could provide robust tools against impersonation and unauthorized commercial use, while also raising complex questions about freedom of expression, cross-border enforcement, and the boundaries of copyright law. Through a comparative and critical lens, the article evaluates the advantages and drawbacks of treating personal identity as intellectual property, and considers the broader implications for legal doctrine, policy, and human dignity in an era of artificial intelligence and deepfakes.

title: Freight Rates and Farmland Values: Causal Evidence from Brazil's Agricultural States
affiliations: Universidade de Brasília (UnB)

detail.title: Freight Rates and Farmland Values: Causal Evidence from Brazil's Agricultural States
detail.abstract: We develop a graphical structural causal model (SCM) to estimate how transportation costs capitalize into farmland values. Using panel data for Brazil's ten largest agricultural states (2001-2017), we combine Pearl's (2009) graphical identification with bias-corrected dynamic panel methods to identify the causal effect of freight rates on land prices. A 1% reduction in freight rates increases average farmland values by 1.59% in the first year and 2.35% in the long run, exceeding 3% in the Center-West grain frontier. Policy targets in Brazil's National Logistics Plan (PNL2035) imply potential long-run increases of up to 54%. The SCM approach generalizes to infrastructure evaluation worldwide.

title: International Arbitration's Paradoxical Strengths in a Fragmenting World
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Law

detail.title: International Arbitration's Paradoxical Strengths in a Fragmenting World
detail.abstract:
Investment arbitration has become a primary focus of academic and policy debates about legitimacy in international adjudication. Many who challenge the legitimacy of investment arbitration argue that it should be replaced with a standing investment court. Proponents of this view often use the World Trade Organization dispute settlement regime—often celebrated as the “crown jewel” of international adjudication—as the best model to replace investment arbitration. This Essay argues that that reform trajectory collides with the current fragility of international courts.

Today, standing international courts and tribunals are proving increasingly vulnerable to politicization as States block judicial appointments, strategically withdraw consent, and refuse to comply with their outcomes. The World Trade Organization dispute system itself was brought to a standstill in 2019 through blockage of its appointment processes. This process of dejudicialization threatens to get worse, not better, in light of the increasingly fractious international politics.

The Essay develops an Anti-fragility Thesis, which argues that features  of investment arbitration commonly treated as illegitimate—ad hoc tribunals, party appointment, and decentralized enforcement—should instead be understood as sources of resiliency in an era of global fragmentation and direct political attacks. Its decentralized ad hoc-ism allows investment arbitration to bend without breaking, even in the face of dramatic reforms. Party-appointment internalizes States’ “voice” within tribunals, while reducing their potential efforts to “control” those tribunals through centralized appointment politics. The Essay further highlights the professional and institutional ecology of arbitration—rulemaking, soft-law guidance, shared procedural techniques, and the professional project of international arbitrators—as a source of continuous adaptation on key issues such as fact-finding, transparency, and ethics.

The conclusion is not that investment arbitration is a panacea. But it is a warning against efforts to jettison arbitration in favor of a standing court while denying the institutional features of investment arbitration that may be best able preserve credible adjudication in an increasingly fragmented world.

title: Traineeships and the Labor Market Experiences and Expectations of College Graduates
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics,  and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Traineeships and the Labor Market Experiences and Expectations of College Graduates
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the impacts of a large-scale traineeship program on the labor market expectations and experiences of Singaporean college students graduating during the pandemic-induced recession, focusing on students’ perceived ex ante and ex post treatment effects. Specifically, we collect novel data at different time points to recover subjective treatment effects of the traineeship program by collecting information on students’ perceived/realized labor market outcomes, as well as their perceived outcomes in hypothetical counterfactual states, such as in the absence of the traineeship program or the economic downturn itself. We find that graduates anticipate significant negative labor market effects from the economic downturn that persist until age 35; nevertheless, ex ante, they expect the traineeship program to substantially mitigate these impacts on full-time employment, income, and job satisfaction. These perceived treatment effects persist in a follow-up survey conducted two years after graduation. Interestingly, both traineeship participants and non-participants expect, on average, positive effects from the program’s existence, suggesting little evidence of perceived crowd-out effects. Finally, we also elicit perceived participation effects and find that graduates self-select into the scheme based on expected gains.

title: Business Innovation in South Asian Startups: A Conceptual Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Business Innovation in South Asian Startups: A Conceptual Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest related to the preparation or publication of this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual research paper based on a review and synthesis of existing literature. It does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or the use of personal or sensitive data. Therefore, ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Startups are important for economic development and the creation of jobs within South Asia. However, South Asian start-ups face environments that are hampered by limited resources and created by institutional difficulties and high uncertainty within the market environment. Given this background, business innovation stands out as a crucial approach to attaining competitiveness and sustaining start-ups in South Asia. Conversely, despite the rising importance of start-ups in South Asia, literature on the subject does not have a comprehensive framework to explore how business capabilities and external environments contribute to start-up success and business innovation. The paper aims to conceptualize a framework to investigate the drivers and consequences of innovation in South Asian start-ups. This paper proposes a framework by applying the Resource-Based View of the firm, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and Institutional Theory to identify the important predictors of innovation in the firms, which are innovation capability, entrepreneurship orientation, finance access, digital preparedness, and support from institutions. The proposed framework also associates innovation in the firms with their performance, competitive advantage, and sustained innovation. The study contributes to the literature by offering a region-specific conceptual model that furthers the theoretical understanding of startup innovation in emerging economies. Such a framework also has practical implications for entrepreneurs, policy makers, and investors who wish to develop startup ecosystems in South Asia.

title: US Federal Reserve Data Reveals a New Way to Fund the AI Economy: The 0.6% Solution

detail.title: US Federal Reserve Data Reveals a New Way to Fund the AI Economy: The 0.6% Solution
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming a primary source of productive capacity, performing work across manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, energy, medicine, research, and software-work that previous economic systems assumed could only be done by human labor. Traditional frameworks such as capitalism, socialism, and communism were built for a labor-centric world and are increasingly misaligned with an economy in which autonomous AI systems generate most goods and services and where value circulates primarily through digital payments rather than wages. Empirical data from the U.S. Federal Reserve indicate that aggregate gross non-cash payments in the United States exceed $1.4 quadrillion annually once wholesale transfers, ACH, card networks, and other electronic flows are included. For revenue calibration, this paper aligns the tax base with final settlement–level payment magnitudes (Fedwire-scale annual volumes on the order of $1.1– $1.2 quadrillion). At this scale, applying a uniform 0.6% micro-tax to electronic transfers yields approximately $7 trillion per year in revenue-enough to fund a universal basic income of $12,000 per adult (~$4 trillion annually) and roughly $3 trillion in additional government expenditure. This paper outlines the historical trajectory of labor-based economic systems, examines the structural requirements of an AI-first economy, presents a technical architecture for a universal payments micro-tax, and analyzes macroeconomic, behavioral, and philosophical implications of a society no longer dependent on human labor for survival. A key behavioral observation is that individuals and businesses already tolerate 2–3% merchant fees on card-based transactions; a uniform 0.6% public micro-fee embedded into payment rails is significantly smaller and broadly acceptable. This paper introduces a feasible and empirically grounded economic system-which we shall call Abundism. Abundism replaces all major taxes with a single 0.6% universal micro-tax on electronic transfers between economically distinct entities, collected automatically by the nation’s financial infrastructure. The framework is data-validated, technically implementable, and fiscally scalable to the requirements of an AI-driven economy.

title: Farm Specific Digital Advisories Mitigate Fertilizer Overuse and Double Profitability for Smallholding Rice Farmers
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee and Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee

detail.title: Farm Specific Digital Advisories Mitigate Fertilizer Overuse and Double Profitability for Smallholding Rice Farmers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare that they have no competing interests, including personal associations and financial interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work has no funders.

detail.abstract: Smallholding farmers rely on rules of thumb to estimate crop yields and fertilizer requirements because farm-specific edapho-climatological data are often unavailable, leading to prophylactic overapplication driven by perceived risks of crop failure. This fertilizer overapplication has severe consequences, including eutrophication and greenhouse gas emissions, emphasizing the need to model farm dynamics and provide farm-specific agronomic advisories. To address this, we developed a multi-output, datadriven digital advisory framework for rice cultivation in South Asia by optimizing machine and deep learning models trained on 40,328 rice farms and integrated with 47 agro-edapho-socio-climatological variables. Within the framework, farmers can simulate agronomic scenarios, simultaneously predict rice yields and fertilizer application rates (nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium), and obtain agronomic prescriptions to optimize yields, fertilizer use, and benefit-to-cost ratios sustainably. Upon validation, the best-performing model (random forest) achieved superior accuracy (68%) compared with more complex sequential deep learning models and showed high reliability scores (79.54-93.27) across rice farms in South Asia, confirming its suitability for predictions and prescriptions. Following the framework's prescriptions, a farmer could expect increases in yields, fertilizer use efficiency, and the benefit-to-cost ratio by ~13%, ~9%, and ~15%, respectively. Monetarily, this would translate to an increase of ₹ 23,030 ($ 256.51) per hectare, doubling farmers' profitability. This digital advisory framework bridges the gap between scientific research and on-farm practices, mitigating environmental risks and boosting farmers' profitability.

title: IoT based Soil Monitoring & Irrigation System for Agriculture
affiliations: KL University, KL University, KL University and Koneru Lakshmaiah Education Foundation

detail.title: IoT based Soil Monitoring & Irrigation System for Agriculture
detail.abstract: Agriculture is the main resource of the survival of India. This research proposed IoT based smart agriculture systems which help to increase crop production. In addition, Internet of Things (IoT) enabled automated irrigation systems aimed at optimizing water utilization and overcome from the wastage of the water and simultaneously protecting crop health through continuous soil moisture level and requirement of the water in specific area. IoT based systems incorporate soil moisture sensors, microcontrollers, and advanced data processing procedures to enable the automated supply of water. The received sensor data and by using automated decision-making processes, this system improves irrigation efficiency as well lower the labor cost. It will also help in improving farmers’ incomes through increased crop production. Implementation of remote sensing technologies along with real-time data analysis enables truthful water distribution. Also, based on the results received by the sensors data farmers can cultivate the crop which suits the specific soil.

title: Digital Finance Reform in Nigeria: Opportunities, Risks, and the Road Ahead for Crypto Regulators and Businesses

detail.title: Digital Finance Reform in Nigeria: Opportunities, Risks, and the Road Ahead for Crypto Regulators and Businesses

contentType.other: HAVE NOT YET PUBISHED IT IN ANY SOURCE OR CIRCULATED THE DRAFT

detail.abstract:
Nigeria’s entanglement with cryptocurrencies and other digital assets, has evolved from being initially shrouded in regulatory scepticism to a more deliberate and coordinated regulatory posture. Driven by escalating inflation, FX constraints, and a youthful, tech-savvy population, Nigeria has emerged as one of the world’s most active crypto markets.
This paper meticulously examines the country’s shifting regulatory landscape, tracing the transition from early resistance by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to the more harmonised framework established under the current legal framework. It highlights how these reforms seek to balance innovation with financial stability, market integrity, and compliance.
The analysis further considers the broader commercial implications of this regulatory shift, including its impact on financial inclusion, investor protection, fintech innovation, and economic formalisation. While the new framework introduces clarity and legitimacy into the digital asset ecosystem, it also presents challenges around AML/CFT compliance, systemic risk, and the delicate interplay between innovation and regulation. The paper concludes that Nigeria’s digital asset market is on a promising but complex path, one that will require sustained regulatory coordination, adaptive supervision, and strengthened technical capacity to foster responsible growth and long-term financial stability.

title: Re-Examining Geographic Variation in Health and Health Care
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and Stanford University

detail.title: Re-Examining Geographic Variation in Health and Health Care
detail.abstract: A large literature has documented widespread variation in health care spending per capita across areas of the United States without correspondingly better health outcomes. Recent work has used mover designs to estimate the causal impact of place on both health care spending and mortality. In this paper, we investigate whether places that increase health care spending also tend to be places that increase health. We find that they do not and discuss the implications.

title: AI and Its Implications on Cybersecurity

detail.title: AI and Its Implications on Cybersecurity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest in relation to this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The author confirms that this research did not involve human participants, animal experimentation, or any use of identifiable personal data. Therefore, ethical approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author declares that no funding has been received.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a paradoxical role in today’s cybersecurity environment, acting as both a powerful defensive asset and a potential tool for sophisticated cyberattacks. AI-driven systems enhance organizational resilience by accelerating threat detection, anomaly monitoring, and automated incident response. However, the same capabilities that strengthen defense can be inverted for adversarial manipulation, enabling automated hacking, adversarial machine learning, and the expansion of generative AI–based threats. This dual-use dilemma underpins a growing tension between the opportunities and vulnerabilities that AI creates. Successful adoption requires addressing issues such as data quality, transparency, algorithmic bias, and oversight. This study argues that AI must be integrated through a model of augmented intelligence, emphasizing human-AI collaboration to ensure the reliable, secure, and ethical deployment of AI.

title: Cross-Sectional Information in Stock Returns for GDP Growth Forecasting in Japan A Factor-Augmented MIDAS Approach
affiliations: Hosei University

detail.title: Cross-Sectional Information in Stock Returns for GDP Growth Forecasting in Japan A Factor-Augmented MIDAS Approach
detail.abstract: This paper studies how stock-market information contributes to forecasting quarterly GDP growth in Japan. Using a factor-augmented MIDAS framework, we distinguish between higher-frequency information and cross-sectional aggregation in individual stock returns. Recursive out-of-sample forecasts show that, prior to COVID-19, factor-based predictors outperform aggregate indices, highlighting the importance of cross-sectional information. Once such aggregation is taken into account, additional gains from mixed-frequency specifications are limited. The predictive relationship weakens during the COVID-19 period, consistent with a structural change in the stock–macro relationship during the pandemic.

title: Global Convergence Toward Competency-Based Education for the Knowledge Economy
affiliations: Open Christian University

detail.title: Global Convergence Toward Competency-Based Education for the Knowledge Economy
detail.abstract: Background: Education reforms across regions are converging on competency-based education (CBE) as states pursue knowledge-based economic growth and "future-ready" workforces, while navigating dense transnational and regional policy networks. Purpose: This article analyzes how global and regional governance frameworks (OECD skills and assessment initiatives, UNESCO's Education 2030/SDG4 agenda, the African Union's CESA, and ASEAN-linked education visions) shape national curriculum redesign toward broadly defined competencies, and it interrogates the epistemic and ethical trade-offs of this shift. Methods: The study uses a qualitative secondary design, integrating comparative policy analysis with critical literature review of peer-reviewed studies, strategy documents, and official reports. The analysis is guided by World Society Theory, multi-level governance, and a purpose-of-education critique that contrasts market-oriented human-capital rationales with holistic educational ends. Results: Across Africa, Southeast Asia, and Latin America, CBE diffusion is propelled by soft-governance mechanisms including benchmarking, policy borrowing, technical assistance, and donor-aligned reform templates, producing convergent curricular language and outcome-based assessment aspirations. Yet persistent implementation frictions emerge where competency constructs remain underspecified, increasing the risk of "thin" competencies, superficial learning, and uneven classroom enactment. The review also identifies governance tensions around educational sovereignty, equity, and youth epistemologies, as curricula are increasingly justified through employability logics that can marginalize local knowledge and amplify resource-based disparities. Conclusion: CBE convergence is unlikely to reverse, but its educational value depends on conceptual clarity, knowledge integrity, and context-sensitive governance. The article advances an impact-oriented lens for evaluating reforms and recommends balancing competency aims with robust disciplinary learning, culturally resonant curricula, and accountability systems that preserve national and community agency while engaging global innovation.

title: The Suing Paradox: Inferring Applicants‘ Motives from the Decisions of the European Court of Human Rights on Freedom of Assembly
affiliations: Max-Planck-Institut für Verhaltenökonomik

detail.title: The Suing Paradox: Inferring Applicants‘ Motives from the Decisions of the European Court of Human Rights on Freedom of Assembly

publicationDetails.detailsText: MPI Collective Goods Discussion Paper, No. 2026/1
publicationDetails.journalName: Max Planck Institute for Behavioral Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Instrumental motives can only explain a minority of the applications for a violation of freedom of assembly that the European Court of Human Rights has published, even if one includes indirect benefits, like mounting international pressure, or fuelling local mobilisation. For most cases, the cost-benefit balance is clearly negative. One needs non-instrumental, expressive motives to resolve the “suing paradox”. Analysing all 691 published decisions with the help of the large language model gemini 2.5 flash, one finds traces of a substantial list of deontological concerns, and markers for emotional involvement. Applications by human subjects are a necessary condition for human rights institutions to increase the standard of protection in their member states. International law scholars interested in understanding this input by protected individuals should direct their attention to expressive motives and emotional involvement.

reference: Centro Studi Luca d'Agliano Development Studies Working Paper No. 510
title: Power Play: Balancing Efficiency and Protection in Fixed vs. Variable Electricity Pricing
affiliations: Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change (CMCC), University of Milan, CMCC - Centro Euro-Mediterraneo sui Cambiamenti Climatici, Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change (CMCC) and RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment

detail.title: Power Play: Balancing Efficiency and Protection in Fixed vs. Variable Electricity Pricing

publicationDetails.detailsText: Centro Studi Luca d'Agliano Development Studies Working Paper No. 510
publicationDetails.journalName: Centro Studi Luca d'Agliano Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how households respond to being defaulted into an indexed-price electricity contract after a period under fixed prices, using high-frequency data from a major Italian utility during the 2021-2023 energy crisis. Quasi-random timing of the default generates large, unanticipated price shocks. Defaulting increases bills by up to 56 percent, while consumption declines slowly, by up to 9.8 percent after eighteen months, implying low expenditure elasticity. Welfare analysis shows that fixed-price contracts trade efficiency for protection: they distort consumption and generate deadweight losses, yet provide implicit subsidies that are regressive in absolute terms but progressive relative to income, highlighting central equity-efficiency trade-offs.

title: Cyber-Event Resilience as a Fundamental Credit Metric: Assessing EBITDA Sensitivity in the Face of Systemic Outages

detail.title: Cyber-Event Resilience as a Fundamental Credit Metric: Assessing EBITDA Sensitivity in the Face of Systemic Outages
detail.abstract: Systemic cyber outages increasingly behave like operational shocks with credit-relevant consequences: they interrupt revenue generation, force surge remediation spending, and can leave persistent tail effects through customer friction, regulatory exposure, and reputational drag. This paper argues that cyber-event resilience should be treated as a fundamental credit metric by translating resilience into an "EBITDA sensitivity" lens-how deep the earnings drawdown is and how quickly recovery occurs-rather than relying on complex or opaque risk models. Using a hybrid approach that combines publicly disclosed incident impacts with scenario archetypes (vendor blackout, ransomware halt, and data exfiltration), the paper links observable resilience capabilities to expected EBITDA-at-risk. Calibrated case evidence illustrates why loss distributions appear heavy-tailed and why vendor concentration can turn seemingly idiosyncratic IT failures into correlated cash-flow shocks.

title: Target Met, Environment Hurt: The Environmental Externalities of Corporate Performance Benchmarks
affiliations: Jinan University, Hainan University, Jinan University - Management School and Miami University of Ohio

detail.title: Target Met, Environment Hurt: The Environmental Externalities of Corporate Performance Benchmarks
detail.abstract: We examine whether board-set performance targets generate environmental externalities by exploiting China's mandatory disclosure of internal benchmarks. Establishments increase sulfur dioxide emissions by 23.3% when parent firms barely meet sales targets, identified through discontinuity tests at target thresholds. This effect reflects deliberate resource reallocation: managers simultaneously increase production and sales expenditures while cutting research and development and environmental investments. Cross-sectional tests reveal that environmental sacrifice depends critically on governance structure rather than representing an inherent cost of performance measurement. State-owned enterprises show zero emissions increase despite facing similar targets, while private firms increase emissions by 58.8%, demonstrating that multi-dimensional evaluation systems prevent opportunistic behavior. Product market competition amplifies environmental damage, while regulatory enforcement and transparency requirements eliminate it entirely. Establishments in CEO ancestral hometowns show no pollution increase while other facilities in the same firm increase emissions by 37.1%, revealing that personal accountability dominates financial incentives.

title: The Digital Ethnography of Tradition: Analyzing the Modernization and Transmission Dynamics of Urban Folklore in Dhaka

detail.title: The Digital Ethnography of Tradition: Analyzing the Modernization and Transmission Dynamics of Urban Folklore in Dhaka
